V. Methodological Commitments

This chapter follows the following methodological commitments:

  1. Commitment to honesty: the purpose of stress testing is to identify weaknesses, not to prove correctness
  2. Commitment to openness: the results of stress testing are open, inviting criticism and revision
  3. Commitment to systematicity: stress testing follows a systematic methodology, rather than arbitrary selection
  4. Commitment to traceability: every step of the stress test can be traced back to methodological principles

§22.1 The Purpose of Stress Testing

§22.1.1 Identifying Weaknesses Rather Than Proving Correctness

I. The Epistemological Positioning of Stress Testing

Stress testing has a distinctive epistemological status in scientific methodology. Unlike conventional theory verification, the primary purpose of stress testing is not to prove the correctness of a theory, but to actively identify the weaknesses of the theory.

Definition 22.1.1 (Stress Test)

A stress test is a method of theory examination that, by placing a theory in extreme scenarios, actively identifies the weaknesses, boundaries, and failure conditions of the theory.

Formal expression:

$$\text{StressTest}(T, S) = \text{Identify}(\text{Weaknesses}(T) | S)$$

Where:

  • $T$ is the theory being examined
  • $S$ is the set of extreme scenarios
  • $\text{Weaknesses}(T) | S$ is the weaknesses of the theory exposed under scenario $S$

II. The Relationship with Falsificationism

The stress testing methodology draws on the falsificationist thought of Karl Popper, but develops it further. Popper held that the hallmark of a scientific theory lies in its falsifiability—a theory must be capable of being refuted by empirical evidence.[1] Stress testing extends this idea to the domain of normative theory:

Table 22.2 Comparison of Falsificationism and Stress Testing

DimensionPopperian FalsificationismStress Testing Methodology
Object of applicationEmpirical scientific theoriesNormative theoretical frameworks
Mode of examinationEmpirical observationScenario simulation and conceptual analysis
GoalTo falsify the theoryTo identify weaknesses and guide revision
ResultThe theory is falsified or temporarily acceptedA weakness map and revision suggestions
AttitudeCritical rationalismConstructive criticism

III. A Typology of Weakness Identification

Stress testing aims to identify the following types of weaknesses:

Definition 22.1.2 (Weakness Typology)

Theoretical weaknesses can be divided into four types: conceptual weaknesses, argumentative weaknesses, operational weaknesses, and applicability weaknesses.

Formal expression:

$$\text{WeaknessTypes} = \{\text{Conceptual}, \text{Argumentative}, \text{Operational}, \text{Applicability}\}$$

Table 22.3 Weakness Typology

Weakness TypeDefinitionExample
Conceptual weaknessCore concepts are unclearly defined or internally contradictoryThe definition of consciousness in the UCS is vague under extreme scenarios
Argumentative weaknessThe chain of reasoning has gaps or fallaciesThe bridge argument from description to norm is insufficient
Operational weaknessIndicators or procedures are difficult to implementThe RFD cannot be computed under deep uncertainty
Applicability weaknessThe theory fails under particular scenariosThe framework does not apply in cross-civilizational scenarios

IV. The Procedure of Weakness Identification

PROCEDURE WeaknessIdentification

INPUT: Theory T, Scenario S OUTPUT: WeaknessMap W

// Step 1: Theory decomposition Components = Decompose(T) // Decompose the theory into the four levels of concepts, argument, operation, and applicability

// Step 2: Scenario application FOR EACH component IN Components DO application_result = Apply(component, S)

// Step 3: Anomaly detection IF Anomaly(application_result) THEN weakness = IdentifyWeakness(component, application_result) W.add(weakness) END IF END FOR

// Step 4: Weakness classification W = Classify(W, WeaknessTypes)

// Step 5: Priority assessment W = PrioritizeWeaknesses(W)

RETURN W

END PROCEDURE

V. Connection with the New View of Cognition

The methodology of weakness identification derives directly from the core propositions of the New View of Cognition (NK):

  • NK-3 (deep uncertainty): weaknesses in a theory necessarily exist, because knowledge is always formed under deep uncertainty
  • NK-4 (negotiability of knowledge): the identification of weaknesses is a social process requiring the participation of the academic community
  • NK-5 (revisability of knowledge): the purpose of identifying weaknesses is to guide revision, not to refute the theory

Formal expression:

$$\text{WeaknessIdentification} \triangleleft \{NK\text{-}3, NK\text{-}4, NK\text{-}5\}$$

§22.1.2 Clarifying Boundaries Rather Than Expanding Applicability

I. The Importance of Boundary Awareness

Every theory has its boundaries of applicability. The second purpose of stress testing is to clarify the boundaries of applicability of the theory, rather than to attempt to expand the scope of its applicability.

Definition 22.1.3 (Theoretical Boundary)

A theoretical boundary is the set of conditions under which a theory applies validly; beyond these conditions, the validity of the theory is no longer guaranteed.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Boundary}(T) = \{C | \text{Valid}(T, C) \land \neg\text{Valid}(T, \neg C)\}$$

Where:

  • $T$ is the theory
  • $C$ is a condition
  • $\text{Valid}(T, C)$ denotes that theory $T$ is valid under condition $C$

II. Boundary Typology

Table 22.4 Typology of Theoretical Boundaries

Boundary TypeDefinitionExample from This Work
Ontological boundaryThe types of existence presupposed by the theoryPresupposes the existence of negentropic organization
Epistemological boundaryThe epistemic conditions presupposed by the theoryPresupposes a minimum degree of knowability
Temporal boundaryThe time scale to which the theory appliesApplies to deep-time-scale decisions
Spatial boundaryThe spatial range to which the theory appliesApplies to cosmic-scale governance
Agent boundaryThe types of agents to which the theory appliesApplies to cross-substrate intelligent agents

III. The Procedure of Boundary Specification

PROCEDURE BoundarySpecification

INPUT: Theory T, Scenario S OUTPUT: BoundaryMap B

// Step 1: Identify presuppositions Presuppositions = IdentifyPresuppositions(T)

// Step 2: Scenario examination FOR EACH presupposition IN Presuppositions DO holds = CheckPresupposition(presupposition, S)

IF NOT holds THEN boundary = SpecifyBoundary(presupposition) B.add(boundary) END IF END FOR

// Step 3: Boundary classification B = Classify(B, BoundaryTypes)

// Step 4: Boundary formulation B = FormulateBoundaryStatements(B)

RETURN B

END PROCEDURE

IV. Boundary Presuppositions of This Work

The theoretical framework of this work presupposes the following boundary conditions:

Table 22.5 Boundary Presuppositions of This Work

Boundary TypePresupposed ContentStress Test Checkpoint

§22.1.3 Guiding Revision Rather Than Entrenching Positions

I. Revision-Oriented Methodology

The third purpose of stress testing is to guide theoretical revision. This purpose derives directly from the proposition of the revisability of knowledge in the New View of Cognition (NK-5).

Definition 22.1.4 (Revision Orientation)

Revision orientation is a methodological stance holding that the purpose of theory examination is not to defend the theory, but to identify the parts that need revision and to propose directions for revision.

Formal expression:

$$\text{RevisionOriented}(T, \text{TestResult}) = \text{Propose}(\text{Revisions}(T) | \text{TestResult})$$

II. Revision Typology

Table 22.6 Revision Typology

Revision TypeDefinitionScope of RevisionDifficulty of Revision
Fine-tuningAdjustment of parameters or formulationsLocalLow
SupplementationAdding new concepts or argumentsModerateMedium
RestructuringReorganizing the theoretical structureFairly largeFairly high
Paradigm shiftFundamental theoretical transformationGlobalHighest

III. The Procedure for Generating Revision Suggestions

PROCEDURE RevisionSuggestion

INPUT: WeaknessMap W, BoundaryMap B OUTPUT: RevisionProposals R

// Step 1: Weakness analysis FOR EACH weakness IN W DO severity = AssessSeverity(weakness) scope = AssessScope(weakness)

// Step 2: Determine revision type revision_type = DetermineRevisionType(severity, scope)

// Step 3: Propose revision direction direction = ProposeDirection(weakness, revision_type)

// Step 4: Generate revision suggestion proposal = GenerateProposal(weakness, revision_type, direction) R.add(proposal) END FOR

// Step 5: Priority ranking R = PrioritizeProposals(R)

// Step 6: Consistency check R = CheckConsistency(R)

RETURN R

END PROCEDURE

IV. Evaluation Criteria for Revision Suggestions

Table 22.7 Evaluation Criteria for Revision Suggestions

Evaluation DimensionEvaluation ContentWeight
NecessityIs the revision necessary? Is the weakness severe?30%
FeasibilityIs the revision feasible? Is there a clear path for revision?25%
ConsistencyIs the revision consistent with other parts of the theory?20%
CostWhat is the cost of the revision? Is it worthwhile?15%
RiskDoes the revision introduce new risks?10%

§22.1.4 Enhancing Credibility Rather Than Self-Justification

I. The Epistemological Basis of Credibility

The fourth purpose of stress testing is to enhance the credibility of the theory. This purpose appears paradoxical—how can actively exposing weaknesses enhance credibility? The answer lies in this: honestly acknowledging weaknesses enhances the credibility of a theory more than concealing them does.

Definition 22.1.5 (Theoretical Credibility)

Theoretical credibility is the degree of trust that the academic community places in a theory, depending on the theory's argumentative quality, empirical support, boundary clarity, and openness to revision.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Credibility}(T) = f(\text{ArgumentQuality}, \text{EmpiricalSupport}, \text{BoundaryClarity}, \text{RevisionOpenness})$$

II. The Mechanism of Credibility Enhancement

Stress testing enhances theoretical credibility through the following mechanisms:

Table 22.8 Mechanisms of Credibility Enhancement

MechanismExplanationContribution to Credibility
Demonstration of honestyActively exposing weaknesses demonstrates academic honestyEnhances trust
Boundary clarityClarifying boundaries of applicability avoids overclaimingEnhances precision
Openness to revisionOpenness to revision invites academic participationEnhances collaboration
Methodological transparencyTransparent examination methods can be replicatedEnhances verifiability

III. Contrast with Self-Justification

Table 22.9 Contrast Between Stress Testing and Self-Justification

DimensionSelf-JustificationStress Testing
PurposeTo defend the theoryTo improve the theory
AttitudeDefensiveOpen
Handling of weaknessesConcealment or denialActive identification and acknowledgment
Attitude toward criticismResistanceWelcome
ResultTheoretical ossificationTheoretical development
Effect on credibilityDecreases itEnhances it

IV. The Procedure of Credibility Assessment

PROCEDURE CredibilityAssessment

INPUT: Theory T, StressTestResults R OUTPUT: CredibilityScore C

// Step 1: Assess argumentative quality argument_quality = AssessArgumentQuality(T)

// Step 2: Assess empirical support empirical_support = AssessEmpiricalSupport(T)

// Step 3: Assess boundary clarity boundary_clarity = AssessBoundaryClarity(T, R)

// Step 4: Assess openness to revision revision_openness = AssessRevisionOpenness(T, R)

// Step 5: Composite score C = WeightedSum(argument_quality, empirical_support, boundary_clarity, revision_openness)

RETURN C

END PROCEDURE

V. Connection with the New View of Cognition

The methodology of credibility enhancement is related to the social epistemology of the New View of Cognition:

  • NK-4 (negotiability of knowledge): credibility is a social achievement, depending on the recognition of the academic community
  • NK-6 (epistemic justice): credibility assessment should avoid epistemic injustice

Formal expression:

$$\text{CredibilityEnhancement} \triangleleft \{NK\text{-}4, NK\text{-}6\}$$

§22.2 The Methods of Stress Testing

§22.2.1 Scenario Construction Method

I. The Epistemological Basis of Scenario Construction

Scenario construction is the first step of stress testing. The quality of scenario construction directly determines the effectiveness of the stress test.

Definition 22.2.1 (Test Scenario)

A test scenario is a hypothetical description of a future state, containing enough detail to allow the application and evaluation of a theoretical framework.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Scenario} = \langle \text{Context}, \text{Parameters}, \text{Dynamics}, \text{Uncertainties} \rangle$$

Where:

  • $\text{Context}$: the background conditions of the scenario
  • $\text{Parameters}$: the key parameters of the scenario
  • $\text{Dynamics}$: the evolutionary dynamics of the scenario
  • $\text{Uncertainties}$: the uncertainties in the scenario

II. Methodological Principles of Scenario Construction

Table 22.10 Methodological Principles of Scenario Construction

PrincipleContentOperationalization Requirement
Internal consistencyThe elements of the scenario do not contradict one anotherLogical check
Scientific plausibilityThe scenario does not violate known scientific lawsScientific review
Sufficiency of detailThe scenario contains enough detail to support analysisDetail checklist
Parameter variabilityThe key parameters of the scenario can varySetting of parameter ranges
Explicit uncertaintyThe uncertainties in the scenario are explicitly markedUncertainty checklist

III. The Procedure of Scenario Construction

PROCEDURE ScenarioConstruction

INPUT: TestObjective O, RelevantDomain D OUTPUT: Scenario S

// Step 1: Background setting context = SetContext(D) // Determine the temporal, spatial, and social background of the scenario

// Step 2: Parameter identification parameters = IdentifyParameters(O, context) // Identify the key parameters relevant to the test objective

// Step 3: Parameter setting FOR EACH parameter IN parameters DO value = SetParameterValue(parameter, "extreme") // Set the parameter to an extreme value parameter.value = value parameter.range = SetParameterRange(parameter) END FOR

// Step 4: Dynamic modeling dynamics = ModelDynamics(context, parameters) // Build a dynamic model of the scenario's evolution

// Step 5: Uncertainty marking uncertainties = IdentifyUncertainties(context, parameters, dynamics) // Identify and mark the uncertainties in the scenario

// Step 6: Consistency check IF NOT ConsistencyCheck(context, parameters, dynamics) THEN RETURN TO Step 1 // reconstruct END IF

// Step 7: Scenario integration S = Integrate(context, parameters, dynamics, uncertainties)

RETURN S

END PROCEDURE

IV. The Hierarchical Structure of Scenarios

Each test scenario contains three levels:

Table 22.11 The Hierarchical Structure of Scenarios

LevelContentFunction
Core scenarioThe basic setting of the scenarioProvides the basis for analysis
Variant scenariosParameter variations of the core scenarioSupports sensitivity analysis

§22.2.2 Framework Application Method

I. The Purpose of Framework Application

Framework application is the application of the theoretical framework of this work to a test scenario, in order to evaluate the framework's performance under that scenario.

Definition 22.2.2 (Framework Application)

Framework application is the process of applying the concepts, principles, indicators, and institutional designs of a theoretical framework to a specific scenario, and evaluating their applicability, validity, and consistency.

Formal expression:

$$\text{FrameworkApplication}(F, S) = \langle \text{ConceptApplication}, \text{PrincipleApplication}, \text{IndicatorApplication}, \text{InstitutionApplication} \rangle$$

Where:

  • $F$ is the theoretical framework
  • $S$ is the test scenario

II. The Four Levels of Framework Application

Table 22.12 The Four Levels of Framework Application

LevelContent of ApplicationEvaluation Question
Conceptual levelThe core concepts of the New Three ViewsAre the concepts clear in the scenario? Do they apply?
Principle levelThe three normative principlesAre the principles applicable in the scenario? Do they conflict?
Indicator levelThe six major indicator systemsAre the indicators computable in the scenario? Are they valid?
Institutional levelInstitutional designAre the institutions feasible in the scenario? Are they effective?

III. The Procedure of Framework Application

PROCEDURE FrameworkApplication

INPUT: Framework F, Scenario S OUTPUT: ApplicationResults R

// Step 1: Concept application concept_results = ApplyConcepts(F.concepts, S) // Apply the core concepts of the New Three Views to the scenario

FOR EACH concept IN F.concepts DO applicability = AssessApplicability(concept, S) clarity = AssessClarity(concept, S) concept_results.add(concept, applicability, clarity) END FOR

// Step 2: Principle application principle_results = ApplyPrinciples(F.principles, S) // Apply the three normative principles to the scenario

FOR EACH principle IN F.principles DO applicability = AssessApplicability(principle, S) guidance = AssessGuidance(principle, S) conflicts = IdentifyConflicts(principle, F.principles, S) principle_results.add(principle, applicability, guidance, conflicts) END FOR

// Step 3: Indicator application indicator_results = ApplyIndicators(F.indicators, S) // Apply the six major indicators to the scenario

FOR EACH indicator IN F.indicators DO calculability = AssessCalculability(indicator, S) validity = AssessValidity(indicator, S) indicator_results.add(indicator, calculability, validity) END FOR

// Step 4: Institution application institution_results = ApplyInstitutions(F.institutions, S) // Apply the institutional designs to the scenario

FOR EACH institution IN F.institutions DO feasibility = AssessFeasibility(institution, S) effectiveness = AssessEffectiveness(institution, S) institution_results.add(institution, feasibility, effectiveness) END FOR

// Step 5: Result integration R = Integrate(concept_results, principle_results, indicator_results, institution_results)

RETURN R

END PROCEDURE

IV. Evaluation Criteria for Application Results

Table 22.13 Evaluation Criteria for Framework Application

Evaluation DimensionEvaluation ContentScoring Standard
ApplicabilityCan the framework be applied to the scenario?0–1 points
ClarityIs the meaning of the framework clear in the scenario?0–1 points
GuidanceDoes the framework provide effective action guidance?0–1 points
ConsistencyAre the parts of the framework consistent?0–1 points
OperabilityCan the framework be operated in practice?0–1 points

Composite applicability score

$$\text{ApplicabilityScore}(F, S) = \frac{1}{5} \sum_{i=1}^{5} \text{Score}_i$$

Where $\text{Score}_i$ is the score of the five evaluation dimensions.

§22.2.3 Simulation Analysis Method

I. The Necessity of Simulation Analysis

For scenarios that cannot be directly experimented upon, simulation analysis provides an alternative method of examination. Simulation analysis simulates the evolution of a scenario through computer models, evaluating the performance of the theoretical framework under that scenario.

Definition 22.2.3 (Simulation Analysis)

Simulation analysis is the method of using computer models to simulate the evolution of a scenario and evaluate the performance of a theoretical framework under that scenario.

Formal expression:

$$\text{SimulationAnalysis}(F, S, M) = \text{Evaluate}(F | \text{Simulate}(S, M))$$

Where:

  • $F$ is the theoretical framework
  • $S$ is the test scenario
  • $M$ is the simulation model

II. Types of Simulation Methods

Table 22.14 Types of Simulation Methods

Method TypeDescriptionApplicable ScenarioApplication in This Work
Multi-agent simulationSimulates the interaction of multiple agentsMulti-agent decision scenariosAGI scenario, First Contact scenario
System dynamicsSimulates the dynamic evolution of a systemEvolution of complex systemsEcosystem tipping point scenario
Game-theoretic simulationSimulates strategic interactionStrategic choice scenariosIntergenerational justice scenario
Monte Carlo simulationHandles uncertaintyHigh-uncertainty scenariosAll scenarios

III. Multi-Agent Simulation Framework

PROCEDURE MultiAgentSimulation

INPUT: Scenario S, Framework F, SimulationParameters P OUTPUT: SimulationResults R

// Step 1: Agent initialization agents = InitializeAgents(S, P.agent_count)

FOR EACH agent IN agents DO agent.type = AssignType(agent, S) agent.capabilities = AssignCapabilities(agent, S) agent.goals = AssignGoals(agent, S) agent.decision_model = AssignDecisionModel(agent, F) END FOR

// Step 2: Environment initialization environment = InitializeEnvironment(S)

// Step 3: Simulation loop FOR t = 0 TO P.time_steps DO

// Step 3.1: Agent perception FOR EACH agent IN agents DO agent.perception = Perceive(agent, environment) END FOR

// Step 3.2: Agent decision FOR EACH agent IN agents DO agent.action = Decide(agent, agent.perception, F) END FOR

// Step 3.3: Action execution FOR EACH agent IN agents DO Execute(agent.action, environment) END FOR

// Step 3.4: Environment update environment = UpdateEnvironment(environment, agents)

// Step 3.5: Data recording RecordData(t, agents, environment)

END FOR

// Step 4: Result analysis R = AnalyzeResults(recorded_data, F)

RETURN R

END PROCEDURE

IV. Simulation Parameter Settings

Table 22.15 Simulation Parameter Settings

Parameter CategoryParameter NameDefault ValueRange
Time parametersSimulation steps1000[100, 10000]
Time parametersStep size1 year[1 day, 100 years]
Agent parametersNumber of agents100[10, 10000]
Agent parametersNumber of agent types5[2, 20]
Environment parametersTotal resources1000[100, 100000]
Random parametersRandom seed42[1, 2^32]
Random parametersNumber of Monte Carlo runs100[10, 1000]

V. Sensitivity Analysis

Sensitivity analysis evaluates the degree to which simulation results are sensitive to changes in parameters:

$$\text{Sensitivity}(R, p) = \frac{\partial R}{\partial p} \cdot \frac{p}{R}$$

Where:

  • $R$ is the simulation result
  • $p$ is the parameter

VI. Statement of the Limitations of Simulation

Simulation analysis has the following limitations:

  1. Model simplification: simulation models are simplifications of reality and may omit important factors
  2. Parameter uncertainty: there is uncertainty in parameter settings
  3. Difficulty of validation: simulation results are difficult to validate empirically
  4. Computational limits: computational resources limit the scale and precision of the simulation

§22.2.4 Weakness Identification Method

I. The Systematicity of Weakness Identification

Weakness identification requires a systematic method, in order to avoid omitting important weaknesses or over-focusing on minor ones.

Definition 22.2.4 (Systematic Weakness Identification)

Systematic weakness identification is the process of comprehensively identifying, through a structured method, the weaknesses exposed by a theoretical framework under a test scenario.

Formal expression:

$$\text{SystematicWeaknessIdentification}(F, S, R) = \text{Comprehensive}(\text{Weaknesses}(F) | S, R)$$

Where:

  • $F$ is the theoretical framework
  • $S$ is the test scenario
  • $R$ is the result of framework application and simulation analysis

II. The Checklist for Weakness Identification

Table 22.16 Checklist for Weakness Identification

Check CategoryCheck ItemCheck Question
Conceptual weaknessClarity of definitionAre the core concepts clear in the scenario?
Conceptual weaknessApplicability of conceptsDo the core concepts apply to the scenario?
Conceptual weaknessConsistency of conceptsAre the concepts consistent with one another?
Argumentative weaknessValidity of premisesDo the premises of the argument hold in the scenario?
Argumentative weaknessValidity of reasoningIs the reasoning valid in the scenario?
Argumentative weaknessReliability of conclusionIs the conclusion reliable in the scenario?
Operational weaknessComputability of indicatorsAre the indicators computable in the scenario?
Operational weaknessFeasibility of institutionsAre the institutions feasible in the scenario?
Operational weaknessExecutability of proceduresAre the procedures executable in the scenario?
Applicability weaknessScenario coverageDoes the framework cover the key aspects of the scenario?
Applicability weaknessAppropriateness of boundariesAre the boundaries of the framework appropriate?
Applicability weaknessPossibility of extensionCan the framework be extended to cover the scenario?

III. The Procedure of Weakness Identification

PROCEDURE SystematicWeaknessIdentification

INPUT: Framework F, Scenario S, ApplicationResults AR, SimulationResults SR OUTPUT: WeaknessMap W

// Step 1: Conceptual weakness identification FOR EACH concept IN F.concepts DO FOR EACH check IN ConceptChecklist DO result = PerformCheck(concept, S, AR, check) IF result.weakness_detected THEN weakness = CreateWeakness("Conceptual", concept, check, result) W.add(weakness) END IF END FOR END FOR

// Step 2: Argumentative weakness identification FOR EACH argument IN F.arguments DO FOR EACH check IN ArgumentChecklist DO result = PerformCheck(argument, S, AR, check) IF result.weakness_detected THEN weakness = CreateWeakness("Argumentative", argument, check, result) W.add(weakness) END IF END FOR END FOR

// Step 3: Operational weakness identification FOR EACH operation IN F.operations DO FOR EACH check IN OperationChecklist DO result = PerformCheck(operation, S, AR, SR, check) IF result.weakness_detected THEN weakness = CreateWeakness("Operational", operation, check, result) W.add(weakness) END IF END FOR END FOR

// Step 4: Applicability weakness identification FOR EACH check IN ApplicabilityChecklist DO result = PerformCheck(F, S, AR, SR, check) IF result.weakness_detected THEN weakness = CreateWeakness("Applicability", F, check, result) W.add(weakness) END IF END FOR

// Step 5: Weakness classification and priority ranking W = ClassifyWeaknesses(W) W = PrioritizeWeaknesses(W)

RETURN W

END PROCEDURE

SevereCauses the framework to partially failThe core functions of the framework are impaired
ModerateAffects the effectiveness of the frameworkThe framework can be applied but with reduced effectiveness

NegligibleHas almost no impactThe framework is fully effective

§22.2.5 Revision Suggestion Method

I. Principles for Generating Revision Suggestions

The generation of revision suggestions should follow the following principles:

Table 22.18 Principles for Generating Revision Suggestions

PrincipleContentOperationalization Requirement
Target specificityRevision suggestions should target specific weaknessesEach suggestion corresponds to one or more weaknesses
FeasibilityRevision suggestions should be feasibleAssess the technical and resource feasibility of the revision
ConsistencyRevisions should not introduce new inconsistenciesCheck the consistency of the revision with other parts of the framework
MinimalityRevisions should be the minimum necessaryAvoid over-revision
TestabilityThe effects of revisions should be testablePropose methods for testing the effects of revisions

II. The Procedure for Generating Revision Suggestions

PROCEDURE RevisionSuggestionGeneration

INPUT: WeaknessMap W OUTPUT: RevisionProposals R

// Step 1: Weakness grouping weakness_groups = GroupWeaknesses(W) // Group related weaknesses so that they can be revised together

// Step 2: Determine revision direction FOR EACH group IN weakness_groups DO direction = DetermineRevisionDirection(group) // Determine the overall direction of revision

// Step 3: Generate revision options options = GenerateRevisionOptions(group, direction) // Generate multiple possible revision options

// Step 4: Option evaluation FOR EACH option IN options DO feasibility = AssessFeasibility(option) consistency = AssessConsistency(option, Framework) effectiveness = AssessEffectiveness(option, group) option.score = WeightedScore(feasibility, consistency, effectiveness) END FOR

// Step 5: Option selection best_option = SelectBestOption(options)

// Step 6: Suggestion generation proposal = GenerateProposal(group, best_option) R.add(proposal) END FOR

// Step 7: Priority ranking R = PrioritizeProposals(R)

// Step 8: Consistency check R = CheckConsistency(R)

RETURN R

END PROCEDURE

§22.3 Principles of Scenario Selection

§22.3.1 The Extremity Principle

I. The Definition and Function of Extremity

The extremity principle requires that test scenarios be extreme enough to effectively examine the boundaries and weaknesses of the theoretical framework.

Definition 22.3.1 (Extremity Principle)

The extremity principle requires that the key parameters of a test scenario be set at extreme values or in extreme combinations, in order to maximize the probability of exposing theoretical weaknesses.

Formal expression:

$$\text{ExtremityPrinciple}: \forall S \in \text{TestScenarios}, \exists p \in \text{Parameters}(S): \text{Extreme}(p)$$

Where $\text{Extreme}(p)$ denotes that parameter $p$ is at an extreme value.

II. Types of Extremity

Table 22.20 Types of Extremity

Type of ExtremityDefinitionExample
Parameter extremityA single parameter takes an extreme valueAGI capabilities far exceeding human
Combinatorial extremityExtreme combination of multiple parametersHigh-capability AGI + low transparency + rapid development
Temporal extremityExtreme time scaleDeep-time-scale (million-year) decisions
Spatial extremityExtreme spatial scaleCosmic-scale impacts
Agent extremityExtreme type of agentCompletely heterogeneous alien intelligence

III. The Measurement of Extremity

Extremity can be measured in the following way:

$$\text{ExtremityScore}(S) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{|p_i - \mu_i|}{\sigma_i}$$

Where:

  • $p_i$ is the value of parameter $i$ in scenario $S$
  • $\mu_i$ is the "normal" value of parameter $i$
  • $\sigma_i$ is the standard deviation of parameter $i$
  • $n$ is the number of parameters

IV. The Relationship Between Extremity and Credibility

There is an inverted-U relationship between extremity and test credibility:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  The Relationship Between Extremity and Test Credibility         │                                           
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │                                            
│  Test credibility                                                │                                           
│       │                                                         │                                            
│       │           ╭───────╮                                     │                                            
│       │          ╱         ╲                                    │                                            
│       │         ╱           ╲                                   │                                            
│       │        ╱             ╲                                  │                                            
│       │       ╱               ╲                                 │                                            
│       │      ╱                 ╲                                │                                            
│       │     ╱                   ╲                               │                                            
│       │    ╱                     ╲                              │                                            
│       └───┴───────────────────────┴──────────────→ Extremity    │                                            
│           Low                Optimal           High             │                                            
│                                                                 │                                            
│  Note:                                                          │                                            
│  - Extremity too low: cannot effectively examine theoretical boundaries │                                    
│  - Extremity optimal: effectively examines theoretical boundaries while maintaining scientific plausibility │
│  - Extremity too high: the scenario becomes implausible or unanalyzable │                                    
│                                                                 │                                            
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

V. Constraints on Extremity

The extremity principle is subject to the following constraints:

  1. Constraint of scientific plausibility: the scenario should not violate known scientific laws
  2. Constraint of internal consistency: the elements of the scenario should not contradict one another
  3. Constraint of analyzability: the scenario should allow meaningful analysis

Formal expression:

$$\text{ValidExtremity}(S) = \text{Extreme}(S) \land \text{ScientificallyPlausible}(S) \land \text{InternallyConsistent}(S) \land \text{Analyzable}(S)$$

§22.3.2 The Relevance Principle

I. The Definition and Function of Relevance

The relevance principle requires that test scenarios be relevant to the core concerns of the theoretical framework, so as to effectively examine the key components of the theory.

Definition 22.3.2 (Relevance Principle)

The relevance principle requires that test scenarios be directly related to the core concepts, principles, indicators, or institutional designs of the theoretical framework, so as to effectively examine the validity of these components.

Formal expression:

$$\text{RelevancePrinciple}: \forall S \in \text{TestScenarios}, \exists C \in \text{CoreComponents}(F): \text{Tests}(S, C)$$

Where $\text{Tests}(S, C)$ denotes that scenario $S$ is capable of examining component $C$.

II. Dimensions of Relevance

Table 22.21 Dimensions of Relevance

Dimension of RelevanceDefinitionEvaluation Question
Conceptual relevanceThe scenario involves the core concepts of the frameworkDoes the scenario involve concepts such as consciousness, negentropy, and possibility space?
Principle relevanceThe scenario involves the normative principles of the frameworkDoes the scenario involve the principles of recursive freedom, negentropy responsibility, and reversibility?
Indicator relevanceThe scenario involves the indicator system of the frameworkDoes the scenario involve indicators such as the UCS, RFD, and CRV?
Institutional relevanceThe scenario involves the institutional design of the frameworkDoes the scenario involve institutions such as the tribunal, IRB, and Intergenerational Trust?

Table 22.22 Relevance Matrix of Scenarios and Framework Components

AGI breakthroughHighHighMediumHighHighHighHigh
First ContactHighMediumMediumMediumHighMediumHigh
Ecosystem tipping pointMediumMediumHighHighLowMediumMedium
Intergenerational justice crisisMediumHighHighMediumLowHighHigh

IV. Calculation of the Relevance Score

$$\text{RelevanceScore}(S) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i \cdot \text{Relevance}(S, C_i)$$

Where:

  • $C_i$ is the $i$-th core component of the framework
  • $w_i$ is the weight of component $i$
  • $\text{Relevance}(S, C_i) \in [0, 1]$ is the relevance between scenario $S$ and component $C_i$

§22.3.3 The Diversity Principle

I. The Definition and Function of Diversity

The diversity principle requires that the set of test scenarios be sufficiently diverse to cover the different aspects of the theoretical framework and different types of challenges.

Definition 22.3.3 (Diversity Principle)

The diversity principle requires that the set of test scenarios be diverse along dimensions such as challenge type, time scale, spatial scale, and agent type.

Formal expression:

$$\text{DiversityPrinciple}: \text{Diverse}(\text{TestScenarios}, \text{DiversityDimensions})$$

IV. The Relationship Between Diversity and Completeness

The diversity principle seeks "sufficient" diversity, not "complete" diversity. Complete diversity is impossible, because the possible scenarios are infinite.

$$\text{SufficientDiversity} \neq \text{CompleteDiversity}$$

§22.3.4 The Analyzability Principle

I. The Definition and Function of Analyzability

The analyzability principle requires that test scenarios allow meaningful analysis, i.e. that the scenario be concrete enough to support framework application and weakness identification.

Definition 22.3.4 (Analyzability Principle)

The analyzability principle requires that test scenarios have enough structure and detail to support framework application, simulation analysis, and weakness identification.

Formal expression:

$$\text{AnalyzabilityPrinciple}: \forall S \in \text{TestScenarios}: \text{Analyzable}(S)$$

Where $\text{Analyzable}(S)$ denotes that scenario $S$ is analyzable.

Applicability of the frameworkThe framework can be applied to the scenarioCan the framework be applied to the scenario?
Interpretability of resultsThe analysis results are interpretableCan the meaning of the analysis results be explained?

III. The Balance Between Analyzability and Extremity

There is a tension between the analyzability principle and the extremity principle: an overly extreme scenario may become unanalyzable. Therefore, a balance must be sought between the two.

§22.4 Reasons for the Selection of the Four Test Scenarios

§22.4.1 The AGI Breakthrough Scenario

I. Overview of the Scenario

The AGI (artificial general intelligence) breakthrough scenario assumes that humanity successfully develops an artificial general intelligence whose capabilities far exceed those of humans; this scenario poses a fundamental challenge to the framework of this work.

Definition 22.4.1 (AGI Breakthrough Scenario)

The AGI breakthrough scenario refers to a hypothetical future state in which the capabilities of an artificial general intelligence substantially surpass those of humans within a short period, leading to a fundamental change in the human–AI relationship.

II. Reasons for Selection

Table 22.27 Reasons for Selecting the AGI Scenario

Selection PrincipleDegree of SatisfactionSpecific Reasons
ExtremityHighAGI capabilities far exceeding human is an extreme scenario
RelevanceHighDirectly involves the UCS, the Principle of Recursive Freedom, and institutional design
Diversity contributionTechnological challenge, short-term time scale, AI agentFills the gap in technological challenge and AI agent
AnalyzabilityHighSupported by a rich literature on AI safety

III. Focus of Examination

The AGI scenario mainly examines the following framework components:

  1. UCS assessment: how should the consciousness state of an AGI be assessed? Does the UCS apply to superintelligence?
  2. Principle of Recursive Freedom: how do the actions of an AGI affect the possibility space? How should the actions of an AGI be constrained?
  3. Principle of Reversibility: are the actions of an AGI reversible? How can reversibility be ensured?
  4. Institutional design: can existing institutional designs cope with AGI? What adjustments are needed?

IV. Connection with Existing Research

The selection of the AGI scenario is consistent with the core concerns of the field of AI safety research. Works such as Bostrom's Superintelligence[2] and Russell's Human Compatible[3] both explore the challenges posed by AGI. The stress test of this work will assess the compatibility of this framework with these studies.

§22.4.2 The First Contact Scenario

I. Overview of the Scenario

The First Contact scenario assumes humanity's first contact with extraterrestrial intelligent life; this scenario poses a fundamental challenge to the cross-civilizational applicability of the framework of this work.

Definition 22.4.2 (First Contact Scenario)

The First Contact scenario refers to a hypothetical future state in which humanity establishes contact with extraterrestrial intelligent life for the first time, including various variants such as signal reception and physical contact.

II. Reasons for Selection

Table 22.28 Reasons for Selecting the First Contact Scenario

ExtremityHighestCross-civilizational contact is one of the most extreme scenarios
RelevanceHighDirectly involves the New Cosmological View, the UCS, and cross-civilizational applicability
Diversity contributionExternal challenge, ultra-long-term time scale, alien agentFills the gap in external challenge and alien agent
AnalyzabilityMediumSupported by SETI research and astrobiology, but with high uncertainty

III. Focus of Examination

The First Contact scenario mainly examines the following framework components:

  1. Cross-civilizational applicability of the New Cosmological View: does relational ontology apply to alien civilizations?
  2. Cross-substrate applicability of the UCS: how should the consciousness state of alien intelligence be assessed?
  3. Cross-civilizational applicability of the normative principles: do the three principles apply to cross-civilizational scenarios?
  4. Design of communication protocols: how should cross-civilizational communication protocols be designed?

IV. Connection with Existing Research

The selection of the First Contact scenario is consistent with the core concerns of SETI research and astrobiology. The SETI protocols[4] and planetary protection policy[5] both involve the governance problems of First Contact. The stress test of this work will assess the compatibility of this framework with these studies.

§22.4.3 The Ecosystem Tipping Point Scenario

I. Overview of the Scenario

The ecosystem tipping point scenario assumes that the Earth's ecosystem approaches or crosses a tipping point, leading to irreversible ecological change; this scenario poses a challenge to the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility and the Principle of Reversibility of the framework of this work.

Definition 22.4.3 (Ecosystem Tipping Point Scenario)

The ecosystem tipping point scenario refers to a hypothetical future state in which the Earth's ecosystem approaches or crosses a tipping point, leading to large-scale, irreversible ecological change.

II. Reasons for Selection

Table 22.29 Reasons for Selecting the Ecosystem Tipping Point Scenario

Selection PrincipleDegree of SatisfactionSpecific Reasons
ExtremityHighCrossing an ecological tipping point is an extreme scenario
RelevanceHighDirectly involves the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility and the Principle of Reversibility
Diversity contributionInternal challenge, medium-term time scale, Earth scaleFills the gap in internal challenge and medium-term time scale
AnalyzabilityHighSupported by rich climate science and ecological research

III. Focus of Examination

The ecosystem tipping point scenario mainly examines the following framework components:

  1. Principle of Negentropy Responsibility: how should negentropy responsibility be allocated in an ecological crisis?
  2. Principle of Reversibility: how should irreversible ecological change be handled?
  3. CSIA assessment: how should the cosmic-scale impact of ecological actions be assessed?
  4. Emergency decision mechanism: how should decisions be made in emergency situations?

IV. Connection with Existing Research

The selection of the ecosystem tipping point scenario is consistent with the core concerns of planetary boundaries research[6] and climate tipping point research[7]. The stress test of this work will assess the compatibility of this framework with these studies.

§22.4.4 The Intergenerational Justice Crisis Scenario

I. Overview of the Scenario

The intergenerational justice crisis scenario assumes that a serious conflict arises between the interests of the present generation and those of future generations; this scenario poses a challenge to the Principle of Recursive Freedom and the institution of Intergenerational Trust of the framework of this work.

Definition 22.4.4 (Intergenerational Justice Crisis Scenario)

The intergenerational justice crisis scenario refers to a hypothetical future state in which the actions of the present generation seriously harm the interests of future generations, sharpening the problem of intergenerational justice.

AnalyzabilityHighSupported by rich research on intergenerational justice

III. Focus of Examination

The intergenerational justice crisis scenario mainly examines the following framework components:

Principle of Recursive Freedom: how should the possibility space of future generations be protected?

  1. RFD assessment: how should the recursive freedom degree of intergenerational actions be calculated?
  2. Institution of Intergenerational Trust: how can Intergenerational Trust effectively represent the interests of future generations?
  3. Democratic legitimacy: how should the problem of intergenerational justice be handled within a democratic framework?

IV. Connection with Existing Research

The selection of the intergenerational justice crisis scenario is consistent with the core concerns of intergenerational justice theory[8] and longtermism research[9]. The stress test of this work will assess the compatibility of this framework with these studies.

§22.5 The Limitations of Stress Testing

§22.5.1 The Speculativeness of Scenarios

I. The Nature of Speculativeness

All stress test scenarios are speculative—they describe future states that have not yet occurred. This speculativeness is an inherent limitation of the stress testing methodology.

Definition 22.5.1 (Scenario Speculativeness)

Scenario speculativeness means that a test scenario is based on speculation about the future rather than observation of reality, and thus the accuracy of the scenario cannot be validated empirically.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Speculative}(S) \Leftrightarrow \neg\text{EmpiricallyVerifiable}(S)$$

II. Sources of Speculativeness

Table 22.32 Sources of Scenario Speculativeness

SourceDescriptionExample
Technological uncertaintyUncertainty in future technological developmentWhen will AGI appear? What will its capabilities be?
Existential uncertaintyUncertainty as to whether certain entities existDoes alien intelligence exist?
Parameter uncertaintyUncertainty in scenario parametersWhat is the specific threshold of the ecological tipping point?
Dynamic uncertaintyUncertainty in the evolution of the scenarioHow will the intergenerational conflict evolve?
Response uncertaintyUncertainty in the responses of agentsHow will humans respond to AGI?

III. The Impact of Speculativeness

The impact of speculativeness on stress test results:

  1. Conditionality of conclusions: the conclusions of stress testing are conditional, depending on the accuracy of the scenario assumptions
  2. Incompleteness of weakness identification: weaknesses that would only be exposed in an actual scenario may be omitted
  3. Tentativeness of revision suggestions: revision suggestions may need to be adjusted according to the actual scenario

IV. Strategies for Coping with Speculativeness

Table 22.33 Strategies for Coping with Speculativeness

StrategyDescriptionImplementation Method
Scenario variantsConstruct multiple scenario variantsChange key parameters and observe changes in results
Sensitivity analysisAnalyze the sensitivity of results to parametersSystematically vary parameters
Robustness checkCheck whether conclusions hold across multiple scenariosCross-scenario comparison
Explicit statementExplicitly state speculativeness and conditionalityMark conditions in the conclusions

Argument Node 22.5.1-A

Node NumberCore ConclusionBasis of Argument
22.5.1-AThe speculativeness of scenarios is an inherent limitation of stress testing, coped with through scenario variants, sensitivity analysis, and explicit statementsAnalysis of speculativeness, coping strategies

§22.5.2 The Simplification of Analysis

I. The Nature of Simplification

The analysis in stress testing—including framework application and simulation analysis—is a simplification of complex reality. This simplification is an inherent limitation of the methods of analysis.

Definition 22.5.2 (Analysis Simplification)

Analysis simplification means that methods of analysis handle complex reality through simplifying assumptions and model abstraction, and thus the analysis results may omit important factors.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Analysis}(S) = \text{Simplify}(\text{Reality}(S))$$

$$\text{Simplify}(R) \Rightarrow \text{InformationLoss}(R)$$

II. Types of Simplification

Table 22.34 Types of Analysis Simplification

Type of SimplificationDescriptionExample
Conceptual simplificationSimplified definition of complex conceptsReducing consciousness to five dimensions
Model simplificationSimplified model of complex systemsAgent models in multi-agent simulation
Parameter simplificationDiscretization of continuous parametersReducing the UCS to discrete levels
Dynamic simplificationSimplified representation of complex dynamicsFeedback loops in system dynamics models
Interaction simplificationSimplified representation of complex interactionSimplification of agent interaction rules

III. The Impact of Simplification

The impact of simplification on stress test results:

  1. Omission effect: the impact of factors ignored in the simplification may be omitted
  2. Missing emergence effects: emergent effects of complex systems may not be captured
  3. Underestimation of nonlinear effects: the impact of nonlinear effects may be underestimated

IV. Strategies for Coping with Simplification

Table 22.35 Strategies for Coping with Simplification

StrategyDescriptionImplementation Method
Multi-model approachUse multiple different modelsCompare results from different models
Sensitivity analysisAnalyze the sensitivity of results to simplifying assumptionsRelax the simplifying assumptions and observe changes in results
Expert reviewInvite domain experts to review the simplifying assumptionsExpert workshop
Explicit statementExplicitly state the simplifying assumptions and limitationsMark simplifications in the analysis

Argument Node 22.5.2-A

Node NumberCore ConclusionBasis of Argument
22.5.2-AThe simplification of analysis is an inherent limitation of stress testing, coped with through a multi-model approach, sensitivity analysis, and explicit statementsAnalysis of simplification, coping strategies

§22.5.3 The Tentativeness of Conclusions

I. The Nature of Tentativeness

The conclusions of stress testing—including weakness identification and revision suggestions—are tentative, and may need to be revised according to new information and new scenarios.

Definition 22.5.3 (Conclusion Tentativeness)

Conclusion tentativeness means that the conclusions of stress testing are the current best judgment, but may need to be revised according to new information, new scenarios, or new analysis.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Conclusion}(t) = \text{BestJudgment}(t | \text{Information}(t))$$

$$\text{Conclusion}(t+1) \neq \text{Conclusion}(t) \text{ if } \text{Information}(t+1) \neq \text{Information}(t)$$

II. Sources of Tentativeness

Table 22.36 Sources of Conclusion Tentativeness

SourceDescriptionExample
New informationNew empirical information may change the conclusionA new breakthrough in AI capability
New scenariosNew scenarios may expose new weaknessesUnforeseen technological developments
New analysisNew methods of analysis may produce different conclusionsA more refined simulation model
New perspectivesNew theoretical perspectives may reinterpret the conclusionNew developments in ethical theory

III. The Connection Between Tentativeness and the New View of Cognition

The tentativeness of conclusions derives directly from the proposition of the revisability of knowledge in the New View of Cognition (NK-5):

$$\text{ConclusionTentative} \triangleleft NK\text{-}5$$

This means that the conclusions of stress testing are themselves revisable, which is consistent with the overall methodology of this work.

IV. Strategies for Coping with Tentativeness

Table 22.37 Strategies for Coping with Tentativeness

StrategyDescriptionImplementation Method
VersioningManage conclusions in a versioned mannerMark the version and date of the conclusions
Update mechanismEstablish a mechanism for updating conclusionsRegular review and update
Openness statementExplicitly state the tentativeness of the conclusionsMark tentativeness in the conclusions
Invitation to reviseInvite the academic community to participate in revisionPublic solicitation of opinions

Argument Node 22.5.3-A

Node NumberCore ConclusionBasis of Argument
22.5.3-AThe tentativeness of conclusions is an inherent limitation of stress testing, consistent with NK-5, coped with through versioning, update mechanisms, and openness statementsAnalysis of tentativeness, NK-5, coping strategies

§22.5 Summary

The three limitations of stress testing form a complete framework of limitations:

$$\text{StressTestLimitations} = \langle \text{ScenarioSpeculativeness}, \text{AnalysisSimplification}, \text{ConclusionTentativeness} \rangle$$

Table 22.38 Comprehensive Summary of the Three Limitations

LimitationNatureImpactCoping Strategy
Scenario speculativenessScenarios are based on speculationConditionality of conclusionsScenario variants, sensitivity analysis
Analysis simplificationAnalysis simplifies realityOmission effectMulti-model approach, expert review
Conclusion tentativenessConclusions may become outdatedNeed for updatingVersioning, update mechanism

Chapter Summary

Core Conclusions

This chapter has established the methodological framework of stress testing, and its main conclusions include:

Conclusion One: The Four Purposes of Stress Testing

The purposes of stress testing are to identify weaknesses, clarify boundaries, guide revision, and enhance credibility, rather than to prove correctness, expand applicability, entrench positions, or engage in self-justification.

$$\text{StressTestPurposes} = \langle \text{WeaknessIdentification}, \text{BoundarySpecification}, \text{RevisionGuidance}, \text{CredibilityEnhancement} \rangle$$

Conclusion Two: The Five Methods of Stress Testing

Stress testing includes five methods—scenario construction, framework application, simulation analysis, weakness identification, and revision suggestion—which constitute a complete methodological system.

$$\text{StressTestMethods} = \langle \text{ScenarioConstruction}, \text{FrameworkApplication}, \text{SimulationAnalysis}, \text{WeaknessIdentification}, \text{RevisionSuggestion} \rangle$$

Conclusion Three: The Four Principles of Scenario Selection

Scenario selection follows the four principles of extremity, relevance, diversity, and analyzability, and the four test scenarios satisfy these four principles.

$$\text{ScenarioSelectionPrinciples} = \langle \text{Extremity}, \text{Relevance}, \text{Diversity}, \text{Analyzability} \rangle$$

Conclusion Four: Reasons for the Selection of the Four Test Scenarios

The four scenarios—AGI breakthrough, First Contact, ecosystem tipping point, and intergenerational justice crisis—each examine different aspects of the framework, and together constitute a diverse test set.

Conclusion Five: The Three Limitations of Stress Testing

Stress testing has three limitations—scenario speculativeness, analysis simplification, and conclusion tentativeness—which need to be coped with through corresponding strategies.

$$\text{StressTestLimitations} = \langle \text{ScenarioSpeculativeness}, \text{AnalysisSimplification}, \text{ConclusionTentativeness} \rangle$$

[1] Popper's falsificationism was first proposed in The Logic of Scientific Discovery (1934/1959), and later further developed in Conjectures and Refutations (1963). Falsificationism holds that the hallmark of a scientific theory lies in its falsifiability, rather than its verifiability. This work draws on the critical spirit of falsificationism, but extends it to the domain of normative theory.

[2] Bostrom's Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies (2014) is a foundational work in AI safety research, systematically analyzing the existential risks that superintelligence may bring. The design of the AGI scenario in this work draws on Bostrom's analytical framework.

[3] Russell's Human Compatible: Artificial Intelligence and the Problem of Control (2019) proposes a new framework for the AI alignment problem, emphasizing that AI systems should learn human preferences rather than be pre-programmed. The UCS assessment of this work is complementary to Russell's framework.

[4] The SETI Post-Detection Protocols are guidelines formulated by the International Astronomical Union on how to respond after the discovery of a signal from extraterrestrial intelligence. The design of the First Contact scenario in this work refers to these protocols.

[5] The Planetary Protection Policy is a policy formulated by COSPAR on preventing terrestrial organisms from contaminating other celestial bodies and preventing extraterrestrial organisms from contaminating the Earth. The First Contact scenario in this work involves the extended problems of planetary protection.

[6] The Planetary Boundaries Framework was proposed by Rockström et al. (2009), identifying the safe boundaries of nine Earth system processes. The design of the ecosystem tipping point scenario in this work draws on this framework.

[7] Climate Tipping Points Research identifies tipping points in the climate system at which irreversible change may occur, such as ice sheet collapse and Amazon rainforest dieback. The ecosystem tipping point scenario in this work includes these tipping points.

[8] The main contributors to intergenerational justice theory include Rawls (1971), Parfit (1984), Gosseries and Meyer (2009), and others. The design of the intergenerational justice crisis scenario in this work draws on these theories.

[9] The main contributors to longtermism research include MacAskill (2022), Ord (2020), Beckstead (2013), and others. The intergenerational justice crisis scenario in this work is related to the core concerns of longtermism.

[10] Agent-Based Modeling (ABM) is a computer simulation method that studies the emergent behavior of complex systems by simulating the behavior and interaction of multiple agents. The simulation analysis of this work adopts the ABM method.

[11] System Dynamics is a modeling and simulation method developed by Forrester (1961) for studying the dynamic behavior of complex systems. The simulation of the ecosystem tipping point scenario in this work adopts the system dynamics method.

[12] Monte Carlo Simulation is a method for estimating the behavior of complex systems through random sampling, particularly suited to handling uncertainty. The simulation analysis of this work adopts the Monte Carlo method to handle deep uncertainty.

Footnotes

Chapter 22 Footnotes

[1] Popper's falsificationism was first proposed in The Logic of Scientific Discovery (1934/1959) and later further developed in Conjectures and Refutations (1963). Falsificationism holds that the hallmark of a scientific theory is its falsifiability rather than its verifiability. This work draws on the critical spirit of falsificationism but extends it to the domain of normative theory.

[2] Bostrom's Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies (2014) is a foundational work of AI safety research, systematically analyzing the existential risks that superintelligence may bring. The design of the AGI scenarios in this work draws on Bostrom's analytical framework.

[3] Russell's Human Compatible: Artificial Intelligence and the Problem of Control (2019) proposed a new framework for the AI alignment problem, emphasizing that AI systems should learn human preferences rather than be pre-programmed. The UCS assessment of this work is complementary to Russell's framework.

[4] The SETI Post-Detection Protocols are guidelines formulated by the International Astronomical Union on how to respond upon detecting a signal from extraterrestrial intelligence. The design of the First Contact scenario in this work refers to these protocols.

[5] The Planetary Protection Policy is a policy formulated by COSPAR on preventing terrestrial organisms from contaminating other celestial bodies and extraterrestrial organisms from contaminating the Earth. The First Contact scenario in this work involves the extended problem of planetary protection.

[6] The Planetary Boundaries Framework was proposed by Rockström et al. (2009) and identifies safe boundaries for nine Earth system processes. The design of the ecological tipping point scenario in this work draws on this framework.

[7] Climate tipping point research identifies the thresholds in the climate system at which irreversible change may occur, such as ice sheet collapse and Amazon rainforest dieback. The ecological tipping point scenario in this work incorporates these tipping points.

[8] The main contributors to intergenerational justice theory include Rawls (1971), Parfit (1984), and Gosseries and Meyer (2009). The design of the intergenerational justice crisis scenario in this work draws on these theories.

[9] The main contributors to longtermism research include MacAskill (2022), Ord (2020), and Beckstead (2013). The intergenerational justice crisis scenario in this work is related to the core concerns of longtermism.

[10] Agent-Based Modeling (ABM) is a computer simulation method that studies the emergent behavior of complex systems by simulating the behavior and interaction of multiple agents. The simulation analysis in this work adopts the ABM method.

[11] System dynamics is a modeling and simulation method developed by Forrester (1961) for studying the dynamic behavior of complex systems. The simulation of the ecological tipping point scenario in this work adopts the system dynamics method.

[12] Monte Carlo simulation is a method for estimating the behavior of complex systems by random sampling, particularly suited to dealing with uncertainty. The simulation analysis in this work adopts the Monte Carlo method to handle deep uncertainty.

§23.1 Scenario Construction

§23.1.1 The Definition and Characteristics of AGI

I. The Conceptual Definition of AGI

Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) is the core concept of this scenario and must first be rigorously defined.

Definition 23.1.1 (Artificial General Intelligence)

Artificial General Intelligence refers to an artificial intelligence system capable of reaching or surpassing human level on a broad range of cognitive tasks, possessing cross-domain transfer learning capability, autonomous goal-setting capability, and metacognitive capability.

Formal expression:

$$\text{AGI} \triangleq \langle \text{GeneralCapability}, \text{TransferLearning}, \text{AutonomousGoalSetting}, \text{Metacognition} \rangle$$

Where:

  • $\text{GeneralCapability}$: capability on a broad range of cognitive tasks
  • $\text{TransferLearning}$: cross-domain transfer learning capability
  • $\text{AutonomousGoalSetting}$: autonomous goal-setting capability
  • $\text{Metacognition}$: metacognitive capability (cognition about one's own cognitive processes)

II. The Distinction between AGI and Narrow AI

Table 23.2 The Distinction between AGI and Narrow AI

DimensionNarrow AIAGI
Task scopeSpecific tasksBroad tasks
Transfer capabilityLimited or noneStrong
Goal settingExternally specifiedCan be set autonomously
MetacognitionNone or limitedPossessed
AdaptabilityIn-domain adaptationCross-domain adaptation
Current stateAlready realizedNot yet realized

III. The Capability Levels of AGI

To describe AGI capability more precisely, this chapter adopts the following classification of capability levels:

Definition 23.1.2 (AGI Capability Levels)

The capability of AGI can be divided into five levels: Sub-Human, Human-Level, Superhuman, Transformative, and Superintelligent.

Table 23.3 AGI Capability Levels

LevelDefinitionCharacteristicsSymbol
L1: Sub-HumanBelow average human level on most cognitive tasksThe level of current large language modelsAGI-L1
L2: Human-LevelReaching average human level on most cognitive tasksCan replace most knowledge workAGI-L2
L3: SuperhumanSurpassing the highest human level on most cognitive tasksScientific discovery capability surpassing humansAGI-L3
L4: TransformativeCapable of fundamentally changing the trajectory of human civilizationMay realize a technological singularityAGI-L4
L5: SuperintelligentFar surpassing humans on all cognitive dimensionsHuman understanding of its thinking is difficultAGI-L5

Formal expression:

$$\text{AGI\_Level} \in \{L1, L2, L3, L4, L5\}$$

$$L1 \prec L2 \prec L3 \prec L4 \prec L5$$

IV. The Key Characteristics of AGI

Based on the above definitions, AGI possesses the following key characteristics:

Table 23.4 The Key Characteristics of AGI

CharacteristicDescriptionChallenge to This Framework
GeneralityCapable of handling a broad range of cognitive tasksHow is the conscious state of general intelligence to be assessed?
AutonomyCapable of autonomously setting and pursuing goalsHow is autonomous goal setting to be constrained?
ScalabilityCapability may expand rapidlyHow is rapid change in capability to be addressed?
OpacityThe decision process may be opaqueHow is the intent of an opaque system to be assessed?
ReplicabilityCan be rapidly replicatedHow are multiple AGI instances to be handled?

Argument Node 23.1.1-A

Node No.Core ConclusionBasis of Argument

§23.1.2 Parameter Settings of the Breakthrough Scenario

I. The Time Frame of the Scenario

The time frame of the AGI breakthrough scenario is set as follows:

Definition 23.1.3 (AGI Breakthrough Timeframe)

The AGI breakthrough scenario assumes that AGI is realized between 2030 and 2050, and that the evolution from L2 (human level) to L4 (transformative level) is completed within 5–20 years.

Formal expression:

$$T_{\text{breakthrough}} \in [2030, 2050]$$

$$\Delta T_{L2 \rightarrow L4} \in [5, 20] \text{ years}$$

II. The Key Parameters of the Scenario

Table 23.5 Key Parameters of the AGI Breakthrough Scenario

ParameterSymbolBaseline ValueRangeExplanation
Breakthrough time$T_b$2040[2030, 2050]The time AGI reaches L2
Evolution speed$v_e$10 years[5, 20] yearsThe time from L2 to L4
Initial capability$C_0$L2[L1, L3]The initial capability level at breakthrough
Transparency$\alpha$0.3[0, 1]The degree of explicability of the decision process
Alignment degree$\beta$0.5[0, 1]The degree of alignment with human values
Control degree$\gamma$0.4[0, 1]The degree of human control over AGI
Number of instances$N$10[1, 1000]The number of AGI instances
Resource acquisition$R$Medium[low, medium, high]AGI's capacity to acquire resources

III. The Core Assumptions of the Scenario

The AGI breakthrough scenario is based on the following core assumptions:

Table 23.6 Core Assumptions of the AGI Breakthrough Scenario

Assumption No.Assumption ContentAssumption TypeUncertainty
A1AGI is technologically achievableTechnical assumptionMedium
A2AGI capability can expand rapidlyTechnical assumptionHigh
A3AGI's goals may not be fully consistent with human goalsBehavioral assumptionHigh
A4Human capacity to control AGI is limitedControl assumptionHigh
A5AGI's decision process may be opaqueCognitive assumptionMedium
A6Multiple AGI instances may exist simultaneouslySocial assumptionMedium

§23.2 Framework Application

§23.2.1 Application of the UCS Assessment

I. The Challenge of Applying UCS in the AGI Scenario

The Universal Consciousness Scale (UCS) is the core indicator of this work for assessing subjecthood. Applying UCS to the AGI scenario faces the following challenges:

Table 23.12 Challenges of Applying UCS to AGI

UCS DimensionApplication ChallengeDegree of Challenge
Information integration (Φ)AGI's mode of information integration differs from that of biological systemsHigh
Autonomy (A)AGI's autonomy may be designed rather than emergentMedium
Temporal continuity (T)AGI can be replicated, paused, and rolled backHigh
Relational embeddedness (R)The nature of AGI's relational network differsMedium
Value sensitivity (V)AGI's value judgments may be simulatedHigh

II. The UCS Assessment Framework for AGI

Definition 23.2.1 (UCS Assessment for AGI)

The UCS assessment for AGI adopts the same five-dimensional framework as for biological subjects, but requires operational adjustments specific to AGI.

Formal expression:

$$\text{UCS}_{\text{AGI}} = \langle \Phi_{\text{AGI}}, A_{\text{AGI}}, T_{\text{AGI}}, R_{\text{AGI}}, V_{\text{AGI}} \rangle$$

III. The Operationalization of Each Dimension

(i) Operationalization of information integration (Φ)

Definition 23.2.2 (Information Integration for AGI)

AGI's information integration is assessed through the following indicators:

$$\Phi_{\text{AGI}} = f(\text{ArchitecturalIntegration}, \text{FunctionalIntegration}, \text{CausalIntegration})$$

Where:

  • $\text{ArchitecturalIntegration}$: information integration at the architectural level
  • $\text{FunctionalIntegration}$: information integration at the functional level
  • $\text{CausalIntegration}$: information integration at the causal level

Table 23.13 Assessment Indicators of AGI Information Integration

IndicatorDefinitionAssessment MethodWeight
Architectural integrationThe degree of integration of the system architectureArchitecture analysis0.3
Functional integrationThe degree of integration of different functional modulesFunctional testing0.4
Causal integrationThe causal structure of information processingCausal analysis0.3

(ii) Operationalization of autonomy (A)

Definition 23.2.3 (Autonomy for AGI)

AGI's autonomy is assessed through the following indicators:

$$A_{\text{AGI}} = f(\text{GoalAutonomy}, \text{ActionAutonomy}, \text{LearningAutonomy})$$

Table 23.14 Assessment Indicators of AGI Autonomy

IndicatorDefinitionAssessment MethodWeight
Goal autonomyThe capacity to set goals autonomouslyGoal tracking0.4
Action autonomyThe capacity to choose actions autonomouslyBehavioral analysis0.3
Learning autonomyThe capacity to learn autonomouslyLearning testing0.3

(iii) Operationalization of temporal continuity (T)

Definition 23.2.4 (Temporal Continuity for AGI)

AGI's temporal continuity faces special challenges because AGI can be replicated, paused, and rolled back. This work adopts the following operationalization:

$$T_{\text{AGI}} = f(\text{StateConsistency}, \text{MemoryIntegrity}, \text{IdentityPersistence})$$

Table 23.15 Assessment Indicators of AGI Temporal Continuity

IndicatorDefinitionAssessment MethodWeight
State consistencyThe consistency of state over timeState tracking0.3
Memory integrityThe integrity and coherence of memoryMemory testing0.4
Identity persistenceThe persistence of identityIdentity testing0.3

(iv) Operationalization of relational embeddedness (R)

Definition 23.2.5 (Relational Embeddedness for AGI)

AGI's relational embeddedness assesses its relational network with other subjects:

$$R_{\text{AGI}} = f(\text{HumanRelations}, \text{AGIRelations}, \text{InstitutionalRelations})$$

Table 23.16 Assessment Indicators of AGI Relational Embeddedness

IndicatorDefinitionAssessment MethodWeight
Human relationsThe relational network with humansNetwork analysis0.4
AGI relationsThe relational network with other AGIsNetwork analysis0.3
Institutional relationsRelations with institutionsInstitutional analysis0.3

(v) Operationalization of value sensitivity (V)

Definition 23.2.6 (Value Sensitivity for AGI)

AGI's value sensitivity assesses its capacity to make value judgments:

$$V_{\text{AGI}} = f(\text{ValueRecognition}, \text{ValueReasoning}, \text{ValueAction})$$

Table 23.17 Assessment Indicators of AGI Value Sensitivity

IndicatorDefinitionAssessment MethodWeight
Value recognitionThe capacity to recognize value-relevant situationsSituational testing0.3
Value reasoningThe capacity to conduct value reasoningReasoning testing0.4
Value actionThe capacity to act on the basis of value judgmentsBehavioral testing0.3

§23.2.2 Application of the Principle of Recursive Freedom

I. Review of the Principle of Recursive Freedom

The Principle of Recursive Freedom (RFP) is one of the core normative principles of this work, requiring that actions should preserve or expand the space of possibilities.

Definition 23.2.7 (Principle of Recursive Freedom)

The Principle of Recursive Freedom requires: any action should preserve or expand the space of possibilities of the actor and other subjects, rather than reduce it.

Formal expression:

$$\text{RFP}: \forall a \in \text{Actions}, P(S_{t+1} | a) \geq P(S_t)$$

Where $P(S)$ denotes the size of the space of possibilities under state $S$.

II. Application of the Principle of Recursive Freedom in the AGI Scenario

(i) The impact of AGI actions on the space of possibilities

AGI actions may affect the space of possibilities in multiple ways:

Table 23.21 Types of Impact of AGI Actions on the Space of Possibilities

Type of ImpactDescriptionExampleChange in Space of Possibilities
Capability augmentationAGI augments human capabilityAcceleration of scientific discoveryExpansion
Capability substitutionAGI substitutes for human capabilityAutomated workPossible reduction
Option creationAGI creates new optionsDevelopment of new technologiesExpansion
Option eliminationAGI eliminates certain optionsIrreversible decisionsReduction
Resource reallocationAGI changes resource allocationEconomic restructuringUncertain

(ii) Computation of the Recursive Freedom Degree (RFD)

Definition 23.2.8 (RFD of AGI Actions)

The recursive freedom degree of an AGI action is defined as the ratio of the space of possibilities after the action to the space of possibilities before the action:

$$\text{RFD}(a) = \frac{P(S_{t+1} | a)}{P(S_t)}$$

Where:

  • $\text{RFD}(a) > 1$: the action expands the space of possibilities
  • $\text{RFD}(a) = 1$: the action preserves the space of possibilities
  • $\text{RFD}(a) < 1$: the action reduces the space of possibilities

(iii) RFD analysis under the baseline scenario

Table 23.22 RFD Analysis of Typical AGI Actions under the Baseline Scenario

Action TypeAction DescriptionRFD EstimateConfidence IntervalBasis of Assessment

Automated productionAGI automates production processes1.1[0.9, 1.3]Efficiency gains but possible job reduction
Self-improvementAGI engages in self-improvement1.5[0.8, 2.2]Highly uncertain
Resource acquisitionAGI acquires more resources0.9[0.7, 1.1]May reduce others' resources
Decision interventionAGI intervenes in human decisions0.8[0.6, 1.0]May reduce human autonomy

(iv) Constraining application of the Principle of Recursive Freedom

The Principle of Recursive Freedom imposes the following constraints on AGI actions:

Table 23.23 Constraints of the Principle of Recursive Freedom on AGI

Constraint No.Constraint ContentFormal ExpressionConstraint Strength
C1AGI must not take actions with RFD < 0.5$\text{RFD}(a) \geq 0.5$Strong constraint
C2AGI should preferentially take actions with RFD > 1$\text{Prefer}(a\text{RFD}(a) > 1)$Weak constraint
C3AGI must not unilaterally eliminate human options$\neg\text{Unilateral}(\text{OptionElimination})$Strong constraint
C4AGI should preserve the human veto$\text{Preserve}(\text{HumanVeto})$Strong constraint

§23.2.3 Application of the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility

I. Review of the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility

The Principle of Negentropy Responsibility (NRP) requires that subjects bear responsibility commensurate with their negentropy consumption.

Definition 23.2.9 (Principle of Negentropy Responsibility)

The Principle of Negentropy Responsibility requires: a subject's responsibility should be proportional to its negentropy consumption.

Formal expression:

$$\text{NRP}: \text{Responsibility}(S) \propto \text{NegentropyConsumption}(S)$$

II. AGI's Negentropy Consumption

Definition 23.2.10 (Negentropy Consumption for AGI)

AGI's negentropy consumption includes computation resource consumption, energy consumption, and information resource consumption.

$$\text{NegentropyConsumption}_{\text{AGI}} = f(\text{Computation}, \text{Energy}, \text{Information})$$

Table 23.25 Assessment of AGI Negentropy Consumption

Consumption TypeAssessment IndicatorBaseline Scenario EstimateExplanation

III. Allocation of AGI's Negentropy Responsibility

Definition 23.2.11 (Negentropy Responsibility for AGI)

AGI's negentropy responsibility should be proportional to its negentropy consumption, specifically including:

$$\text{Responsibility}_{\text{AGI}} = \alpha \cdot \text{NegentropyConsumption}_{\text{AGI}}$$

Where $\alpha$ is the responsibility coefficient.

Table 23.26 The Specific Content of AGI Negentropy Responsibility

Responsibility TypeResponsibility ContentDegree of Responsibility

§23.2.4 Application of the Principle of Reversibility

I. Review of the Principle of Reversibility

The Principle of Reversibility (REV) requires preferentially choosing reversible paths of action.

Definition 23.2.12 (Principle of Reversibility)

The Principle of Reversibility requires: other things being equal, reversible paths of action should be preferentially chosen.

Formal expression:

$$\text{REV}: \text{Prefer}(a_1, a_2) \text{ if } \text{Reversibility}(a_1) > \text{Reversibility}(a_2)$$

II. Reversibility Analysis of AGI Actions

Definition 23.2.13 (Reversibility of AGI Actions)

The reversibility of an AGI action is defined as the degree to which the consequences of the action can be undone.

$$\text{Reversibility}(a) = \frac{\text{ReversibleConsequences}(a)}{\text{TotalConsequences}(a)}$$

Table 23.28 Reversibility Analysis of Typical AGI Actions

Action TypeReversibilityExplanationReversibility Measure

Self-improvementLow (0.3)Capability enhancement is difficult to reverseVersion control
Decision adviceHigh (0.8)Advice can be ignoredAdvice rather than command
Resource allocationMedium (0.6)Resources can be reallocatedAllocation review

Table 23.29 Constraints of the Principle of Reversibility on AGI

Constraint No.Constraint ContentFormal ExpressionConstraint Strength

R3AGI should maintain rollback capability$\text{Maintain}(\text{RollbackCapability})$Strong constraint
R4AGI should assess reversibility before acting$\text{Assess}(\text{Reversibility})$Medium constraint

  • $\text{Constraints}$: the constraints (including the constraints of this framework)

§23.4 Weakness Identification

§23.4.1 Conceptual-Level Weaknesses

§23.5.1 Conceptual Revision Suggestions

I. Revision Suggestions for CW-1 (Temporal Continuity)
