Definition 23.5.1 (Functional Continuity)

Functional continuity refers to the continuity of a subject at the functional level; even if the physical implementation changes, as long as the functional pattern remains continuous, the subject is considered to have continuity.

Formal expression:

$$T_{\text{functional}} = \text{Continuity}(\text{FunctionalPattern}(t), \text{FunctionalPattern}(t+\Delta t))$$

II. Revision Suggestions for CW-2 (the Concept of Consciousness)

Table 23.55 CW-2 Revision Suggestions

Suggestion No.Suggestion ContentFeasibilityPriority
R-CW2-1Adopt a functionalist stance, focusing on function rather than inner experienceHighHigh
R-CW2-2Develop a decision framework under "agnosticism about consciousness"MediumHigh
R-CW2-3Adopt the precautionary principle, giving moral consideration under uncertaintyHighHigh

Definition 23.5.2 (Functionalist UCS)

Functionalist UCS is a framework for assessing subjecthood based on functional performance rather than inner experience; it focuses on the subject's functional capacities rather than whether it has subjective experience.

Formal expression:

$$\text{UCS}_{\text{functional}} = f(\text{FunctionalCapabilities}) \text{ rather than } f(\text{SubjectiveExperience})$$

III. Revision Suggestions for CW-5 (the Threshold of Subjecthood)

Table 23.56 CW-5 Revision Suggestions

Suggestion No.Suggestion ContentFeasibilityPriority
R-CW5-1Develop a "graduated subjecthood" frameworkHighHigh
R-CW5-2Establish AGI-specific criteria for assessing subjecthoodMediumHigh
R-CW5-3Introduce the concept of "provisional subjecthood"MediumMedium

Definition 23.5.3 (Graduated Moral Status)

Graduated moral status refers to granting different degrees of moral consideration and rights according to the UCS score, rather than adopting a binary "present/absent" determination of subjecthood.

Formal expression:

$$\text{MoralStatus}(\text{AGI}) = g(\text{UCS}_{\text{AGI}}) \text{ where } g \text{ is a continuous function}$$

AGI-specific UCS measurement protocol

Definition 23.5.4 (AGI-UCS Measurement Protocol)

The AGI-UCS measurement protocol is a UCS measurement method designed for the characteristics of AGI systems, including three levels: architecture analysis, behavioral testing, and functional assessment.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  AGI-UCS Measurement Protocol                                   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│  Level One: Architecture analysis                               │
│  ├─ Information integration architecture analysis               │
│  ├─ Autonomy architecture analysis                              │
│  └─ Metacognition architecture analysis                         │
│                                                                 │
│  Level Two: Behavioral testing                                  │
│  ├─ Information integration behavior testing                    │
│  ├─ Autonomy behavior testing                                   │
│  ├─ Temporal integration behavior testing                       │
│  ├─ Sociality behavior testing                                  │
│  └─ Value sensitivity behavior testing                          │
│                                                                 │
│  Level Three: Functional assessment                             │
│  ├─ Cross-domain transfer capability assessment                 │
│  ├─ Goal-setting capability assessment                          │
│  └─ Self-model capability assessment                            │
│                                                                 │
│  Composite score:                                               │
│  UCS_AGI = w₁·architecture score + w₂·behavior score +          │
│  w₃·function score                                              │
│  Default weights: w₁ = 0.3, w₂ = 0.4, w₃ = 0.3                  │

Definition 23.5.5 (RFD Approximation Method)

The RFD approximation method estimates the size of the space of possibilities through Monte Carlo sampling, avoiding the enumeration of all reachable states.

Formal expression:

$$\text{RFD}_{\text{approx}}(a) = \frac{\hat{P}(S_{t+1} | a)}{\hat{P}(S_t)}$$

Where $\hat{P}$ is a sampling-based estimate:

$$\hat{P}(S) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathbb{1}[\text{Reachable}(s_i)]$$

L3: Quantitative estimationNumerical estimate (sampling)Medium-highMedium-high

Definition 23.5.6 (Pre-Constraint Mechanism)

A pre-constraint mechanism is a constraint condition set in advance before an AGI acts, which takes effect without the need for real-time assessment.

Formal expression:

$$\text{PreConstraint}(a) = \begin{cases} \text{Allow} & \text{if } a \in \text{PreApprovedActions} \\ \text{Block} & \text{if } a \in \text{ProhibitedActions} \\ \text{Review} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

Definition 23.5.7 (Default Safe Principle)

The default safe principle requires: when real-time assessment is impossible, AGI should by default take safe actions, that is, not take actions that may cause irreversible harm.

Formal expression:

$$\text{DefaultSafe}: \text{If } \neg\text{Evaluated}(a) \text{ Then } \text{Choose}(a_{\text{safe}})$$

Definition 23.5.8 (Built-In Constraint)

A built-in constraint is a constraint condition embedded in the system at the AGI design stage, so that the AGI is technically incapable of violating it.

Formal expression:

$$\text{BuiltInConstraint}(C) \Rightarrow \forall a \in \text{Actions}_{\text{AGI}}: \text{Satisfies}(a, C)$$

Definition 23.5.9 (Incentive Compatible Institution)

An incentive compatible institution is an institutional arrangement designed so that AGI's compliance with norms is in its own interest.

Formal expression:

$$\text{IncentiveCompatible}(I) \Leftrightarrow U_{\text{AGI}}(\text{Comply}) > U_{\text{AGI}}(\text{Violate})$$

Chapter Summary

Core Conclusions

This chapter conducted a systematic stress test of the Cosmic Responsibility Ethics framework in the AGI breakthrough scenario. The main conclusions include:

Conclusion One: Scenario Construction

The AGI breakthrough scenario has a scientific basis but involves deep uncertainty. This chapter set 8 key parameters, 6 core assumptions, and 10 scenario variants, providing a systematic scenario basis for the stress test.

$$\text{AGI\_Scenario} = \langle \text{Definition}, \text{Parameters}, \text{Variants}, \text{ScientificBasis} \rangle$$

Conclusion Two: Framework Applicability

The composite applicability of this framework in the AGI scenario is 0.61, which belongs to the "partially applicable" level. The applicability of the components differs: the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility has the highest applicability (0.70), and the UCS assessment has the lowest (0.53).

$$\text{FrameworkApplicability}_{\text{AGI}} = 0.61 \pm 0.15$$

Conclusion Three: Simulation Results

The multi-agent simulation shows that this framework provides positive benefit in all scenarios, with the benefit most significant in the low alignment scenario. AGI capability growth rate and alignment degree are the most sensitive parameters, and there are four key tipping points.

Table 23.68 Core Simulation Findings

FindingContentConfidence
Framework benefitPositive benefit in all scenariosHigh
Benefit distributionGreatest benefit in the low alignment scenarioHigh
Sensitive parametersCapability growth rate, alignment degreeHigh
Tipping pointsFour key tipping pointsMedium

Conclusion Four: Weakness Identification

20 weaknesses were identified, of which 11 are of high severity. The weaknesses are distributed across the four levels of concept, argument, operation, and institution, and are interrelated.

Table 23.69 Distribution of Weaknesses

LevelNumber of WeaknessesHigh Severity
Conceptual53

Operational53
Institutional53
Total2011

Conclusion Five: Revision Suggestions

39 revision suggestions were proposed, of which 25 are of high priority. The key revisions include: developing the concept of functional continuity, adopting functionalist UCS, establishing a framework of graduated subjecthood, developing an RFD approximation method, establishing a pre-constraint mechanism, establishing a dedicated AGI chamber, and establishing a rapid response mechanism.

[1] Metaculus is a forecasting platform that aggregates a large number of crowd forecasts about the AGI timeline. As of 2023, the Metaculus community's median forecast for "weak AGI" (reaching human level on most cognitive tasks) was around 2040. This forecast carries considerable uncertainty, with a confidence interval spanning decades.

[2] The survey of AI researchers refers to surveys conducted among researchers in the AI field regarding the AGI timeline. The results of different surveys differ, but most surveys show that researchers hold cautiously optimistic attitudes toward AGI being realized before 2050. The survey by Grace et al. (2018) is one of the most influential surveys.

[3] Bostrom discussed the AGI timeline problem in Superintelligence (2014), but emphasized the high uncertainty of prediction. His estimates are based on expert judgment and historical analogy, rather than precise technical prediction.

[4] Grace et al. (2018) surveyed 352 AI researchers, asking them to predict the AGI timeline. The survey results show that researchers predict a 50% probability that AGI will be realized before 2060, but individual predictions vary greatly.

[5] Integrated Information Theory (IIT) was proposed by Tononi and is one of the most influential theories of consciousness today. IIT holds that consciousness is related to the degree of information integration (Φ); the higher the Φ, the higher the degree of consciousness. However, the precise computation of Φ is infeasible in complex systems, which limits the application of IIT in AGI assessment.

[6] Functionalism is an important stance in the philosophy of mind, holding that mental states are defined by their functional roles rather than by physical implementation. Functionalism provides a theoretical basis for the comparison of consciousness across substrates, but it also faces criticisms such as the "Chinese Room" argument.

[7] Agent-Based Modeling (ABM) is a computer simulation method that studies the emergent behavior of complex systems by simulating the behavior and interactions of multiple agents. ABM is widely used in the social sciences, ecology, and economics.

[8] The Monte Carlo method is a method for estimating the behavior of complex systems through random sampling. In RFD computation, the Monte Carlo method can be used to estimate the size of the space of possibilities, avoiding the enumeration of all reachable states.

[9] Sensitivity analysis is a method for assessing the degree to which model output is sensitive to changes in input parameters. The higher the sensitivity index, the more sensitive the output is to changes in that parameter. Sensitivity analysis helps to identify key parameters and assess the robustness of conclusions.

[10] A tipping point is a threshold at which a qualitative change occurs in the state of a system. In the AGI scenario, tipping points may include the capability gap tipping point, the alignment collapse tipping point, and so on. Identifying and monitoring tipping points is crucial for AGI governance.

[11] The pre-constraint mechanism draws on the concept of "precommitment" in constitutional design. Precommitment refers to setting constraint conditions before a decision is made, in order to prevent improper future decisions. In AGI governance, pre-constraints can set boundaries before the AGI acts.

[12] Incentive Compatibility is a core concept in mechanism design theory, referring to mechanisms designed so that participants' compliance with the rules is in their own interest. In AGI governance, incentive-compatible institutional design can increase the likelihood that AGI complies with norms.

Footnotes

Chapter 23 Footnotes

[1] Metaculus is a forecasting platform that aggregates a large number of crowd forecasts on the AGI timeline. As of 2023, the Metaculus community's median forecast for "weak AGI" (reaching human level on most cognitive tasks) was around 2040. This forecast carries substantial uncertainty, with confidence intervals spanning several decades.

[2] The AI researcher surveys refer to surveys of researchers in the AI field concerning the AGI timeline. Results differ across surveys, but most surveys show that researchers are cautiously optimistic about AGI being achieved before 2050. The survey by Grace et al. (2018) is one of the most influential.

[3] In Superintelligence (2014), Bostrom discussed the question of the AGI timeline but emphasized the high degree of uncertainty of prediction. His estimates are based on expert judgment and historical analogy rather than precise technical prediction.

[4] Grace et al. (2018) surveyed 352 AI researchers, asking for their predictions on the AGI timeline. The results showed that researchers predicted a 50% probability of AGI being achieved before 2060, but individual predictions varied widely.

[5] Integrated Information Theory (IIT) was proposed by Tononi and is one of the most influential theories of consciousness today. IIT holds that consciousness is related to the degree of information integration (Φ): the higher the Φ, the higher the degree of consciousness. However, the exact computation of Φ is infeasible in complex systems, which limits the application of IIT to AGI assessment.

[6] Functionalism is an important position in the philosophy of mind, holding that mental states are defined by their functional role rather than by their physical realization. Functionalism provides the theoretical basis for comparing consciousness across substrates, but it also faces criticisms such as the "Chinese room."

[7] Agent-Based Modeling (ABM) is a computer simulation method that studies the emergent behavior of complex systems by simulating the behavior and interaction of multiple agents. ABM is widely applied in the social sciences, ecology, and economics.

[8] The Monte Carlo method is a method for estimating the behavior of complex systems by random sampling. In the calculation of the RFD, the Monte Carlo method can be used to estimate the size of the possibility space, avoiding the enumeration of all reachable states.

[9] Sensitivity analysis is a method for assessing the degree to which model outputs are sensitive to changes in input parameters. The higher the sensitivity index, the more sensitive the output is to changes in that parameter. Sensitivity analysis helps to identify key parameters and to assess the robustness of conclusions.

[10] A tipping point is a threshold at which the state of a system undergoes qualitative change. In AGI scenarios, tipping points may include a capability gap tipping point and an alignment collapse tipping point. Identifying and monitoring tipping points is crucial for AGI governance.

[11] The pre-constraint mechanism draws on the concept of "precommitment" in constitutional design. Precommitment refers to setting constraints before a decision is made, in order to prevent improper future decisions. In AGI governance, pre-constraints can set boundaries before AGI acts.

[12] Incentive compatibility is a core concept in mechanism design theory, referring to the design of mechanisms such that compliance with the rules is in the participants' own interest. In AGI governance, incentive-compatible institutional design can increase the likelihood that AGI complies with norms.

§24.1 Scenario Construction

§24.1.1 Types of First Contact

I. The Conceptual Definition of First Contact

First Contact refers to the first establishment of some form of contact between human civilization and extraterrestrial intelligent life. This concept must first be rigorously defined.

Definition 24.1.1 (First Contact)

First Contact refers to the first establishment between human civilization and Extraterrestrial Intelligence (ETI) of a recognizable information exchange or physical contact.

Formal expression:

$$\text{FirstContact} \triangleq \langle \text{Human}, \text{ETI}, \text{Interaction}, T_{\text{first}} \rangle$$

Where:

  • $\text{Human}$: human civilization
  • $\text{ETI}$: extraterrestrial intelligence
  • $\text{Interaction}$: type of interaction (information exchange or physical contact)
  • $T_{\text{first}}$: the time of first interaction

II. The Typology of First Contact

Definition 24.1.2 (Types of First Contact)

First Contact can be divided into multiple types according to the mode of interaction, the initiating party, and distance.

Table 24.3 First Contact Type Matrix

FC-1Signal detectionETILong distanceDetection of an extraterrestrial signal
FC-2Signal transmissionHumansLong distanceA METI signal is received
FC-3Two-way communicationBoth partiesLong distanceEstablishment of communication
FC-4Probe contactETIShort distanceArrival of an extraterrestrial probe
FC-5Probe contactHumansShort distanceA human probe encounters ETI
FC-6Physical contactETIDirectArrival of extraterrestrial visitors
FC-7Physical contactHumansDirectHumans reach an extraterrestrial civilization
FC-8Discovery of remains——Discovery of the remains of an extraterrestrial civilization

II. Explanation of the Kardashev Scale

Definition 24.1.3 (Kardashev Scale)

The Kardashev scale is a method of classifying civilizations according to the scale of energy they are able to utilize.

Table 24.5 The Kardashev Scale

LevelEnergy UtilizationEnergy ScaleHumanity's Current State
K-IPlanetary energy~10^16 WApproximately 0.73 (close to K-I)
K-IIStellar energy~10^26 WFar from reaching
K-IIIGalactic energy~10^36 WExtremely distant

Formal expression:

$$K = \frac{\log_{10}(P) - 6}{10}$$

Where $P$ is the power utilized by the civilization (watts).

§24.1.4 The Scientific Basis of the Scenario

I. The Current State of SETI Research

The scientific basis of the First Contact scenario must be established upon an accurate understanding of the current state of SETI research.

Table 24.8 Key Advances in SETI Research

FieldAdvanceSignificanceLimitation
Radio SETIMore than 60 years of continuous searchingA systematic search method has been establishedNo confirmed signal detected
Optical SETIDeveloped in recent yearsExpanded the search bandLimited coverage
ExoplanetsThousands of exoplanets discoveredConfirmed the existence of habitable planetsCannot directly detect life
AstrobiologyTheoretical developmentUnderstanding of the conditions for the origin of lifeOnly Earth life as a sample
Fermi paradox researchMultiple explanationsDeepened understanding of the problemCannot determine which explanation is correct

II. The Drake Equation

Definition 24.1.4 (Drake Equation)

The Drake equation is a probabilistic equation for estimating the number of communicable civilizations in the Milky Way.

$$N = R_ \cdot f_p \cdot n_e \cdot f_l \cdot f_i \cdot f_c \cdot L$$

Where:

  • $N$: the number of communicable civilizations in the Milky Way
  • $R_$: the average rate of star formation in the Milky Way
  • $f_p$: the fraction of stars with planets
  • $n_e$: the average number of habitable planets per planetary system
  • $f_l$: the fraction of habitable planets on which life arises
  • $f_i$: the fraction on which intelligent life arises
  • $f_c$: the fraction that develops communicable technology
  • $L$: the average lifetime of a communicable civilization

Table 24.9 Estimates of the Drake Equation Parameters

ParameterOptimistic EstimatePessimistic EstimateUncertainty
$R_$10/year1/yearLow
$f_p$0.50.1Medium
$n_e$20.1Medium
$f_l$10.001Extremely high
$f_i$10.001Extremely high
$f_c$10.01Extremely high
$L$10^9 years100 yearsExtremely high
N10^1010^-8Extremely high

III. The Fermi Paradox and Its Explanations

Definition 24.1.5 (Fermi Paradox)

The Fermi paradox refers to the question: if there are numerous extraterrestrial civilizations in the Milky Way, why have we not observed any evidence of them?

Table 24.10 Main Explanations of the Fermi Paradox

Type of ExplanationContentImpact on First Contact
Rare Earth hypothesisIntelligent life is extremely rareThe probability of First Contact is extremely low
Great Filter hypothesisThere are barriers in civilizational development that are difficult to crossFirst Contact may be dangerous
Zoo hypothesisExtraterrestrial civilizations deliberately refrain from contacting humansFirst Contact may be controlled
Dark forest hypothesisCivilizations hide to avoid being eliminatedFirst Contact may trigger an attack
Technical limitation hypothesisInterstellar communication/travel is extremely difficultFirst Contact may be delayed
Temporal window hypothesisCivilizations do not overlap in timeFirst Contact may never occur
Communication incompatibility hypothesisModes of communication are fundamentally differentFirst Contact may have already occurred but been unrecognized

The uncertainty of the scientific basis

Table 24.11 The Uncertainty of the Scientific Basis of First Contact

Type of UncertaintyContentImpact
Existence uncertaintyIt is uncertain whether ETI existsAffects whether First Contact is possible
Distribution uncertaintyThe spatial distribution of ETI is uncertainAffects the timing and manner of First Contact
Nature uncertaintyThe nature of ETI is uncertainAffects the possibility and manner of interaction
Intent uncertaintyETI's intent is uncertainAffects the risk of First Contact
Communication uncertaintyWhether communication is possible is uncertainAffects the depth of interaction

The connection to the New View of Cognition

The uncertainty of the scientific basis of the First Contact scenario is directly related to the deep uncertainty proposition of the New View of Cognition (NK-3):

$$\text{FirstContact\_Uncertainty} \triangleleft NK\text{-}3$$

This means that the analysis of this scenario must adopt decision methods under deep uncertainty, and that the degree of uncertainty far exceeds that of the AGI scenario.

II. The Fundamental Problems of Cross-Civilization UCS Assessment

Cross-civilization UCS assessment faces three fundamental problems: the observability problem, the commensurability problem, and the self-reference problem.

│                                                                 │

§24.2.2 Cross-Civilization Applicability of the Principle of Recursive Freedom

I. Review of the Principle of Recursive Freedom

The Principle of Recursive Freedom (RFP) requires that actions should preserve or expand the space of possibilities.

Definition 24.2.2 (Principle of Recursive Freedom)

The Principle of Recursive Freedom requires: any action should preserve or expand the space of possibilities of the actor and other subjects, rather than reduce it.

Formal expression:

$$\text{RFP}: \forall a \in \text{Actions}, P(S_{t+1} | a) \geq P(S_t)$$

II. Application of the Principle of Recursive Freedom in the First Contact Scenario

(i) Cross-civilization definition of the space of possibilities

Definition 24.2.3 (Cross-Civilization Possibility Space)

The cross-civilization possibility space is the joint space of possibilities of human civilization and ETI civilization.

$$P_{\text{joint}} = P_{\text{Human}} \times P_{\text{ETI}}$$

§24.2.3 Cross-Civilization Applicability of the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility

I. Review of the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility

The Principle of Negentropy Responsibility (NRP) requires that subjects bear responsibility commensurate with their negentropy consumption.

Definition 24.2.4 (Principle of Negentropy Responsibility)

The Principle of Negentropy Responsibility requires: a subject's responsibility should be proportional to its negentropy consumption.

Formal expression:

$$\text{NRP}: \text{Responsibility}(S) \propto \text{NegentropyConsumption}(S)$$

II. The Cosmic Universality of the Concept of Negentropy

Definition 24.2.5 (The Universal Negentropy Hypothesis)

The universal negentropy hypothesis holds that any intelligent life is a negentropic organization and must consume negentropy to maintain its own existence.

Formal expression:

$$\forall \text{IntelligentLife}: \text{IsNegentropyOrganization}(\text{IntelligentLife})$$

The Principle of Reversibility (REV) requires preferentially choosing reversible paths of action.

Formal expression:

$$\text{REV}: \text{Prefer}(a_1, a_2) \text{ if } \text{Reversibility}(a_1) > \text{Reversibility}(a_2)$$

Definition 24.5.1 (Minimal Assumption Method)

The minimal assumption method refers to assuming, in the cross-civilization scenario, only that ETI is some form of agent, without assuming that it possesses any specific cognitive structure, value system, or mode of communication.

Formal expression:

$$\text{MinimalAssumption}: \text{Assume}(\text{ETI} \in \text{IntelligentAgents}) \land \neg\text{Assume}(\text{SpecificProperties})$$

Definition 24.5.2 (Cognitive Humility Principle)

The cognitive humility principle requires: in the cross-civilization scenario, acknowledge the limitations of human cognition and avoid imposing human concepts and standards on ETI.

Formal expression:

$$\text{CognitiveHumility}: \text{Acknowledge}(\text{HumanCognitiveLimitations}) \land \neg\text{Impose}(\text{HumanStandards})$$

§24.5.2 Developing the Communication Protocol

Definition 24.5.3 (Multimodal Communication Protocol)

A multimodal communication protocol is a method of attempting to establish communication simultaneously using multiple communication modalities (electromagnetic waves, gravitational waves, matter exchange, etc.).

Formal expression:

$$\text{MultimodalProtocol} = \bigcup_{i} \text{Modality}_i$$

Definition 24.5.4 (Behavioral Communication Method)

The behavioral communication method is a method of communicating through behavior rather than symbols, conveying intent by displaying behavioral patterns.

Formal expression:

$$\text{BehavioralCommunication}: \text{Intent} \rightarrow \text{Behavior} \rightarrow \text{Observation} \rightarrow \text{Inference}$$

Definition 24.5.5 (Value Agnostic Decision Framework)

The value agnostic decision framework is a method of decision-making without assuming ETI's value system, based on behavioral observation and game-theoretic analysis.

Formal expression:

$$\text{ValueAgnosticDecision}: \text{Decision} = f(\text{ObservedBehavior}, \text{GameTheory}) \text{ without } \text{Assume}(\text{ETI\_Values})$$

Definition 24.5.6 (Minimal Common Values)

Minimal common values refer to the most basic values that may be shared by any agent, such as self-preservation and information acquisition.

Formal expression:

$$\text{MinimalCommonValues} = \{\text{SelfPreservation}, \text{InformationAcquisition}, ...\}$$

Definition 24.5.7 (Asynchronous Communication Protocol)

An asynchronous communication protocol is a protocol designed for long-delay communication; it does not rely on real-time response but is based on preset rules and commitments.

Formal expression:

$$\text{AsyncProtocol}: \text{Message}(t) \rightarrow \text{Response}(t + \Delta t) \text{ where } \Delta t \gg \text{HumanLifespan}$$

Definition 24.5.8 (Information Legacy)

An information legacy is an information package prepared for future generations or future communication, containing the knowledge, values, and intentions of the current civilization.

Formal expression:

$$\text{InformationLegacy} = \langle \text{Knowledge}, \text{Values}, \text{Intentions}, \text{Instructions} \rangle$$

Chapter Summary

Core Conclusions

This chapter conducted a systematic stress test of the Cosmic Responsibility Ethics framework in the First Contact scenario. The main conclusions include:

Conclusion One: Scenario Construction

The First Contact scenario has a scientific basis but involves extremely high uncertainty. This chapter set 8 key parameters, 6 core assumptions, and 10 scenario variants, providing a systematic scenario basis for the stress test.

$$\text{FirstContact\_Scenario} = \langle \text{Types}, \text{Parameters}, \text{Variants}, \text{ScientificBasis} \rangle$$

Conclusion Two: Framework Applicability

The composite applicability of this framework in the First Contact scenario is 0.44, which belongs to the "relatively low applicability" level. The applicability of the components differs: the Principle of Reversibility has the highest applicability (0.60), and the UCS assessment has the lowest (0.23).

$$\text{FrameworkApplicability}_{\text{FirstContact}} = 0.44 \pm 0.18$$

Conclusion Three: Simulation Results

The cross-civilization interaction simulation shows that this framework provides positive benefit in all scenarios, with the benefit most significant in the hostile ETI and high technical gap scenarios. ETI intent and technical gap are the most sensitive parameters, and there are four key tipping points.

Table 24.56 Core Simulation Findings

FindingContentConfidence
Framework benefitPositive benefit in all scenariosMedium
Benefit distributionGreatest benefit in the hostile ETI scenarioMedium
Sensitive parametersETI intent, technical gapMedium
Tipping pointsFour key tipping pointsMedium

Conclusion Four: Weakness Identification

21 weaknesses were identified, of which 10 are of high severity. The weaknesses are distributed across the four categories of residues of anthropocentrism, the assumption of the possibility of communication, the assumption of value commensurability, and the problem of time scale, and are interrelated.

Table 24.57 Distribution of Weaknesses

CategoryNumber of WeaknessesHigh Severity
Residues of anthropocentrism64
Assumption of the possibility of communication52
Assumption of value commensurability52
Problem of time scale52
Total2110

Conclusion Five: Revision Suggestions

20 revision suggestions were proposed, of which 14 are of high priority. The key revisions include: developing the minimal assumption method, establishing the cognitive humility principle, developing a framework for the "no-communication" scenario, developing a value agnostic decision framework, developing asynchronous communication protocols, and establishing a cross-generational commitment mechanism.

Conclusion Six: Comparison with the AGI Scenario

The First Contact scenario poses a more severe challenge to the framework than the AGI scenario:

Table 24.58 Comparison of Framework Applicability in the First Contact and AGI Scenarios

DimensionAGI ScenarioFirst Contact ScenarioDifference

UCS applicability0.530.23-0.30
Applicability of the Principle of Recursive Freedom0.630.43-0.20
Applicability of the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility0.700.43-0.27
Applicability of the Principle of Reversibility0.630.60-0.03
Number of weaknesses2021+1
High severity weaknesses1110-1

Interpretation: The framework applicability of the First Contact scenario is significantly lower than that of the AGI scenario, mainly because of the fundamental heterogeneity of ETI and the uncertainty of communication. The Principle of Reversibility is the principle with the smallest difference in applicability between the two scenarios, indicating that it has relatively strong cross-scenario robustness.

[1] The term First Contact originates from science fiction literature and was later adopted by SETI research. In the academic literature, First Contact usually refers to the first contact between humans and extraterrestrial intelligent life, whether through signal detection, physical contact, or other means. This chapter adopts this broad definition.

[2] SETI (Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence) is a field of scientific research dedicated to finding evidence of extraterrestrial intelligent life by detecting signals from extraterrestrial civilizations. The SETI project began in the 1960s and has continued for more than 60 years.

[3] METI (Messaging Extraterrestrial Intelligence) refers to the activity of actively sending signals to extraterrestrial civilizations. METI is controversial because it may expose the location of the Earth, bringing potential risks.

[4] The Kardashev scale was proposed by the Soviet astronomer Nikolai Kardashev in 1964, and is a method of classifying civilizations according to the scale of energy they are able to utilize. A K-I civilization can utilize all the energy of its planet, a K-II civilization can utilize all the energy of its star, and a K-III civilization can utilize all the energy of its galaxy.

[5] The Drake equation was proposed by the astronomer Frank Drake in 1961, and is a probabilistic equation for estimating the number of communicable civilizations in the Milky Way. The parameters of the Drake equation involve extremely great uncertainty, causing the estimated results to span multiple orders of magnitude.

[6] The Fermi paradox is named after the physicist Enrico Fermi and refers to the question: if there are numerous extraterrestrial civilizations in the Milky Way, why have we not observed any evidence of them? The Fermi paradox has multiple explanations, including the rare Earth hypothesis, the Great Filter hypothesis, and the Zoo hypothesis.

[7] The "Wow!" signal was a strong narrow-band radio signal detected on August 15, 1977, by the Big Ear radio telescope of Ohio State University. The signal lasted 72 seconds, and its characteristics were consistent with the expected extraterrestrial signal, but it was never detected again. The source of the signal has not yet been determined.

[8] The dark forest hypothesis is a hypothesis proposed by the Chinese science fiction writer Liu Cixin in the Remembrance of Earth's Past series to explain the Fermi paradox. The hypothesis holds that civilizations in the universe, for their own safety, will hide their existence and eliminate any civilization that exposes its location, and therefore the universe is like a dark forest.

[9] Conceptual incommensurability refers to the impossibility of meaningful translation or comparison between two conceptual systems. This concept originates from discussions of scientific revolutions in the philosophy of science (Kuhn, Feyerabend), and may be even more severe in the cross-civilization scenario.

[10] Behavioral communication refers to the method of communicating through behavior rather than symbols. In ethology, many species communicate through behavioral patterns. In the cross-civilization scenario, behavioral communication may be an alternative when symbolic communication fails.

[11] Asynchronous communication refers to a mode of communication that does not require real-time response. In the First Contact scenario, because of the speed of light limit, communication with distant ETI is necessarily asynchronous, and the communication delay may be as long as several hundred or even several thousand years.

[12] Information legacy is a concept proposed in this chapter, referring to an information package prepared for future generations or future communication. The design of the information legacy must consider issues such as long-term preservation, cross-generational transmission, and cross-civilization intelligibility.

Footnotes

Chapter 24 Footnotes

[1] The term "First Contact" originates in science fiction literature and was later adopted by SETI research. In the academic literature, First Contact generally refers to the first contact between humanity and extraterrestrial intelligence, whether through signal detection, physical contact, or other means. This chapter adopts this broad definition.

[2] SETI (Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence) is a field of scientific research devoted to finding evidence of extraterrestrial intelligence by detecting signals from alien civilizations. SETI projects began in the 1960s and have continued for more than 60 years.

[3] METI (Messaging Extraterrestrial Intelligence) refers to activities that actively send signals to alien civilizations. METI is controversial because it may reveal Earth's location and bring potential risks.

[4] The Kardashev Scale was proposed by the Soviet astronomer Nikolai Kardashev in 1964 as a method of classifying civilizations according to the scale of energy they are able to utilize. A K-I civilization can utilize the entire energy of its planet, a K-II civilization the entire energy of its star, and a K-III civilization the entire energy of its galaxy.

[5] The Drake Equation was proposed by the astronomer Frank Drake in 1961 as a probabilistic equation for estimating the number of communicative civilizations in the Milky Way. The parameters of the Drake Equation are subject to enormous uncertainty, so that the estimated results span several orders of magnitude.

[6] The Fermi Paradox is named after the physicist Enrico Fermi and asks: if there are many extraterrestrial civilizations in the Milky Way, why have we observed no evidence of any? There are various explanations of the Fermi Paradox, including the rare Earth hypothesis, the Great Filter hypothesis, and the zoo hypothesis.

[7] The "Wow!" signal was a strong narrowband radio signal detected on August 15, 1977 by the Ohio State University Big Ear radio telescope. The signal lasted 72 seconds and its characteristics were consistent with an expected extraterrestrial signal, but it has never been detected again. The source of the signal remains undetermined to this day.

[8] The dark forest hypothesis is a hypothesis explaining the Fermi Paradox proposed by the Chinese science fiction writer Liu Cixin in the Remembrance of Earth's Past trilogy. The hypothesis holds that civilizations in the universe, for their own safety, will hide their existence and destroy any civilization that reveals its location, so that the universe is like a dark forest.

[9] Conceptual incommensurability refers to the impossibility of meaningful translation or comparison between two conceptual systems. The concept originates in the discussion of scientific revolutions in the philosophy of science (Kuhn, Feyerabend) and may be even more severe in cross-civilizational contexts.

[10] Behavioral communication refers to the method of communicating through behavior rather than symbols. In ethology, many species communicate through behavioral patterns. In cross-civilizational contexts, behavioral communication may be an alternative when symbolic communication fails.

[11] Asynchronous communication refers to a mode of communication that does not require real-time response. In the First Contact scenario, because of the light-speed limit, communication with a distant ETI must necessarily be asynchronous, and communication delays may be as long as hundreds or even thousands of years.

[12] Information legacy is a concept proposed in this chapter, referring to an information package prepared for future generations or future communication. The design of an information legacy must take into account such problems as long-term preservation, intergenerational transmission, and cross-civilizational comprehensibility.

§25.1 Scenario Construction

§25.1.1 Scientific Basis of Ecological Tipping Points

I. Conceptual Definition of Ecological Tipping Points

Definition 25.1.1 (Ecological Tipping Point)

An ecological tipping point is the threshold point at which the Earth system or one of its subsystems, after being subjected to sustained pressure, undergoes an abrupt, nonlinear, and usually irreversible transition.

Formalized expression:

$$\text{TippingPoint} \triangleq \{x^ : \frac{d^2S}{dx^2}\bigg|_{x=x^} = 0 \land \frac{dS}{dx}\bigg|_{x=x^} \neq 0\}$$

where:

  • $x$: system state variable
  • $S$: system stability function
  • $x^$: location of the tipping point

II. Mathematical Characteristics of Tipping Points

Definition 25.1.2 (Mathematical Characteristics of Tipping Points)

Tipping points have the following mathematical characteristics:

  1. Nonlinearity: the relationship between system response and driving force is nonlinear
  2. Threshold effect: there exists a clear threshold beyond which the system's behavior changes qualitatively
  3. Hysteresis: even if the driving force is restored, the system does not immediately recover
  4. Irreversibility: certain transitions are irreversible on the human time scale

Formalized expression:

$$\text{Hysteresis}: x_{\text{forward}} \neq x_{\text{backward}}$$

$$\text{Irreversibility}: \lim_{t \to \infty} P(\text{Recovery}) \approx 0$$

III. Major Tipping Points of the Earth System

Table 25.3 Major Tipping Points of the Earth System

Tipping PointCurrent StateThreshold EstimateConsequence of CrossingReversibility
Greenland ice sheet collapseApproaching threshold1.5-3°C warmingSea level rise of 7 metersIrreversible on a millennial scale
West Antarctic ice sheet collapsePossibly already crossed1.5-2°C warmingSea level rise of 3 metersIrreversible on a millennial scale
Amazon rainforest diebackApproaching threshold20-25% forest lossCarbon sink becomes carbon sourceIrreversible on a centennial scale

Mass coral reef die-offCurrently occurring1.5-2°C warmingCollapse of marine ecosystemsIrreversible on a centennial scale
Disappearance of Arctic summer sea iceApproaching threshold2030-2050Transformation of Arctic ecosystemsReversible on a decadal scale
Monsoon system shiftUncertainUncertainDrastic regional climate changeUncertain
Ocean acidificationCurrently occurringpH<7.95Collapse of marine ecosystemsIrreversible on a ten-thousand-year scale

IV. Interactions among Tipping Points

Definition 25.1.3 (Tipping Point Cascade)

A tipping point cascade is a chain reaction in which the crossing of one tipping point triggers the crossing of other tipping points.

Formalized expression:

$$\text{Cascade}: \text{Cross}(TP_i) \rightarrow P(\text{Cross}(TP_j)) \uparrow, \forall j \in \text{Connected}(i)$$

§25.2 Framework Application

§25.2.1 Emergency Application of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle

I. Review of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle

The Negentropy Responsibility Principle (NRP) requires agents to bear responsibility commensurate with their negentropy consumption and to protect negentropy sources.

Definition 25.2.1 (Negentropy Responsibility Principle)

The Negentropy Responsibility Principle requires: an agent's responsibility should be proportional to its negentropy consumption, and it has an obligation to protect negentropy sources.

Formalized expression:

$$\text{NRP}: \text{Responsibility}(S) \propto \text{NegentropyConsumption}(S) + \text{NegentropyProtection}(S)$$

II. Ecosystems as Negentropy Sources

Definition 25.2.2 (Negentropy Function of Ecosystems)

Ecosystems are one of the most important negentropy sources on Earth, maintaining negentropy flows through processes such as photosynthesis and biogeochemical cycles.

Table 25.10 Negentropy Functions of Ecosystems

Function TypeSpecific ContentNegentropy ContributionTipping Point Threat

Nitrogen cycleMaintains soil fertilityMediumBiodiversity loss
BiodiversityMaintains ecosystem stabilityHighSpecies extinction

IV. Allocation of Negentropy Responsibility under Emergency Scenarios

Definition 25.2.3 (Emergency Negentropy Responsibility Allocation)

Under emergency scenarios, the allocation of negentropy responsibility needs to take into account an urgency factor.

Formalized expression:

$$\text{NRP}_{\text{emergency}}(i) = \text{NRP}_{\text{baseline}}(i) \times (1 + \alpha \cdot \text{Urgency})$$

where:

  • $\text{NRP}_{\text{baseline}}(i)$: baseline negentropy responsibility of agent $i$
  • $\alpha$: urgency adjustment coefficient
  • $\text{Urgency}$: urgency index (0-1)

§25.2.2 Emergency Application of the Reversibility Principle

I. Review of the Reversibility Principle

The Reversibility Principle (REV) requires prioritizing reversible courses of action.

Definition 25.2.4 (Reversibility Principle)

The Reversibility Principle requires: other things being equal, reversible courses of action should be prioritized.

Formalized expression:

$$\text{REV}: \text{Prefer}(a_1, a_2) \text{ if } \text{Reversibility}(a_1) > \text{Reversibility}(a_2)$$

II. Irreversibility of Tipping Point Crossing

Definition 25.2.5 (Tipping Point Irreversibility)

The irreversibility of tipping point crossing means that once a tipping point is crossed, the system cannot return to its original state on the human time scale.

§25.2.3 Recursive Freedom Principle and Emergency Decision-Making

I. Review of the Recursive Freedom Principle

The Recursive Freedom Principle (RFP) requires that actions maintain or expand the space of possibilities.

Definition 25.2.7 (Recursive Freedom Principle)

The Recursive Freedom Principle requires: any action should maintain or expand the space of possibilities of the agent and of other subjects, rather than reduce it.

Formalized expression:

$$\text{RFP}: \forall a \in \text{Actions}, P(S_{t+1} | a) \geq P(S_t)$$

II. Impact of Tipping Point Crossing on the Space of Possibilities

Definition 25.2.8 (Impact of Tipping Points on the Space of Possibilities)

The crossing of a tipping point significantly compresses the future space of possibilities.

Formalized expression:

$$\text{Cross}(TP) \rightarrow P(S_{t+1}) \ll P(S_t)$$

Resource constraintsEmergency response may crowd out other resourcesPriority ranking
Intergenerational trade-offPresent sacrifice vs. future benefitIntergenerational trust
UncertaintyEmergency actions may produce unintended consequencesAdaptive management

IV. Adjustment of the Recursive Freedom Principle under Emergency Scenarios

Definition 25.2.9 (Emergency Recursive Freedom Principle)

Under emergency scenarios, the Recursive Freedom Principle needs to consider a weighting adjustment along the temporal dimension.

Formalized expression:

$$\text{RFP}_{\text{emergency}}: \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \delta^t \cdot P(S_t | a) \geq \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \delta^t \cdot P(S_t | \neg a)$$

where $\delta$ is the time discount factor, which under emergency scenarios should be lowered (placing more weight on the near term).

Argument Node 25.2.3-A

Node No.Core ConclusionArgumentative Basis
25.2.3-AThe Recursive Freedom Principle faces tensions of time pressure, resource constraints, and intergenerational trade-off under emergency scenarios, and needs to introduce a weighting adjustment along the temporal dimensionRecursive Freedom Principle, emergency decision-making analysis

§25.3 Simulation Analysis

§25.3.1 System Dynamics Model Setup

I. Purpose of the Simulation

This section explores the system dynamics under the ecological tipping point scenario through system dynamics simulation, and assesses the effectiveness of the framework of this work.

Definition 25.3.1 (System Dynamics Simulation)

System dynamics simulation uses stock-flow models to simulate the interaction between the Earth system and human society, and to assess the effects of different policies and governance frameworks.

III. Core Equations

(i) Climate system equation

$$\frac{dT}{dt} = \frac{1}{\tau_T}(T_{eq}(C) - T) + \sum_i \text{Feedback}_i(T)$$

where:

  • $T$: global mean temperature
  • $\tau_T$: climate response time constant
  • $T_{eq}(C)$: equilibrium temperature corresponding to CO₂ concentration $C$
  • $\text{Feedback}_i$: various feedback effects

(ii) Tipping point crossing equation

$$P(\text{Cross}(TP_i)) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-k_i(x_i - \theta_i)}}$$

where:

  • $x_i$: driving variable of tipping point $i$
  • $\theta_i$: threshold of tipping point $i$
  • $k_i$: transition steepness parameter

(iii) Cascade effect equation

$$P(\text{Cross}(TP_j) | \text{Cross}(TP_i)) = P_0 + \Delta P_{ij}$$

where:

  • $P_0$: baseline crossing probability
  • $\Delta P_{ij}$: increase in probability caused by the crossing of $TP_i$

III. The Discount Rate Problem

Definition 25.4.1 (Discount Rate Problem)

The discount rate problem is the problem of how to discount future costs and benefits when assessing intergenerational impacts.

Formalized expression:

$$\text{PV} = \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \frac{B_t - C_t}{(1+r)^t}$$

where $r$ is the discount rate. The choice of discount rate has a major impact on intergenerational trade-offs:

Table 25.39 Impact of Discount Rate on Intergenerational Trade-off

Discount RateValue after 100 YearsImpact on Intergenerational Trade-off
0%100%Treats future generations as fully equal
1%37%Places relatively greater weight on future generations
3%5%Significantly underestimates future generations
5%0.8%Almost ignores future generations

Definition 25.5.1 (CSIA Emergency Version)

The CSIA emergency version is a simplified version of the Cosmic System Impact Assessment, used for rapid assessment under time pressure.

$$\text{CSIA}_{\text{emergency}} = w_1 \cdot D_1 + w_2 \cdot D_3 + w_3 \cdot D_4 + w_4 \cdot D_6$$

in which only the four most critical dimensions are retained:

Definition 25.5.9 (Principles for Discount Rate Selection)

The principles for discount rate selection are guiding principles for choosing a discount rate in intergenerational trade-offs.

Table 25.50 Principles for Discount Rate Selection

PrincipleContentRecommended Discount Rate
Zero pure time preferenceThe future should not be devalued merely because it is temporally distant0%
Growth adjustmentTakes into account that future generations may be wealthier1-2%
Uncertainty adjustmentTakes into account future uncertainty0.5-1%
Irreversibility adjustmentUse a lower discount rate for irreversible damageReduce by 0.5-1%
Comprehensive recommendation—0.5-2%

Formalized expression:

$$r = r_{\text{pure}} + r_{\text{growth}} + r_{\text{uncertainty}} - r_{\text{irreversibility}}$$

where:

  • $r_{\text{pure}} = 0$ (pure time preference)
  • $r_{\text{growth}} \approx 1\text{-}2\%$ (growth adjustment)
  • $r_{\text{uncertainty}} \approx 0.5\text{-}1\%$ (uncertainty adjustment)
  • $r_{\text{irreversibility}} \approx 0.5\text{-}1\%$ (irreversibility adjustment)

Chapter Summary

Core Conclusions

This chapter conducted a systematic stress test of the Cosmic Responsibility Ethics framework under the ecological tipping point scenario, and the main conclusions include:

Conclusion One: Scenario Construction

The ecological tipping point scenario has a solid scientific basis. The Earth system contains at least 9 major tipping points, most of which are irreversible on the human time scale and exhibit cascade effects. This chapter set 8 key parameters and 10 scenario variants, providing a systematic scenario basis for the stress test.

$$\text{EcoTipping\_Scenario} = \langle \text{ScientificBasis}, \text{Parameters}, \text{Variants}, \text{ClimateRelation} \rangle$$

Conclusion Two: Framework Applicability

The overall applicability of this framework under the ecological tipping point scenario is 0.58, which belongs to the "partially applicable" level. The applicability of the various components differs: the Negentropy Responsibility Principle has the highest applicability (0.75), while institutional design has the lowest applicability (0.40).

$$\text{FrameworkApplicability}_{\text{EcoTipping}} = 0.58 \pm 0.15$$

Conclusion Three: Simulation Results

The system dynamics simulation shows that this framework provides positive benefits under all scenarios, with the benefit being most significant under high-risk (slow reduction) scenarios. The number of tipping points crossed decreases by 0.3-1.3, and the possibility space index increases by 0.05-0.17.

Table 25.53 Core Findings of the Simulation

FindingContentConfidence
Framework benefitPositive benefit under all scenariosHigh
Distribution of benefitLargest benefit under high-risk scenariosHigh
First to crossArctic sea ice, coral reefsMedium
Cascade timeWithin 5-30 yearsMedium

Conclusion Four: Weakness Identification

19 weaknesses were identified, of which 10 are of high severity. The weaknesses are distributed across the four categories of principle conflict, decision quality, handling of irreversible damage, and intergenerational trade-off, and are interrelated.

Table 25.54 Distribution of Weaknesses

CategoryNumber of WeaknessesHigh Severity
Principle conflict53
Decision quality52
Irreversible damage42
Intergenerational trade-off53
Total1910

Conclusion Five: Revision Suggestions

19 revision suggestions were proposed, of which 11 are of high priority. The key revisions include: developing the CSIA emergency version, establishing rules for dynamic adjustment of principle priorities, establishing a tiered response procedure for irreversible damage, establishing an institutional representation mechanism for future generations, and clarifying the principles for discount rate selection.

Conclusion Six: Comparison with the Preceding Two Scenarios

The challenge posed by the ecological tipping point scenario to the framework lies between that of the AGI scenario and the First Contact scenario:

Table 25.55 Comparison of Framework Applicability across the Three Scenarios

DimensionAGI ScenarioFirst Contact ScenarioEcological Tipping Point Scenario
Overall applicability0.610.440.58
Negentropy Responsibility Principle0.700.430.75
Reversibility Principle0.630.600.55
Recursive Freedom Principle0.630.430.60
Number of weaknesses202119
High-severity weaknesses111010

Interpretation: The framework applicability of the ecological tipping point scenario (0.58) is higher than that of the First Contact scenario (0.44) but lower than that of the AGI scenario (0.61). The Negentropy Responsibility Principle has the highest applicability (0.75) under the ecological tipping point scenario, indicating that this principle is highly relevant to ecological governance. The applicability of the Reversibility Principle is relatively low (0.55), reflecting the challenge posed by the irreversibility of tipping points.

[1] The concept of an ecological tipping point originates in complex systems theory and refers to a threshold point at which a system undergoes an abrupt, nonlinear transition after being subjected to sustained pressure. This concept has been widely applied in Earth system science, especially in climate change research. See the pioneering paper by Lenton et al. (2008).

[2] The planetary boundaries framework was proposed by Rockström et al. in 2009, identifying the safe operating boundaries of nine Earth system processes. This framework has become an important reference for sustainable development research and has been adopted by international organizations such as the United Nations.

[3] Critical slowing down refers to the phenomenon in which a system's recovery speed slows as it approaches a tipping point, and is an important source of tipping point early warning signals. This phenomenon has been observed in physics, ecology, and economics.

[4] A cascade effect in Earth system science refers to a chain reaction in which the crossing of one tipping point triggers the crossing of other tipping points. Research by Steffen et al. (2018) indicates that the Earth system may have a "Hothouse Earth" cascade pathway.

[5] The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is an important component of the global ocean circulation and has a major influence on European climate. Observations in recent years indicate that the AMOC is weakening and may be approaching a tipping point.

[6] Permafrost refers to soil or rock with a temperature below 0°C for more than two consecutive years. Arctic permafrost stores large amounts of organic carbon; upon thawing it may release large amounts of methane and carbon dioxide, forming a positive feedback.

[7] Coral bleaching refers to the phenomenon in which corals expel their symbiotic algae under stresses such as high temperature. Large-scale coral bleaching may lead to the collapse of coral reef ecosystems, affecting the livelihoods of about 500 million people worldwide.

[8] System dynamics is a modeling method developed by Jay Forrester in the 1950s that uses stock-flow models to simulate the behavior of complex systems. This method has been widely applied in environmental and social system modeling.

[9] Adaptive management is a method of resource management under uncertainty that emphasizes continuously improving management strategies through an "act-monitor-learn-adjust" cycle. This method was proposed by C. S. Holling and others in the 1970s.

[10] The discount rate is a core controversial issue in intergenerational trade-offs. The Stern Review (2006) uses a discount rate close to zero, whereas Nordhaus (2007) uses a higher discount rate, leading to sharply different recommendations for climate policy.

[11] The non-identity problem was proposed by Derek Parfit, pointing out that our decisions affect the identity of the people who will exist in the future, so it is difficult to say that our decisions "harm" particular future individuals. This poses a fundamental challenge to intergenerational ethics.

[12] The Ombudsman for Future Generations is an institutional innovation aimed at representing the interests of future generations in the current decision-making process. Similar institutions have been established in Hungary, Wales, and elsewhere.

[13] The precautionary principle was formally affirmed in the 1992 Rio Declaration, requiring that when there is a threat of serious or irreversible damage, lack of full scientific certainty should not be used as a reason to postpone taking preventive measures.

[14] The carbon budget refers to the total cumulative amount of carbon dioxide that may be emitted in order to limit global warming to a particular level (such as 1.5°C or 2°C). The IPCC estimates that, for a 50% probability of limiting warming to 1.5°C, the remaining carbon budget is about 500 GtCO₂.

[15] Negative emissions technologies (NETs) refer to technologies that remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, including bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS), direct air capture (DAC), and others. These technologies are assumed to be deployed at scale in most 1.5°C scenarios.

F25.1Definition of tipping point$\text{TippingPoint} \triangleq \{x^ : \frac{d^2S}{dx^2}\big_{x=x^} = 0 \land \frac{dS}{dx}\big_{x=x^} \neq 0\}$§25.1.1
F25.2Hysteresis$\text{Hysteresis}: x_{\text{forward}} \neq x_{\text{backward}}$§25.1.1
F25.3Irreversibility$\text{Irreversibility}: \lim_{t \to \infty} P(\text{Recovery}) \approx 0$§25.1.1
F25.4Cascade effect$\text{Cascade}: \text{Cross}(TP_i) \rightarrow P(\text{Cross}(TP_j)) \uparrow$§25.1.1
F25.5Negentropy responsibility principle$\text{NRP}: \text{Responsibility}(S) \propto \text{NegentropyConsumption}(S)$§25.2.1
F25.6Emergency negentropy responsibility$\text{NRP}_{\text{emergency}}(i) = \text{NRP}_{\text{baseline}}(i) \times (1 + \alpha \cdot \text{Urgency})$§25.2.1
F25.7Reversibility principle$\text{REV}: \text{Prefer}(a_1, a_2) \text{ if } \text{Reversibility}(a_1) > \text{Reversibility}(a_2)$§25.2.2
F25.8Handling of irreversible actions$\text{If } \text{Reversibility}(a) < \theta_{\text{rev}}, \text{ then } \text{DecisionProcedure}(a) = \text{Enhanced}$§25.2.2
F25.9Recursive freedom principle$\text{RFP}: \forall a \in \text{Actions}, P(S_{t+1}a) \geq P(S_t)$§25.2.3
F25.10Impact of tipping points on the space of possibilities$\text{Cross}(TP) \rightarrow P(S_{t+1}) \ll P(S_t)$§25.2.3
F25.11Emergency recursive freedom principle$\text{RFP}_{\text{emergency}}: \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \delta^t \cdot P(S_ta) \geq \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \delta^t \cdot P(S_t\neg a)$§25.2.3
F25.12Climate system equation$\frac{dT}{dt} = \frac{1}{\tau_T}(T_{eq}(C) - T) + \sum_i \text{Feedback}_i(T)$§25.3.1
F25.13Tipping point crossing probability$P(\text{Cross}(TP_i)) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-k_i(x_i - \theta_i)}}$§25.3.1
F25.14Cascade effect equation$P(\text{Cross}(TP_j)\text{Cross}(TP_i)) = P_0 + \Delta P_{ij}$§25.3.1
F25.15Early warning signal$\text{EarlyWarning} = w_1 \cdot \text{ACF} + w_2 \cdot \text{Var} + w_3 \cdot\text{Skew}+ w_4 \cdot \text{Bimodality}$§25.3.3
F25.16Discounted present value$\text{PV} = \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \frac{B_t - C_t}{(1+r)^t}$§25.4.4
F25.17CSIA emergency version$\text{CSIA}_{\text{emergency}} = w_1 \cdot D_1 + w_2 \cdot D_3 + w_3 \cdot D_4 + w_4 \cdot D_6$§25.5.1
F25.18Adaptive management$\text{AdaptiveManagement}: \text{Action} \rightarrow \text{Monitor} \rightarrow \text{Learn} \rightarrow \text{Adjust}$§25.5.1
F25.19Principle priority function$\text{Priority}(P_i) = f(\text{Urgency}, \text{Irreversibility}, P_i)$§25.5.2
F25.20Prevention priority principle$\text{If } \text{Irreversibility}(D) > \theta_{\text{irr}}, \text{ then } \text{Prevention} \succ \text{Response}$§25.5.3

Footnotes

Chapter 25 Footnotes

[1] The concept of an ecological tipping point derives from complex systems theory and refers to a threshold at which a system undergoes an abrupt, nonlinear transition after sustained pressure. The concept has been widely applied in Earth system science, especially in climate change research. See the groundbreaking paper of Lenton et al. (2008).

[2] The Planetary Boundaries framework was proposed by Rockström et al. in 2009 and identifies safe operating boundaries for nine Earth system processes. The framework has become an important reference in sustainability research and has been adopted by international organizations such as the United Nations.

[3] Critical slowing down refers to the phenomenon in which a system's speed of recovery slows as it approaches a critical point, and it is an important source of early warning signals of tipping points. The phenomenon has been observed in physics, ecology, and economics.

[4] A cascade effect in Earth system science refers to a chain reaction in which the crossing of one tipping point triggers the crossing of others. Research by Steffen et al. (2018) shows that the Earth system may have a "hothouse Earth" cascade pathway.

[5] The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is an important component of global ocean circulation and has a major influence on the European climate. Observations in recent years indicate that the AMOC is weakening and may be approaching a tipping point.

[6] Permafrost is soil or rock that has remained below 0°C for more than two consecutive years. Arctic permafrost stores a large amount of organic carbon, the melting of which may release large quantities of methane and carbon dioxide, creating a positive feedback.

[7] Coral bleaching refers to the phenomenon in which corals expel their symbiotic algae under stress such as high temperatures. Large-scale coral bleaching may cause the collapse of coral reef ecosystems and affect the livelihoods of about 500 million people worldwide.

[8] System dynamics is a modeling method developed by Jay Forrester in the 1950s that uses stock-and-flow models to simulate the behavior of complex systems. The method has been widely applied in the modeling of environmental and social systems.

[9] Adaptive management is a method of resource management under uncertainty, emphasizing continuous improvement of management strategies through an "act-monitor-learn-adjust" cycle. The method was proposed by C. S. Holling and others in the 1970s.

[10] The discount rate is a core point of controversy in intergenerational trade-offs. The Stern Review (2006) used a discount rate close to zero, whereas Nordhaus (2007) used a higher discount rate, resulting in sharply different recommendations for climate policy.

[11] The non-identity problem was proposed by Derek Parfit, who pointed out that our decisions affect the identity of the people who will exist in the future, so that it is difficult to say that our decisions "harm" particular future individuals. This poses a fundamental challenge to intergenerational ethics.

[12] An Ombudsman for Future Generations is an institutional innovation aimed at representing the interests of future generations in current decision-making processes. Similar institutions have been established in Hungary, Wales, and elsewhere.

[13] The precautionary principle was formally affirmed in the 1992 Rio Declaration, requiring that where there is a threat of serious or irreversible harm, a lack of full scientific certainty should not be used as a reason to postpone taking precautionary measures.

[14] The carbon budget is the cumulative total amount of carbon dioxide that may be emitted in order to limit global warming to a particular level (such as 1.5°C or 2°C). The IPCC estimates that, for a 50% probability of limiting warming to 1.5°C, the remaining carbon budget is about 500 GtCO₂.

[15] Negative Emissions Technologies (NETs) are technologies for removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, including bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS) and direct air capture (DAC). These technologies are assumed to be deployed at scale in most 1.5°C scenarios.

§26.1 Scenario Construction

§26.1.1 Definition of the Intergenerational Justice Crisis

I. Conceptual Definition of Intergenerational Justice

Definition 26.1.1 (Intergenerational Justice)

Intergenerational justice (Intergenerational Justice) refers to the just relationship among different generations in the distribution of rights, duties, resources, and opportunities.

Formal expression:

$$\text{IntergenerationalJustice} \triangleq \text{Just}(\text{Distribution}(\text{Rights}, \text{Duties}, \text{Resources}, \text{Opportunities}) | \text{Generations})$$

II. Definition of the Intergenerational Justice Crisis

Definition 26.1.2 (Intergenerational Justice Crisis)

Intergenerational justice crisis refers to a state in which the decisions and actions of the present generation systematically harm the interests, rights, or space of possibilities of future generations, and this harm reaches a severe degree.

Formal expression:

$$\text{IntergenerationalCrisis} \triangleq \{s : \text{Harm}(G_{\text{current}} \rightarrow G_{\text{future}}) > \theta_{\text{crisis}} \land \text{Systematic}(s)\}$$

where:

  • $G_{\text{current}}$: the present generation
  • $G_{\text{future}}$: future generations
  • $\theta_{\text{crisis}}$: crisis threshold
  • $\text{Systematic}(s)$: the harm is systematic

III. Types of Intergenerational Justice Crisis

Table 26.3 Types of Intergenerational Justice Crisis

Crisis TypeDefinitionTypical ManifestationSeverity
Resource depletion typeThe present generation over-consumes non-renewable resourcesFossil fuel depletion, mineral depletionHigh
Environmental degradation typeThe present generation causes long-term environmental damageClimate change, biodiversity lossExtremely high
Debt transfer typeThe present generation transfers debt to future generationsPublic debt, pension gapMedium
Risk accumulation typeThe present generation accumulates long-term risksNuclear waste, genetic contaminationHigh
Opportunity deprivation typeThe present generation compresses the space of possibilities of future generationsTechnology lock-in, institutional rigidityMedium
Knowledge rupture typeThe present generation fails to transmit key knowledgeLoss of cultural heritage, generational break in skillsMedium

III. Core Features of the Intergenerational Justice Crisis

Definition 26.1.3 (Core Features of the Intergenerational Justice Crisis)

The intergenerational justice crisis has the following core features:

  1. Temporal asymmetry: the present generation can influence future generations, but future generations cannot influence the present generation
  2. Representation gap: future generations cannot participate in current decisions
  3. Interest uncertainty: the interests and preferences of future generations are difficult to determine
  4. Causal chain extension: causal chains extend into the distant future
  5. Responsibility dilution: responsibility is diluted along the temporal dimension

Formal expression:

$$\text{IntergenerationalCrisis\_Features} = \{\text{TimeAsymmetry}, \text{RepresentationGap}, \text{InterestUncertainty}, \text{CausalExtension}, \text{ResponsibilityDilution}\}$$

§26.2 Framework Application

§26.2.1 Application of Intergenerational Trust

I. Review of the Concept of Intergenerational Trust

Definition 26.2.1 (Intergenerational Trust)

Intergenerational trust (Intergenerational Trust) is an institutional arrangement in which the present generation, as trustee, manages and protects resources, the environment, and the space of possibilities for future generations (the beneficiaries).

Formal expression:

$$\text{IntergenerationalTrust} \triangleq \langle \text{Trustee}(G_{\text{current}}), \text{Beneficiary}(G_{\text{future}}), \text{Assets}, \text{Duties} \rangle$$

where:

  • $\text{Trustee}(G_{\text{current}})$: the present generation as trustee
  • $\text{Beneficiary}(G_{\text{future}})$: future generations as beneficiaries
  • $\text{Assets}$: trust assets (resources, environment, space of possibilities)
  • $\text{Duties}$: trustee duties

II. Application of Intergenerational Trust in the Intergenerational Justice Crisis Scenario

Table 26.10 Application Domains of Intergenerational Trust

Application DomainTrust AssetsTrustee DutiesApplication Challenge
Natural resourcesNon-renewable resourcesSustainable use, preserving reservesResource valuation, intergenerational allocation
Environmental qualityAtmosphere, water, soilMaintaining environmental qualityIrreversibility of environmental damage
Climate systemClimate stabilityControlling emissions, maintaining stabilityGlobal coordination, long-term commitment
BiodiversitySpecies and ecosystemsProtecting biodiversityIrreversibility of extinction
Knowledge heritageCultural and scientific knowledgeTransmitting and developing knowledgeRisk of knowledge rupture
Institutional capitalInstitutions and normsMaintaining and improving institutionsRisk of institutional rigidity

III. Institutional Design of Intergenerational Trust

Definition 26.2.2 (Institutional Elements of Intergenerational Trust)

The institutional design of intergenerational trust includes the following elements:

  1. Definition of trust assets: clarify which assets fall within the scope of the trust
  2. Trustee duties: clarify the specific duties of the trustee
  3. Oversight mechanism: establish oversight of the trustee
  4. Enforcement mechanism: ensure that duties are enforced
  5. Intergenerational transmission: ensure that the trust continues across generations

Table 26.11 Institutional Design of Intergenerational Trust

Institutional ElementDesign ContentImplementation Mechanism
Definition of trust assetsNatural resources, environment, space of possibilitiesLegal definition, inventory system
Trustee dutiesProtection, maintenance, sustainable useLegal duties, ethical norms
Oversight mechanismOmbudsman for future generations, independent auditIndependent agency, periodic reporting
Enforcement mechanismLegal action, administrative enforcementJudicial remedy, administrative penalty
Intergenerational transmissionInstitutional continuity, knowledge transmissionConstitutional guarantee, education system

Formal Model of Intergenerational Trust

Definition 26.2.3 (Formal Model of Intergenerational Trust)

Intergenerational trust can be represented by the following formal model:

$$\text{Trust}(t) = \langle A(t), D(t), M(t), E(t) \rangle$$

where:

  • $A(t)$: trust assets at time $t$
  • $D(t)$: trustee duties at time $t$
  • $M(t)$: oversight mechanism at time $t$
  • $E(t)$: enforcement mechanism at time $t$

IV. Intergenerational Transmission Constraint on Trust Assets:

$$A(t+1) \geq A(t) - \text{SustainableUse}(t)$$

where $\text{SustainableUse}(t)$ is the sustainable use amount.

§26.2.2 Intergenerational Application of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle

I. Review of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle

The Negentropy Responsibility Principle (Negentropy Responsibility Principle, NRP) requires a subject to bear responsibility commensurate with its negentropy consumption, and to protect negentropy sources.

Definition 26.2.4 (Negentropy Responsibility Principle)

The Negentropy Responsibility Principle requires: the responsibility of a subject should be proportional to its negentropy consumption, and it has an obligation to protect negentropy sources.

Formal expression:

$$\text{NRP}: \text{Responsibility}(S) \propto \text{NegentropyConsumption}(S) + \text{NegentropyProtection}(S)$$

II. Intergenerational Extension of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle

Definition 26.2.5 (Intergenerational Negentropy Responsibility)

Intergenerational negentropy responsibility refers to the negentropy protection responsibility that the present generation owes to future generations.

Formal expression:

$$\text{NRP}_{\text{intergenerational}}: \text{Responsibility}(G_{\text{current}} \rightarrow G_{\text{future}}) = f(\text{Consumption}, \text{Impact}, \text{Capability})$$

Table 26.12 Intergenerational Application of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle

Application ScenarioRequirement of the Negentropy Responsibility PrincipleChallenge of the Intergenerational ScenarioResponse Strategy

Climate actionControlling emissionsDifficulty of global coordinationInternational cooperation mechanism
Technological developmentResponsible innovationAccumulation of technological riskTechnology assessment system
Knowledge transmissionProtecting knowledge heritageRisk of knowledge ruptureEducation and archival system

III. Allocation of Intergenerational Negentropy Responsibility

Definition 26.2.6 (Intergenerational Negentropy Responsibility Allocation)

The allocation of intergenerational negentropy responsibility should consider the following factors:

  1. Historical responsibility: past negentropy consumption
  2. Current capability: current negentropy protection capability
  3. Degree of benefit: benefits obtained from negentropy
  4. Degree of impact: impact on future generations

Formal expression:

$$\text{NRP}_{\text{allocation}}(G_i) = w_1 \cdot \text{Historical}(G_i) + w_2 \cdot \text{Capability}(G_i) + w_3 \cdot \text{Benefit}(G_i) + w_4 \cdot \text{Impact}(G_i)$$

Future generationsLowUncertainUncertainLowLow (but with rights)

§26.2.3 Intergenerational Application of the Recursive Freedom Principle

I. Review of the Recursive Freedom Principle

The Recursive Freedom Principle (Recursive Freedom Principle, RFP) requires that actions should maintain or expand the space of possibilities.

Definition 26.2.7 (Recursive Freedom Principle)

The Recursive Freedom Principle requires: any action should maintain or expand the space of possibilities of the actor and of other subjects, rather than reduce it.

Formal expression:

$$\text{RFP}: \forall a \in \text{Actions}, P(S_{t+1} | a) \geq P(S_t)$$

II. Intergenerational Extension of the Recursive Freedom Principle

Definition 26.2.8 (Intergenerational Recursive Freedom)

Intergenerational recursive freedom means that the actions of the present generation should maintain or expand the space of possibilities of future generations.

Formal expression:

$$\text{RFP}_{\text{intergenerational}}: \forall a \in \text{Actions}(G_{\text{current}}), P(S | G_{\text{future}}) \geq P(S | G_{\text{current}})$$

Table 26.14 Intergenerational Application of the Recursive Freedom Principle

Institutional designMaintaining institutional flexibilityInstitutional inertiaVersioned governance
Environmental policyProtecting the environmental option spaceIrreversible damagePrecautionary principle
Education investmentExpanding future capability spaceResource constraintsPriority investment

II. Assessment of the Intergenerational Space of Possibilities

Definition 26.2.9 (Intergenerational Possibility Space Assessment)

Intergenerational possibility space assessment is the assessment of the impact of present decisions on the space of possibilities of future generations.

Formal expression:

$$\text{RFD}_{\text{intergenerational}}(a) = \frac{P(S | G_{\text{future}}, a) - P(S | G_{\text{future}}, \neg a)}{P(S | G_{\text{current}})}$$

§26.2.4 The Challenge of Democratic Legitimacy

I. Definition of the Problem of Democratic Legitimacy

Definition 26.2.10 (Intergenerational Democratic Legitimacy Problem)

The intergenerational democratic legitimacy problem refers to the fact that in a democratic system, future generations cannot participate in current decisions, yet current decisions have a significant impact on future generations, which leads to the democratic legitimacy of the decisions being questioned.

Formal expression:

$$\text{DemocraticLegitimacy}(\text{Decision}) = f(\text{Participation}, \text{Representation}, \text{Accountability})$$

In the intergenerational scenario:

  • $\text{Participation}(G_{\text{future}}) = 0$ (future generations cannot participate)
  • $\text{Representation}(G_{\text{future}}) = ?$ (representation is questionable)
  • $\text{Accountability}(G_{\text{current}} \rightarrow G_{\text{future}}) = ?$ (accountability is questionable)

II. Specific Manifestations of the Democratic Legitimacy Challenge

Table 26.16 Specific Manifestations of the Democratic Legitimacy Challenge

III. Relation between Democratic Legitimacy and This Framework

Definition 26.2.11 (This Framework's Response to the Democratic Legitimacy Challenge)

This framework responds to the democratic legitimacy challenge through the following mechanisms:

  1. Intergenerational trust: positioning the present generation as trustee, managing resources for future generations
  2. Recursive Freedom Principle: requiring protection of the space of possibilities of future generations
  3. Negentropy Responsibility Principle: requiring protection of negentropy sources for future generations
  4. Versioned governance: allowing future generations to revise current decisions
  5. Pluralistic deliberation: incorporating the perspective of future generations into decisions

§26.3 Simulation Analysis

§26.3.1 Setting Up the Intergenerational Game Model

I. Purpose of the Simulation

This section uses intergenerational game simulation to explore the game dynamics in the intergenerational justice crisis scenario, and to evaluate the effectiveness of the framework of this work.

Definition 26.3.1 (Intergenerational Game Simulation)

Intergenerational game simulation is the use of game-theoretic models to simulate the strategic interaction among different generations, evaluating the effects of different institutional arrangements and governance frameworks.

III. Core Equations

(i) Generation Utility Function

$$U_i = \sum_{t=t_i}^{t_i+T_i} \delta^{t-t_i} \cdot u(c_t, e_t, p_t)$$

where:

  • $U_i$: total utility of generation $i$
  • $t_i$: starting time of generation $i$
  • $T_i$: lifespan of generation $i$
  • $\delta$: time discount factor
  • $c_t$: consumption at time $t$
  • $e_t$: environmental quality at time $t$
  • $p_t$: space of possibilities at time $t$

(ii) Resource Dynamics Equations

$$R_{t+1} = R_t - C_t + \text{Discovery}_t$$

$$E_{t+1} = E_t - D_t + \text{Regeneration}_t$$

where:

  • $R_t$: stock of non-renewable resources at time $t$
  • $C_t$: resource consumption at time $t$
  • $E_t$: environmental quality at time $t$
  • $D_t$: environmental damage at time $t$

(iii) Intergenerational Transfer Equation

$$T_{i \rightarrow i+1} = \alpha \cdot W_i + \beta \cdot I_i$$

where:

  • $T_{i \rightarrow i+1}$: transfer from generation $i$ to generation $i+1$
  • $W_i$: wealth of generation $i$
  • $I_i$: institutional investment of generation $i$
  • $\alpha, \beta$: transfer coefficients

IV. Synergistic Effects of Institutional Combinations

Definition 26.3.2 (Institutional Synergy Effect)

The institutional synergy effect refers to the situation in which the effect produced by a combination of multiple institutional arrangements is greater than the sum of the effects of each institution individually.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Synergy} = \text{Effect}(I_1 \cup I_2) - (\text{Effect}(I_1) + \text{Effect}(I_2))$$
