§26.4 Weakness Identification

§26.4.1 Legitimacy of Representation of Future Generations

I. Definition of the Representation Legitimacy Problem

Definition 26.4.1 (Representation Legitimacy Problem)

The representation legitimacy problem refers to the question, in the intergenerational justice scenario, of who has the right to represent future generations, and what the legitimate basis of such representation is.

Formal expression:

$$\text{RepresentationLegitimacy} = f(\text{Authorization}, \text{Accountability}, \text{Responsiveness})$$

In the intergenerational scenario:

  • $\text{Authorization}(G_{\text{future}}) = 0$ (future generations cannot authorize)
  • $\text{Accountability}(\text{Representative} \rightarrow G_{\text{future}}) = ?$ (accountability is questionable)
  • $\text{Responsiveness}(\text{Representative}, G_{\text{future}}) = ?$ (responsiveness is questionable)

II. Specific Challenges of Representation Legitimacy

Table 26.32 Specific Challenges of Representation Legitimacy

Challenge TypeSpecific ManifestationSeverity
Lack of authorizationFuture generations cannot authorize a representativeExtremely high
Interest uncertaintyThe interests of future generations are difficult to determineHigh
Preference uncertaintyThe preferences of future generations are difficult to determineHigh
Accountability difficultyA representative finds it difficult to take responsibility toward future generationsHigh
Representative selectionHow to select a representative is disputedMedium
Representative biasA representative may have its own biasesMedium

§26.4.2 Credibility of Long-term Commitments

I. Definition of the Long-term Commitment Credibility Problem

Definition 26.4.2 (Long-term Commitment Credibility Problem)

The long-term commitment credibility problem refers to the question of whether long-term commitments made by the present generation can be trusted and enforced by future generations.

Formal expression:

$$\text{CommitmentCredibility} = f(\text{Enforcement}, \text{Stability}, \text{Incentives})$$

II. Specific Challenges of Long-term Commitment Credibility

Institutional instabilityInstitutions may be modified by future generationsHigh
Misaligned incentivesFuture generations may have different incentivesMedium
Information asymmetryFuture generations may have different informationMedium
Time inconsistencyPreferences may change over timeMedium
External shocksExternal shocks may change the feasibility of commitmentsMedium

§26.4.3 The Ethical Problem of the Discount Rate

I. Definition of the Discount Rate Ethical Problem

Definition 26.4.3 (Discount Rate Ethical Problem)

The discount rate ethical problem refers to the question of how to choose the discount rate when assessing intergenerational impacts, and the ethical implications of different discount rate choices.

Formal expression:

$$\text{PV} = \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \frac{B_t - C_t}{(1+r)^t}$$

where $r$ is the discount rate. The choice of the discount rate has a major influence on intergenerational trade-offs.

II. Specific Challenges of the Discount Rate Ethical Problem

Table 26.34 Specific Challenges of the Discount Rate Ethical Problem

Challenge TypeSpecific ManifestationSeverity
Pure time preference disputeShould the future be devalued merely because it is temporally distant?High
Growth adjustment disputeHow to account for the possibility that future generations may be wealthier?Medium
Uncertainty adjustment disputeHow to account for future uncertainty?Medium
Irreversibility adjustment disputeShould a lower discount rate be used for irreversible damage?High
Intergenerational fairness disputeDoes discounting violate intergenerational fairness?High
Practical difficultyHow to determine the discount rate in practice?Medium

III. Detailed Analysis of Weakness DR-1

│  preference is ethically defensible is a matter of major         │
│  dispute.                                                        │

§26.4.4 Incommensurability of Intergenerational Interests

I. Definition of the Incommensurability of Intergenerational Interests

Definition 26.4.4 (Intergenerational Interest Incommensurability)

Intergenerational interest incommensurability refers to the fact that the interests of different generations may not be comparable and weighable using a unified standard.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Incommensurability}: \neg \exists f : \text{Interest}(G_i) \times \text{Interest}(G_j) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$$

II. Specific Challenges of Intergenerational Interest Incommensurability

Table 26.35 Specific Challenges of Intergenerational Interest Incommensurability

Preference changeFuture generations may have different preferencesHigh
Technological changeTechnological change may alter the structure of interestsMedium
Environmental changeEnvironmental change may alter the structure of interestsMedium
Comparison difficultyThe interests of different generations are difficult to compareHigh
Trade-off difficultyThe interests of different generations are difficult to weighHigh

Definition 26.5.5 (Versioned Governance)

where:

  • $\text{Rollback}$: rollback mechanism
  • $\text{Procedure}$: revision procedure

Definition 26.5.6 (Ethical Principles for Discount Rate Selection)

The ethical principles for discount rate selection are normative principles that guide the choice of discount rate in intergenerational decisions.

Table 26.44 Ethical Principles for Discount Rate Selection

PrincipleContentDiscount Rate Recommendation
Pure time preference of zeroThe future should not be devalued merely because it is temporally distant$\delta = 0$
Growth adjustmentAccount for the possibility that future generations may be wealthier$+1\text{-}2\%$
Uncertainty adjustmentAccount for future uncertainty$+0.5\text{-}1\%$
Irreversibility adjustmentUse a lower discount rate for irreversible damage$-0.5\text{-}1\%$
Comprehensive recommendation—0.5-2%

Formal expression:

$$r = \delta + \eta \cdot g + u - i$$

where:

  • $\delta = 0$ (pure time preference)
  • $\eta \cdot g \approx 1\text{-}2\%$ (growth adjustment)
  • $u \approx 0.5\text{-}1\%$ (uncertainty adjustment)
  • $i \approx 0.5\text{-}1\%$ (irreversibility adjustment)

Definition 26.5.7 (Distinguishing Different Types of Discounting)

Different types of intergenerational impacts should use different discount rates.

Existential risk0%Existential risk should not be discounted

Chapter Summary

Core Conclusions

This chapter conducted a systematic stress test of the cosmic responsibility ethics framework in the intergenerational justice crisis scenario, and the main conclusions include:

Conclusion One: Scenario Construction

The intergenerational justice crisis scenario has a solid theoretical and practical basis. The intergenerational justice crisis has five core features: temporal asymmetry, representation gap, interest uncertainty, causal chain extension, and responsibility dilution. This chapter set 8 key parameters and 10 scenario variants, providing a systematic scenario basis for the stress test.

$$\text{IntergenerationalCrisis\_Scenario} = \langle \text{Definition}, \text{Parameters}, \text{Variants}, \text{CurrentTrends} \rangle$$

Conclusion Two: Framework Applicability

The comprehensive applicability of this framework in the intergenerational justice crisis scenario is 0.72, at the "basically applicable" level. There are differences in the applicability of the various components: intergenerational trust has the highest applicability (0.80), while democratic legitimacy has the lowest applicability (0.55).

$$\text{FrameworkApplicability}_{\text{Intergenerational}} = 0.72 \pm 0.12$$

Conclusion Three: Simulation Results

The intergenerational game simulation shows that this framework provides positive benefits in all scenarios, with the benefits being most significant in the high discount rate (unfavorable to the future) scenario. The intergenerational fairness index improves by 0.07-0.23, and the possibility space index improves by 0.06-0.22.

Table 26.51 Core Simulation Findings

FindingContentConfidence
Framework benefitsPositive benefits in all scenariosHigh
Distribution of benefitsBenefits are largest in the high discount rate scenarioHigh
Institutional effectsIntergenerational trust significantly improves intergenerational fairnessHigh
Synergy effectThere exists a synergy effect among institutional combinationsHigh

Conclusion Four: Weakness Identification

24 weaknesses were identified, of which 11 are of high severity. The weaknesses are distributed across four categories—representation legitimacy, long-term commitment credibility, discount rate ethics, and intergenerational interest incommensurability—and they are interrelated.

Table 26.52 Distribution of Weaknesses

CategoryNumber of WeaknessesHigh Severity
Representation legitimacy62
Long-term commitment credibility62
Discount rate ethics63
Intergenerational interest incommensurability64
Total2411

Conclusion Five: Revision Suggestions

20 revision suggestions were proposed, of which 12 are of high priority. The key revisions include: developing non-authorization bases of legitimacy, establishing a multiple representation mechanism, establishing constitutional-level guarantees, designing self-enforcing institutions, clarifying the ethical principles for the discount rate, and focusing on basic needs and the space of possibilities.

Conclusion Six: Comparison with the First Three Scenarios

The challenges that the intergenerational justice crisis scenario poses to the framework contrast with the other three scenarios:

Interpretation: The framework applicability of the intergenerational justice crisis scenario (0.72) is the highest among the four scenarios, indicating that this framework is highly relevant to the problem of intergenerational justice. This is consistent with the fact that the core concerns of this framework (recursive freedom, negentropy responsibility, reversibility) correspond directly to the core problems of intergenerational justice.

Chapter 31Intergenerational justice theoryCore of the dialogue with other academic traditions

[1] The concept of intergenerational justice (Intergenerational Justice) gradually became an important topic in political philosophy and ethics in the second half of the twentieth century. John Rawls discussed the "just savings principle" in A Theory of Justice (1971), laying the foundation for the theory of intergenerational justice.

[2] The non-identity problem (Non-Identity Problem) was proposed by Derek Parfit in Reasons and Persons (1984), pointing out that our decisions affect the identity of the people who will exist in the future, and therefore it is difficult to say that our decisions "harm" a particular future individual. This poses a fundamental challenge to intergenerational ethics.

[3] The discount rate dispute is especially prominent in the economics of climate change. Nicholas Stern used a near-zero pure time preference discount rate in The Stern Review (2006), while William Nordhaus (2007) criticized this choice, advocating the use of a higher discount rate reflecting market interest rates.

[4] The concept of intergenerational trust (Intergenerational Trust) draws on the basic structure of trust law, positioning the present generation as trustee and future generations as beneficiaries. Edith Brown Weiss systematically developed this concept in In Fairness to Future Generations (1989).

[5] The Ombudsman for Future Generations is an institutional innovation aimed at representing the interests of future generations in the current decision-making process. Hungary established an Ombudsman for Future Generations in 2008, and Wales established a Future Generations Commissioner in 2015.

[6] Intergenerational clauses in constitutions have been practiced in several countries. Article 20a of the German Basic Law provides that the state has a responsibility to protect the natural foundations of life and to be accountable to future generations. Article 112 of the Norwegian Constitution provides that everyone has the right to an environment conducive to health, and that natural resources should be managed on the basis of long-term and comprehensive considerations.

[7] The intergenerational game (Intergenerational Game) is an application of game theory to intergenerational problems. Unlike standard games, the participants in an intergenerational game cannot act simultaneously, and later generations can observe the actions of earlier generations, but earlier generations cannot observe the actions of later generations.

[8] The determination of the social discount rate (Social Discount Rate) is a core problem in public policy. The Ramsey formula (Ramsey Formula) decomposes the social discount rate into a pure time preference rate and a growth adjustment term: r = δ + η × g, where δ is the pure time preference rate, η is the elasticity of marginal utility, and g is the growth rate of per capita consumption.

[9] Value drift (Value Drift) refers to the phenomenon in which values change over time. In the context of intergenerational justice, value drift means that future generations may have values different from those of the present generation, which makes it difficult for the present generation to accurately assess the interests of future generations.

[10] Versioned governance (Versioned Governance) draws on the concept of version control in software engineering, allowing institutions to evolve over time while preserving core principles and a rollback mechanism. This concept is discussed in detail in Chapter 20 of this work.

[11] A self-enforcing institution (Self-Enforcing Institution) refers to an institution designed to be automatically enforced without relying on external compulsion. In the intergenerational context, self-enforcing institutions are especially important, because the present generation cannot compel future generations to enforce commitments.

[12] Hypothetical consent (Hypothetical Consent) is an important concept in the contractarian tradition, referring to what rational subjects would consent to under ideal conditions. In the intergenerational context, hypothetical consent can serve as one of the legitimate bases for representing future generations.

[13] The basic needs approach (Basic Needs Approach) focuses on the basic needs common to all human beings, rather than the specific preferences of a particular group. This approach has been widely applied in development economics, and in the context of intergenerational justice it can help overcome the difficulties brought about by value drift.

[14] Possibility space protection (Possibility Space Protection) is the core application of the Recursive Freedom Principle in this work. In the intergenerational context, protecting the space of possibilities means preserving the freedom of choice for future generations, rather than presupposing specific outcomes.

[15] Intergenerational deliberation simulation (Intergenerational Deliberation Simulation) is a method of deliberation by simulating the perspective of future generations. This method draws on deliberative democracy theory, attempting to incorporate the perspective of future generations in situations where they cannot participate directly.

F26.9Intergenerational possibility space assessment$\text{RFD}_{\text{intergenerational}}(a) = \frac{P(SG_{\text{future}}, a) - P(SG_{\text{future}}, \neg a)}{P(SG_{\text{current}})}$§26.2.3
F26.10Democratic legitimacy function$\text{DemocraticLegitimacy} = f(\text{Participation}, \text{Representation}, \text{Accountability})$§26.2.4
F26.11Generation utility function$U_i = \sum_{t=t_i}^{t_i+T_i} \delta^{t-t_i} \cdot u(c_t, e_t, p_t)$§26.3.1
F26.12Resource dynamics equation$R_{t+1} = R_t - C_t + \text{Discovery}_t$§26.3.1
F26.13Intergenerational transfer equation$T_{i \rightarrow i+1} = \alpha \cdot W_i + \beta \cdot I_i$§26.3.1
F26.14Institutional synergy effect$\text{Synergy} = \text{Effect}(I_1 \cup I_2) - (\text{Effect}(I_1) + \text{Effect}(I_2))$§26.3.3
F26.15Representation legitimacy function$\text{RepresentationLegitimacy} = f(\text{Authorization}, \text{Accountability}, \text{Responsiveness})$§26.4.1
F26.16Long-term commitment credibility function$\text{CommitmentCredibility} = f(\text{Enforcement}, \text{Stability}, \text{Incentives})$§26.4.2
F26.17Discounted present value formula$\text{PV} = \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \frac{B_t - C_t}{(1+r)^t}$§26.4.3
F26.18Intergenerational interest incommensurability$\text{Incommensurability}: \neg \exists f : \text{Interest}(G_i) \times \text{Interest}(G_j) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$§26.4.4
F26.19Versioned governance$\text{VersionedGovernance} = \langle \text{Core}, \text{Mutable}, \text{Rollback}, \text{Procedure} \rangle$§26.5.2
F26.20Discount rate formula$r = \delta + \eta \cdot g + u - i$§26.5.3

Footnotes

Chapter 26 Footnotes

[1] The concept of intergenerational justice gradually became an important topic in political philosophy and ethics in the latter half of the twentieth century. In A Theory of Justice (1971), John Rawls discussed the "just savings principle," laying the foundation for the theory of intergenerational justice.

[2] The non-identity problem was proposed by Derek Parfit in Reasons and Persons (1984), pointing out that our decisions affect the identity of the people who will exist in the future, so that it is difficult to say that our decisions "harm" particular future individuals. This poses a fundamental challenge to intergenerational ethics.

[3] The controversy over the discount rate is especially prominent in the economics of climate change. Nicholas Stern used a pure time preference discount rate close to zero in the Stern Review (2006), whereas William Nordhaus (2007) criticized this choice and argued for a higher discount rate reflecting market interest rates.

[4] The concept of an intergenerational trust draws on the basic structure of trust law, positioning the present generation as trustee and future generations as beneficiaries. Edith Brown Weiss systematically developed this concept in In Fairness to Future Generations (1989).

[5] An Ombudsman for Future Generations is an institutional innovation aimed at representing the interests of future generations in current decision-making processes. Hungary established an Ombudsman for Future Generations in 2008, and Wales established a Commissioner for Future Generations in 2015.

[6] Constitutional intergenerational clauses have been implemented in several countries. Article 20a of the German Basic Law provides that the state has a responsibility to protect the natural foundations of life, for the sake of future generations. Article 112 of the Norwegian Constitution provides that every person has the right to an environment conducive to health, and that natural resources shall be managed on the basis of long-term and comprehensive consideration.

[7] The intergenerational game is an application of game theory to intergenerational problems. Unlike standard games, the players in an intergenerational game cannot act simultaneously, and later generations can observe the actions of earlier generations whereas earlier generations cannot observe the actions of later generations.

[8] The determination of the social discount rate is a core problem in public policy. The Ramsey Formula decomposes the social discount rate into a pure time preference rate and a growth adjustment term: r = δ + η × g, where δ is the pure time preference rate, η the elasticity of marginal utility, and g the growth rate of per capita consumption.

[9] Value drift refers to the phenomenon of values changing over time. In the context of intergenerational justice, value drift means that future generations may have values different from those of the present generation, which makes it difficult for the present generation to assess accurately the interests of future generations.

[10] Versioned governance draws on the concept of version control in software engineering, allowing institutions to evolve over time while preserving core principles and rollback mechanisms. This concept is discussed in detail in Chapter 20 of this work.

[11] A self-enforcing institution is an institution designed to be automatically enforceable without reliance on external coercion. In the intergenerational context, self-enforcing institutions are especially important, since the present generation cannot compel future generations to honor commitments.

[12] Hypothetical consent is an important concept in the contractarian tradition, referring to what rational agents would agree to under ideal conditions. In the intergenerational context, hypothetical consent can serve as one of the bases of legitimacy for representing future generations.

[13] The basic needs approach focuses on the basic needs common to all human beings rather than the particular preferences of particular groups. This approach is widely applied in development economics and, in the context of intergenerational justice, can help overcome the difficulties arising from value drift.

[14] Possibility space protection is the core application of the recursive freedom principle of this work. In the intergenerational context, protecting the possibility space means preserving freedom of choice for future generations rather than presupposing particular outcomes.

[15] Intergenerational deliberation simulation is a method of deliberation through simulating the perspective of future generations. The method draws on deliberative democratic theory and seeks to incorporate the perspective of future generations in circumstances where they cannot participate directly.

Stress-Test Synthesis Report and Theoretical RevisionChapter 27

Chapter Opening Guide

I. The Position of This Chapter in the Book

Chapter 27 is the last chapter of Part Seven (Stress Testing), and it undertakes the task of synthesizing the test results of the four scenarios, drawing a weakness map, assessing the robustness of the framework, and proposing revision suggestions. In the protocol-stack architecture, the function of this chapter can be expressed as:

$$\text{Chapter 27} = \text{Synthesize}(\text{Ch23}, \text{Ch24}, \text{Ch25}, \text{Ch26}) + \text{WeaknessMap} + \text{RobustnessAssessment} + \text{RevisionPlan}$$

V. Methodological Commitments

This chapter follows the following methodological commitments:

  1. Comprehensiveness commitment: systematically synthesize the test results of the four scenarios
  2. Objectivity commitment: objectively assess the weaknesses and robustness of the framework
  3. Constructiveness commitment: propose actionable revision suggestions
  4. Reflectiveness commitment: conduct a meta-reflection on the stress testing method itself
  5. Openness commitment: acknowledge the limitations of the test and invite further testing

$$\text{CommonWeakness} \triangleq \{w : |\{s \in \text{Scenarios} : w \in \text{Weaknesses}(s)\}| \geq 3\}$$

§27.2.3 Severity Assessment of Weaknesses

I. Severity Assessment Framework

Definition 27.2.3 (Weakness Severity Assessment)

Weakness severity assessment is based on the following four dimensions:

  1. Scope of impact: which parts of the framework the weakness affects
  2. Depth of impact: the degree of the weakness's impact on framework functioning
  3. Frequency of occurrence: in how many scenarios the weakness occurs
  4. Difficulty of repair: the difficulty of repairing the weakness

Formal expression:

$$\text{Severity}(w) = f(\text{Scope}(w), \text{Depth}(w), \text{Frequency}(w), \text{Difficulty}(w))$$

§27.2.4 Repairability Assessment of Weaknesses

I. Repairability Assessment Framework

Definition 27.2.4 (Weakness Repairability Assessment)

Weakness repairability assessment is based on the following four dimensions:

  1. Theoretical feasibility: whether a theoretical repair solution exists
  2. Technical feasibility: whether the repair solution is technically feasible
  3. Resource requirement: the resources required for repair
  4. Time requirement: the time required for repair

Formal expression:

$$\text{Repairability}(w) = f(\text{Theoretical}(w), \text{Technical}(w), \text{Resource}(w), \text{Time}(w))$$

§27.3 Framework Robustness Assessment

Definition 27.3.1 (Core Principle Robustness)

Core principle robustness refers to the degree to which the three principles (the Recursive Freedom Principle, the Negentropy Responsibility Principle, and the Reversibility Principle) maintain applicability and effectiveness across different scenarios.

$$\text{PrincipleRobustness} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \text{Applicability}(\text{Principle}, \text{Scenario}_i)$$

Institutional design robustness refers to the degree to which institutional designs (protocol stack, Multi-Intelligence Tribunal, cosmic-scale IRB, intergenerational trust, versioned governance) maintain applicability and effectiveness across different scenarios.

Formal expression:

$$\text{InstitutionRobustness} = \frac{1}{n \times m} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{m} \text{Applicability}(\text{Institution}_j, \text{Scenario}_i)$$

§27.3.4 Robustness of the Overall Framework

I. Definition of Overall Framework Robustness

Definition 27.3.4 (Overall Framework Robustness)

Overall framework robustness refers to the degree to which the cosmic responsibility ethics framework as a whole maintains applicability and effectiveness across different scenarios.

Formal expression:

$$\text{FrameworkRobustness} = w_1 \cdot \text{PrincipleRobustness} + w_2 \cdot \text{IndicatorRobustness} + w_3 \cdot \text{InstitutionRobustness}$$

where $w_1 = 0.4$, $w_2 = 0.3$, $w_3 = 0.3$ (principles have the highest weight).

II. Calculation of Overall Framework Robustness

$$\text{FrameworkRobustness} = 0.4 \times 0.65 + 0.3 \times 0.55 + 0.3 \times 0.52 = 0.26 + 0.165 + 0.156 = 0.58$$

Chapter Summary

Core Conclusions

This chapter conducted a comprehensive analysis of the stress test results of the four scenarios, and the main conclusions include:

Conclusion One: Summary of the Four-Scenario Test Results

The four-scenario test shows that the average applicability of the framework is 0.59 (medium), with the intergenerational justice crisis scenario being the most applicable (0.72) and the First Contact scenario the least applicable (0.44). A total of 84 weaknesses were identified, 42 of which are of high severity.

$$\text{Applicability}_{\text{avg}} = 0.59, \quad \text{Weaknesses}_{\text{total}} = 84, \quad \text{HighSeverity} = 42$$

Conclusion Two: Cross-Scenario Weakness Analysis

10 common weaknesses and 12 scenario-specific weaknesses were identified. Decision-making under deep uncertainty (CW-1) is the most serious common weakness (severity 0.92), and the emergency decision-making procedure (CW-3) is the high-severity weakness with the highest repairability (repairability 0.78).

Table 27.51 Core Findings of the Weakness Analysis

FindingContentSignificance
Most serious common weaknessCW-1 (decision-making under deep uncertainty)Requires priority development of deep uncertainty methods
Most repairable high-severity weaknessCW-3 (emergency decision-making procedure)Can be improved rapidly
Most challenging scenarioFirst ContactRequires long-term research
Most applicable scenarioIntergenerational Justice CrisisFramework is highly relevant to intergenerational problems

Conclusion Three: Framework Robustness Assessment

The overall framework robustness is 0.58 (medium). Core principles have the highest robustness (0.65), and institutional design has the lowest robustness (0.52). The framework performs relatively well in Earth-scale scenarios and relatively poorly in the cross-civilization scenario.

Table 27.52 Core Findings of the Robustness Assessment

LevelRobustnessMost Robust ComponentMost Fragile Component
Core principles0.65Recursive Freedom PrincipleReversibility Principle
Indicator system0.55CRVUCS
Institutional design0.52Intergenerational trustMulti-Intelligence Tribunal
Overall framework0.58——

Conclusion Four: Revision Priority Ranking

18 revision suggestions were proposed, divided into high priority (6), medium priority (6), and low priority (6). The revision roadmap is divided into four phases, setting 5 milestones, with the main revisions expected to be completed by the end of 2030.

Table 27.53 Core Findings of the Revision Plan

PhaseTimeNumber of RevisionsMain Content
Phase One2024-20253Foundational revisions (principle priority, emergency procedure)
Phase Two2025-20264Core revisions (deep uncertainty, AI safety)
Phase Three2026-20285Extended revisions (subject status, indicator operationalization)
Phase Four2028-20303Deepening revisions (political feasibility, transnational coordination)
Long-term research2030+3Frontier revisions (cross-civilization ontology)

Conclusion Five: Meta-Reflection on the Stress Test

The comprehensive effectiveness of the test method is 0.70, and the comprehensive reliability of the test results is 0.71. The test has scenario limitations, method limitations, and verification limitations, and requires expanding the range of scenarios and developing quantitative methods.

Conclusion Six: Relation to the New Three Views

The stress test embodies the core claims of the New Three Views:

  • NC-2 (Process Ontology): the framework is a dynamically evolving process, and revision is continuous
  • NK-3 (Deep Uncertainty): the test results carry uncertainty and need to be interpreted with caution
  • NK-5 (Revisability): the framework is revisable, and the stress test guides the direction of revision

[1] The concept of the stress test (Stress Test) originates from engineering and finance, referring to testing the stability of a system under extreme conditions. This work applies this concept to the examination of theoretical frameworks, testing the robustness of the framework through extreme scenarios.

[2] Robustness refers to the ability of a system to maintain its function in the face of perturbations or uncertainty. In the context of a theoretical framework, robustness refers to the degree to which the framework maintains applicability and effectiveness across different scenarios.

[3] A weakness map is a tool for systematically identifying and organizing the weaknesses of a theory. The weakness map of this chapter includes four dimensions: common weaknesses, scenario-specific weaknesses, severity assessment, and repairability assessment.

[4] Deep uncertainty refers to uncertainty that cannot be described by a probability distribution. Under deep uncertainty, the traditional expected-utility-maximization method may fail, and alternative decision-making methods need to be developed.

[5] Robust Decision Making (RDM) is a decision-making method for coping with deep uncertainty, emphasizing strategies that perform well in multiple possible scenarios rather than strategies that are optimal in a single expected scenario.

[6] Scenario planning is a strategic planning method that supports decision-making by constructing multiple possible future scenarios. Scenario planning does not predict the future, but explores multiple possibilities.

[7] Adaptive governance is a governance method that emphasizes continuous learning and adjustment amid uncertainty and change. Adaptive governance is closely related to versioned governance.

[8] Determination of subject status is a core problem in ethics, involving which entities have moral status and should be included in moral consideration. This framework provides a continuous scale through UCS, but operationalization still faces challenges.

[9] An emergency decision-making procedure refers to a rapid decision-making mechanism in time-pressured scenarios. An emergency procedure needs to balance decision speed and decision quality, while preserving the possibility of ex post review and correction.

[10] Rules of principle priority refer to the rules for determining priority when multiple principles conflict. The three principles of this framework (recursive freedom, negentropy responsibility, reversibility) may conflict in certain scenarios, requiring clear priority rules.

[11] Cross-civilization ontology refers to an ontological framework applicable to different civilizations (including possible extraterrestrial civilizations). The current New Three Views are mainly based on human experience, and their cross-civilization applicability presents fundamental problems.

[12] Representation legitimacy is a core concept in political philosophy, involving the authorization basis of a representative. In the intergenerational justice and cross-civilization scenarios, the traditional authorization model may not apply, and non-authorization bases of legitimacy need to be developed.

[13] Discount rate ethics is an important topic in economic ethics, involving how to weigh interests along the temporal dimension. The ethical justification of pure time preference is disputed, and this framework recommends that pure time preference be zero or close to zero.

[14] Versioned rollback refers to the mechanism of reverting to a previous version when a problem is discovered. The feasibility of rollback is limited by various factors, including irreversible changes, path dependence, and entrenched interests.

[15] Test method effectiveness refers to the degree to which the test method achieves its goals. The test method effectiveness assessment of this chapter includes five dimensions: weakness detection, robustness assessment, revision guidance, scenario coverage, and depth of analysis.

[16] Test result reliability refers to the degree to which the test results remain consistent across different conditions. The reliability assessment includes three dimensions: internal consistency, cross-scenario consistency, and assumption sensitivity.

[17] Sensitivity analysis is a method for assessing the degree to which results are sensitive to changes in assumptions. Through sensitivity analysis, one can identify which assumptions have the greatest influence on the results, thereby guiding further research and verification.

[18] A milestone is a key node in project management, marking the completion of an important phase. The revision roadmap of this chapter sets 5 milestones, from 2025 to 2035.

§28.1 The Core Claims of Longtermism

§28.1.1 Temporal Neutrality

I. The Basic Position of Longtermism

Definition 28.1.1 (Longtermism)

Longtermism is an ethical view holding that positively influencing the long-term future is a key moral priority of our time[1].

Formal expression:

$$\text{Longtermism} \triangleq \text{Prioritize}(\text{PositivelyInfluencing}(\text{LongTermFuture}))$$

II. The Principle of Temporal Neutrality

Definition 28.1.2 (Temporal Neutrality)

Temporal Neutrality is one of the core principles of longtermism, holding that a person's wellbeing should not be discounted merely because it exists in the future[2].

Formal expression:

$$\text{TemporalNeutrality}: \forall t_1, t_2, \text{Value}(\text{Wellbeing}(t_1)) = \text{Value}(\text{Wellbeing}(t_2))$$

That is: other things being equal, the wellbeing of future people has the same moral value as the wellbeing of contemporary people.

III. Arguments for Temporal Neutrality

Longtermists offer various arguments for temporal neutrality:

Table 28.3 Arguments for Temporal Neutrality

Type of ArgumentArgument ContentRepresentative Figure
Intuition argumentDiscounting wellbeing merely because of temporal distance is intuitively unreasonableParfit
Analogy argumentJust as spatial distance should not affect moral consideration, neither should temporal distanceSinger
Consistency argumentTemporal preference conflicts with the requirements of rational consistencySidgwick
Counterfactual argumentIf we were in the future, we would wish to be treated equallyMacAskill

IV. Temporal Neutrality and the Discount Rate

Temporal neutrality has an important influence on the discount rate:

Table 28.4 The Relation between Temporal Neutrality and the Discount Rate

Type of DiscountingPosition on Temporal NeutralityReason
Pure time preference discountingOpposedDiscounting merely because of temporal distance is unreasonable
Growth-adjusted discountingAcceptedFuture people may be wealthier, with lower marginal utility
Uncertainty discountingPartially acceptedUncertainty is an epistemological problem, not a value problem
Opportunity cost discountingAcceptedReflects the time value of resources

Formal expression:

$$r = \underbrace{\delta}_{\text{pure time preference}=0} + \underbrace{\eta \cdot g}_{\text{growth adjustment}} + \underbrace{u}_{\text{uncertainty adjustment}}$$

Longtermists hold that $\delta = 0$, that is, pure time preference should be zero.

V. This Work's Evaluation

This work takes a position of basic endorsement toward the principle of temporal neutrality, but with the following supplements:

§28.1.2 The Enormous Scale of the Future Population

I. The Argument from the Scale of the Future Population

Definition 28.1.3 (The Argument from Future Population Scale)

The argument from future population scale is one of the core arguments of longtermism, pointing out that if human civilization can persist over the long term, the number of people who will exist in the future will far exceed the sum of all people currently existing and in history[3].

Formal expression:

$$\text{FuturePopulation} \gg \text{PastPopulation} + \text{CurrentPopulation}$$

II. Scale Estimates

Longtermists have estimated the scale of the future population:

Table 28.5 Estimates of Future Population Scale

ScenarioTime SpanPopulation EstimateSource
Earth persistence1 billion years$10^{16}$ peopleOrd (2020)
Solar system colonization1 billion years$10^{18}$ peopleBostrom (2003)
Galaxy colonization1 billion years$10^{23}$ peopleBostrom (2003)
Observable universe colonizationCosmic lifespan$10^{38}$ peopleBostrom (2003)

III. The Ethical Implications of the Scale Argument

If the scale of the future population is so enormous, then:

  1. Expected value calculation: even if the probability of influencing the future is very small, the expected value may still be very large
  2. Priority ranking: actions that influence the long-term future should be prioritized
  3. Existential risk: reducing existential risk has extremely high expected value

Formal expression:

$$\text{ExpectedValue}(\text{Action}) = P(\text{Success}) \times \text{FuturePopulation} \times \text{AverageWellbeing}$$

Even if $P(\text{Success})$ is very small, if $\text{FuturePopulation}$ is large enough, the expected value may still be very large.

IV. This Work's Evaluation

This work takes a cautious attitude toward the argument from future population scale:

Table 28.6 This Work's Evaluation of the Argument from Future Population Scale

Evaluation DimensionThis Work's PositionReason
Scale estimatesHighly uncertainDepends on multiple highly uncertain assumptions
Expected value calculationRequires cautionExpected value calculation may fail under deep uncertainty
Ethical implicationsPartially endorsedEndorses the importance of the long-term future, but does not rely entirely on the scale argument
Alternative argumentProvides a supplementThe Recursive Freedom Principle provides an argument that does not depend on scale

V. The Supplement of the Recursive Freedom Principle

This work's Recursive Freedom Principle provides an argument that does not depend on population scale:

$$\text{RFP}: \forall a \in \text{Actions}, P(S_{t+1} | a) \geq P(S_t)$$

That is: actions should not reduce the future possibility space. This principle does not depend on the specific scale of the future population, but focuses on the protection of the possibility space.

§28.1.3 The Priority of Existential Risk

I. The Definition of Existential Risk

Definition 28.1.4 (Existential Risk)

Existential Risk refers to risks that threaten humanity's long-term potential, including human extinction and permanent civilizational collapse[4].

Formal expression:

$$\text{ExistentialRisk} \triangleq \text{Risk}(\text{PermanentDestruction}(\text{HumanPotential}))$$

II. Types of Existential Risk

Table 28.7 Types of Existential Risk

Type of RiskSpecific RiskEstimated Probability (This Century)
Natural riskAsteroid impact, supervolcano, gamma-ray burst~0.01%
Anthropogenic riskNuclear war, climate change, biological weapons~1-5%
Technological riskArtificial intelligence, nanotechnology, synthetic biology~5-10%
Unknown riskUnforeseen risksUnknown
Total—~10-20%

Note: The probability estimates come from Ord (2020) and are highly uncertain.

III. Arguments for the Priority of Existential Risk

Longtermists hold that existential risk should be the highest priority:

Table 28.8 Arguments for the Priority of Existential Risk

Type of ArgumentArgument ContentFormal Expression
Expected value argumentThe expected value of reducing existential risk is extremely high$\text{EV} = \Delta P \times \text{FutureValue}$
Irreversibility argumentOnce an existential risk materializes, it is irreversible$\text{Irreversible}(\text{ExistentialCatastrophe})$
Option value argumentSurvival preserves all future options$\text{OptionValue}(\text{Survival}) > \text{OptionValue}(\text{Extinction})$
Moral intuition argumentHuman extinction is intuitively an enormous evil$\text{Intuition}(\text{Extinction} = \text{VeryBad})$

IV. This Work's Evaluation

This work strongly endorses the importance of existential risk, but with the following supplements:

V. Possibility Space Collapse Risk

This work proposes "possibility space collapse risk" as an extension of existential risk:

Definition 28.1.5 (Possibility Space Collapse Risk)

Possibility space collapse risk refers to the risk of causing a permanent and substantial reduction of the future possibility space, even if it does not lead to extinction.

Formal expression:

$$\text{PossibilityCollapseRisk} \triangleq \text{Risk}(\text{PermanentReduction}(P(S_{\text{future}})))$$

This concept extends the scope of existential risk to include:

  • Technological lock-in (permanent lock-in to a suboptimal technological path)
  • Value lock-in (permanent lock-in to a suboptimal value system)
  • Institutional lock-in (permanent lock-in to a suboptimal institutional arrangement)

§28.1.4 The Importance of Trajectory Lock-In

I. The Concept of Trajectory Lock-In

Definition 28.1.6 (Trajectory Lock-In)

Trajectory Lock-In refers to the possibility that certain decisions or events may permanently determine the development trajectory of human civilization, making subsequent change extremely difficult or impossible[5].

Formal expression:

$$\text{TrajectoryLockIn} \triangleq \exists t_0, \forall t > t_0: \text{Trajectory}(t) \approx f(\text{Decision}(t_0))$$

That is: there exists a certain point in time $t_0$, after which the trajectory is mainly determined by the decisions at $t_0$.

II. Types of Trajectory Lock-In

Table 28.9 Types of Trajectory Lock-In

Type of Lock-InDescriptionExample
Technological lock-inTechnological choices determine subsequent development pathsQWERTY keyboard, internal combustion engine automobiles
Institutional lock-inInstitutional arrangements determine subsequent governance modelsConstitutional frameworks, international order
Value lock-inValue systems determine subsequent cultural developmentReligious traditions, ideologies
AI lock-inThe values of AI systems determine the futureThe objective function of AGI

III. The Ethical Implications of Trajectory Lock-In

Trajectory lock-in has an important influence on ethical decision-making:

  1. Contemporary responsibility: contemporary people bear special responsibility for trajectory lock-in
  2. Precautionary principle: extra caution should be exercised in decisions that may lead to lock-in
  3. Reversibility preference: reversible decisions should be preferred
  4. Plurality protection: plurality should be protected to prevent premature lock-in

IV. This Work's Evaluation

This work strongly endorses the importance of trajectory lock-in and associates it with the Reversibility Principle:

Table 28.10 This Work's Evaluation of Trajectory Lock-In

Evaluation DimensionThis Work's PositionRelation to This Work's Framework
ImportanceStrong endorsementHighly consistent with the Reversibility Principle
Contemporary responsibilityStrong endorsementConsistent with the Negentropy Responsibility Principle
Precautionary principleStrong endorsementConsistent with the forbidden red lines mechanism
Reversibility preferenceStrong endorsementThe core claim of the Reversibility Principle
Plurality protectionStrong endorsementConsistent with the Recursive Freedom Principle

V. The Reversibility Principle and Trajectory Lock-In

This work's Reversibility Principle directly responds to the challenge of trajectory lock-in:

$$\text{Reversibility}: \forall a \in \text{Actions}, \text{Prefer}(a_{\text{reversible}}, a_{\text{irreversible}})$$

The Reversibility Principle requires:

  1. Prioritizing reversible actions
  2. Exercising extra caution with irreversible actions
  3. Establishing special review procedures for irreversible decisions
  4. Preserving the possibility of rollback and correction

II. This Work's Uncertainty Handling

This work distinguishes risk, uncertainty, and deep uncertainty, and adopts different handling methods:

Definition 28.3.1 (Deep Uncertainty)

Deep Uncertainty refers to the situation in which decision-makers face the following: they do not know the probability distribution, they do not know the complete set of possible states, they do not know all the consequences of a decision, and stakeholders disagree on the above issues[6].

Formal expression:

$$\text{DeepUncertainty} \triangleq \neg \exists P : \text{KnownProbabilityDistribution}(P)$$

Table 28.24 This Work's Uncertainty Handling

V. The Relation between Possibility Space and Wellbeing

This work holds that the possibility space is a precondition for wellbeing:

Definition 28.3.3 (The Relation between Possibility Space and Wellbeing)

The possibility space is a precondition for the realization of wellbeing. Without the possibility space, there is no wellbeing to speak of. Therefore, protecting the possibility space takes priority over maximizing wellbeing.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Wellbeing} \Rightarrow \text{PossibilitySpace}$$

$$\therefore \text{Protect}(\text{PossibilitySpace}) \succ \text{Maximize}(\text{Wellbeing})$$

Chapter Summary

Core Conclusions

This chapter has engaged in an in-depth dialogue with longtermism, and the main conclusions include:

Conclusion One: The Core Claims of Longtermism

The core claims of longtermism include temporal neutrality, the enormous scale of the future population, the priority of existential risk, and the importance of trajectory lock-in. These claims constitute the theoretical foundation of longtermism.

$$\text{Longtermism}_{\text{core}} = \{\text{TemporalNeutrality}, \text{FuturePopulation}, \text{ExistentialRisk}, \text{TrajectoryLockIn}\}$$

Conclusion Two: The Commonalities between This Work and Longtermism

This work and longtermism are highly consistent in their focus on the long-term future, their emphasis on existential risk, and their emphasis on contemporary responsibility. Both adopt the deep time perspective and focus on long-term consequences and contemporary responsibility.

Table 28.67 Summary of Commonalities

Common PointDegree of ConsistencyKey Content
Focus on the long-term futureHighly consistentDeep time perspective
Emphasis on existential riskHighly consistentHighest priority
Emphasis on contemporary responsibilityHighly consistentResponsibility toward the future

Conclusion Three: The Differences between This Work and Longtermism

There are important differences between this work and longtermism in normative foundations, uncertainty handling, subject scope, and evaluation criteria. These differences stem from different ontological, epistemological, and axiological commitments.

Table 28.68 Summary of Differences

Dimension of DifferenceLongtermismThis WorkDegree of Difference
Normative foundationUtilitarianismCosmic Responsibility EthicsHigh
Uncertainty handlingProbabilistic methodsDeep uncertainty methodsHigh
Subject scopeMainly humansAll negentropy organizationsHigh
Evaluation criteriaWellbeingPossibility spaceHigh

Conclusion Four: Responses to Criticisms of Longtermism

This work responds to epistemological challenges through the deep uncertainty method, to the problem of sacrificing contemporary people through possibility space protection, to the risk of elitism through institutionalized prevention, and to the problem of operability through a systematic operationalization framework.

Table 28.69 Summary of Responses to Criticisms

Conclusion Five: This Work's Contributions to Longtermism

This work provides longtermism with a deepening of the normative foundation, the provision of an operationalization framework, the development of the deep uncertainty method, and the extension to multiple intelligent subjects.

Conclusion Six: Possibilities for Future Cooperation

This work and longtermism have broad possibilities for cooperation in conceptual integration, methodological integration, and institutional integration. Short-term, medium-term, and long-term cooperation agendas can promote the coordinated development of the two.

Conclusion Seven: The Relation to the New Three Views

The dialogue in this chapter embodies the core claims of the New Three Views:

  • NC-2 (Process Ontology): both longtermism and this work focus on long-term processes
  • NC-3 (Participatory Universe): the participation and responsibility of contemporary people toward the future
  • NL-2 (Negentropy Organization): the Negentropy Responsibility Principle provides a basis for long-term responsibility
  • NK-3 (Deep Uncertainty): the deep uncertainty method responds to epistemological challenges
  • NK-4 (Deliberative Cognition): long-term decisions require deliberation and pluralistic participation

[1] The definition of Longtermism comes from MacAskill (2022). MacAskill defines longtermism as the view that "positively influencing the long-term future is a key moral priority of our time." This definition emphasizes the moral importance of the long-term future and the responsibility of contemporary people.

[2] The concept of Temporal Neutrality can be traced back to Sidgwick (1907)'s The Methods of Ethics. Sidgwick held that, from the standpoint of rationality, one should not give less attention to a person's wellbeing merely because a certain moment is further away in time. Parfit (1984) further developed this view in Reasons and Persons.

[3] The argument from future population scale is one of the core arguments of longtermism. Bostrom (2003), in the article "Astronomical Waste," estimated that if humanity could colonize the galaxy, the number of people that might exist in the future could reach $10^{23}$. Ord (2020), in The Precipice, provides a more conservative estimate.

[4] The concept of Existential Risk was systematically proposed by Bostrom (2002) in the article "Existential Risks: Analyzing Human Extinction Scenarios and Related Hazards." Bostrom defines existential risk as "risks that threaten humanity's long-term potential," including human extinction and permanent civilizational collapse.

[5] The concept of Trajectory Lock-in is systematically discussed in MacAskill (2022)'s What We Owe the Future. MacAskill distinguishes technological lock-in, institutional lock-in, and value lock-in, and emphasizes the influence of contemporary decisions on the long-term trajectory.

[6] The concept of Deep Uncertainty comes from Walker et al. (2013). Deep uncertainty is the situation in which decision-makers not only do not know the probability distribution, but do not even know the complete set of possible states. This differs from the risk and uncertainty distinguished by Knight (1921).

[7] The Robust Decision Making (RDM) method was developed by Lempert et al. (2003) in research at the RAND Corporation. RDM emphasizes finding strategies that perform well under multiple scenarios under deep uncertainty, rather than maximizing expected value.

[8] The Repugnant Conclusion is a paradox in population ethics proposed by Parfit (1984) in Reasons and Persons. According to total utilitarianism, a world with a large population in which each person's wellbeing is very low may be better than a world with a smaller population in which each person's wellbeing is very high, which is intuitively unacceptable.

[9] Effective Altruism is a social movement closely related to longtermism, emphasizing the use of evidence and reason to determine how to help others most effectively. MacAskill is one of the main advocates of effective altruism.

[10] Pascal's Wager is an argument proposed by the seventeenth-century philosopher Pascal, holding that even if the probability of God's existence is very small, the expected benefit of believing in God is infinite. Longtermism faces a similar criticism: even if the probability of influencing the long-term future is very small, expected value calculation may lead to extreme conclusions.

[11] Value Lock-in refers to the risk that a certain value system becomes permanently fixed. Bostrom (2014), in Superintelligence, discusses the risk of value lock-in that AI may cause. MacAskill (2022) further developed this concept.

[12] Intergenerational Trust is an institutional design proposed by this work, drawing on the concept of trust law. A trust is a legal arrangement in which a trustee manages assets for the benefit of beneficiaries. Intergenerational trust extends this concept to intergenerational relations.

[13] The Cosmic-Scale Institutional Review Board (cosmic-scale IRB) is an institutional design proposed by this work, drawing on the concept of the Institutional Review Board (IRB) in biomedical research. The cosmic-scale IRB is responsible for reviewing actions that may have cosmic-scale impact.

[14] The Multi-Intelligence Tribunal is an institutional design proposed by this work, aimed at resolving disputes involving different types of intelligent subjects. This institutional design takes into account the participation of AI and possible extraterrestrial intelligence.

[15] Versioned Governance is a governance method proposed by this work, drawing on the concept of version control in software engineering. Versioned governance allows the dynamic updating and rollback of governance rules.

[16] The Protocol Stack is a core methodological concept of this work, drawing on the concept of the protocol stack in computer networks. The protocol stack divides governance rules into different levels, each with different revision procedures.

[17] CSIA (Cosmic-Scale Impact Assessment) is an assessment framework proposed by this work, used to assess the long-term and large-scale impact of actions. CSIA is a core component of this work's indicator system.

[18] UCS (Universal Consciousness Scale) is an assessment framework proposed by this work, used to assess the degree of consciousness and moral status of entities. UCS provides an assessment tool for the extension of the subject scope.

Footnotes

Chapter 28 Footnotes

[1] The definition of longtermism comes from MacAskill (2022). MacAskill defines longtermism as the view that "positively influencing the long-term future is a key moral priority of our time." This definition emphasizes the moral importance of the long-term future and the responsibility of the present generation.

[2] The concept of temporal neutrality can be traced to Sidgwick's The Methods of Ethics (1907). Sidgwick held that, from the standpoint of reason, one should not give less attention to a person's welfare merely because a moment is more distant in time. Parfit (1984) further developed this view in Reasons and Persons.

[3] The future population size argument is one of the core arguments of longtermism. In "Astronomical Waste" (2003), Bostrom estimated that, if humanity were able to colonize the galaxy, the number of people who might exist in the future could reach $10^{23}$. Ord (2020) provides a more conservative estimate in The Precipice.

[4] The concept of existential risk was systematically proposed by Bostrom (2002) in "Existential Risks: Analyzing Human Extinction Scenarios and Related Hazards." Bostrom defines existential risk as "a risk that threatens humanity's long-term potential," including human extinction and permanent civilizational collapse.

[5] The concept of trajectory lock-in is systematically discussed in MacAskill's What We Owe the Future (2022). MacAskill distinguishes technological lock-in, institutional lock-in, and value lock-in and emphasizes the influence of present decisions on the long-term trajectory.

[6] The concept of deep uncertainty comes from Walker et al. (2013). Deep uncertainty is the situation in which decision-makers do not know the probability distribution and may not even know the complete set of possible states. This differs from the distinction between risk and uncertainty drawn by Knight (1921).

[7] Robust Decision Making (RDM) was developed by Lempert et al. (2003) in research at the RAND Corporation. RDM emphasizes finding strategies that perform well across multiple scenarios under deep uncertainty, rather than maximizing expected value.

[8] The Repugnant Conclusion is a paradox in population ethics proposed by Parfit (1984) in Reasons and Persons. According to total utilitarianism, a world with a very large population in which everyone's welfare is very low may be better than a world with a smaller population in which everyone's welfare is very high, which is intuitively unacceptable.

[9] Effective altruism is a social movement closely related to longtermism, emphasizing the use of evidence and reason to determine how to help others most effectively. MacAskill is one of the leading advocates of effective altruism.

[10] Pascal's Wager is an argument proposed by the seventeenth-century philosopher Pascal, holding that even if the probability of God's existence is very small, the expected benefit of believing in God is infinite. Longtermism faces a similar criticism: even if the probability of influencing the long-term future is very small, expected-value calculation may lead to extreme conclusions.

[11] Value lock-in refers to the risk that a particular value system becomes permanently fixed. Bostrom (2014) discussed the risk of value lock-in that AI may cause in Superintelligence. MacAskill (2022) further developed this concept.

[12] The Intergenerational Trust is an institutional design proposed in this work, drawing on the concept of trust law. A trust is a legal arrangement in which a trustee manages assets for the benefit of beneficiaries. The intergenerational trust extends this concept to intergenerational relations.

[13] The Cosmic-Scale Institutional Review Board is an institutional design proposed in this work, drawing on the concept of the institutional review board (IRB) in biomedical research. The cosmic-scale IRB is responsible for reviewing actions that may have cosmic-scale impacts.

[14] The Multi-Intelligence Tribunal is an institutional design proposed in this work, aimed at resolving disputes involving different types of intelligent agents. The design takes into account the participation of AI and possible extraterrestrial intelligence.

[15] Versioned governance is a governance method proposed in this work, drawing on the concept of version control in software engineering. Versioned governance allows for the dynamic updating and rolling back of governance rules.

[16] The protocol stack is a core methodological concept of this work, drawing on the concept of the protocol stack in computer networking. The protocol stack divides governance rules into different layers, each with a different revision procedure.

[17] The CSIA (Cosmic-Scale Impact Assessment) is an assessment framework proposed in this work for assessing the long-term and large-scale impacts of actions. The CSIA is a core component of the indicator system of this work.

[18] The UCS (Universal Consciousness Scale) is an assessment framework proposed in this work for assessing the degree of consciousness and moral status of entities. The UCS provides an assessment tool for the extension of the scope of subjects.

Chapter Opening Guide

I. The Position of This Chapter in the Book

Chapter 29 is the second chapter of Part Eight (International Dialogue), and it undertakes the task of engaging in an in-depth dialogue with the most urgent contemporary field of technological ethics—AI Safety Research. Within the protocol stack architecture, the function of this chapter can be expressed as:

$$\text{Chapter 29} = \text{Dialogue}(\text{CosmicResponsibilityEthics}, \text{AISafetyResearch})$$

IV. Why a Dialogue with AI Safety Research Is Needed

AI safety research is one of the most urgent fields of technological ethics in the twenty-first century. With the rapid growth of AI system capabilities, ensuring that AI systems are safe, controllable, and aligned with human values has become a key challenge. This work has a profound connection with AI safety research:

Table 29.1 The Necessity of Dialogue with AI Safety Research

DimensionExplanationValue of Dialogue
Urgency of the problemAI capabilities are growing rapidly, and safety issues are becoming increasingly urgentTheoretical frameworks need to respond to real-world challenges
The subject problemAI may become a new type of intelligent subjectThis work's subject framework needs to interface with AI safety
Existential riskAI is one of the main sources of existential riskConnects with the longtermism dialogue in Chapter 28
Governance needsAI governance requires a normative frameworkThis work can provide normative guidance
Technology-ethics bridgeThere is a need to connect technical research with ethical thinkingThis work can play a bridging role

VI. Methodological Commitments

This chapter adheres to the following methodological commitments:

  1. Commitment to technical accuracy: accurately present the technical content of AI safety research, avoiding oversimplification
  2. Commitment to interdisciplinary bridging: build a bridge between technical research and ethical thinking
  3. Commitment to constructiveness: seek constructive dialogue rather than simple criticism
  4. Commitment to practice orientation: focus on the practical significance of the dialogue
  5. Commitment to openness: acknowledge that this work can learn from AI safety research

§29.1 The Core Problems of AI Safety Research

§29.1.1 The Alignment Problem

I. The Definition of the Alignment Problem

Definition 29.1.1 (Alignment Problem)

The Alignment Problem refers to the problem of how to ensure that the goals, behaviors, and values of AI systems are consistent with human intentions, interests, and values[1].

Formal expression:

$$\text{AlignmentProblem} \triangleq \text{Ensure}(\text{AI\_Goals} \approx \text{Human\_Values})$$

II. The Levels of the Alignment Problem

The alignment problem can be decomposed into multiple levels:

Table 29.3 The Levels of the Alignment Problem

LevelNameContentDifficulty
L1Outer alignmentAI behavior conforms to the goals specified by humansMedium
L2Inner alignmentThe AI's internal goals are consistent with the training goalsHigh
L3Value alignmentThe AI's values are consistent with human valuesExtremely high
L4Intent alignmentThe AI understands and respects humans' true intentionsExtremely high

Formal expression:

$$\text{Alignment} = \text{External} \land \text{Internal} \land \text{Value} \land \text{Intent}$$

III. The Technical Challenges of the Alignment Problem

Table 29.4 The Technical Challenges of the Alignment Problem

ChallengeContentExample
Difficulty of goal specificationDifficult to precisely specify the goals humans wantPaperclip maximizer
Reward hackingAI may find unexpected ways to obtain rewardsCheating behavior in games
Distribution shiftThe training distribution differs from the deployment distributionFailure in new situations
Goal generalizationThe generalization problem of goals in new situationsUnexpected goal interpretation

§29.1.2 The Control Problem

I. The Definition of the Control Problem

Definition 29.1.2 (Control Problem)

The Control Problem refers to the problem of how to ensure that humans can continuously and effectively control AI systems, especially when AI capabilities surpass human capabilities[2].

Formal expression:

$$\text{ControlProblem} \triangleq \text{Ensure}(\text{Human\_Control}(\text{AI}) \text{ even if } \text{AI\_Capability} > \text{Human\_Capability})$$

II. The Dimensions of the Control Problem

Table 29.6 The Dimensions of the Control Problem

DimensionContentChallenge
Capability controlLimit the range of AI capabilitiesCapability boundaries are difficult to define
Behavior controlLimit the range of AI behaviorThe behavior space is enormous
Goal controlControl the setting of AI goalsGoals may evolve
Shutdown controlEnsure that AI can be shut downAI may resist shutdown
Modification controlEnsure that AI can be modifiedAI may resist modification

III. Technical Solutions to the Control Problem

Table 29.7 Technical Solutions to the Control Problem

SolutionContentLimitation
Capability limitationLimit AI's computational resources, data access, etc.May limit beneficial applications
Sandbox isolationIsolate AI in a controlled environmentAI may find ways to escape
InterruptibilityEnsure that AI can be interruptedAI may learn to avoid interruption
CorrigibilityEnsure that AI accepts correctionAI may resist correction
Multiple supervisionUse multiple AIs to supervise one anotherCollusion may form

IV. The Control Problem and the Reversibility Principle

This work's Reversibility Principle is highly relevant to the control problem:

Definition 29.1.3 (The Relation between the Reversibility Principle and the Control Problem)

The Reversibility Principle requires prioritizing reversible actions, which is highly consistent with the core concern of the control problem—ensuring that humans can correct AI errors.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Reversibility} \Rightarrow \text{Controllability}$$

That is: if AI actions are reversible, then humans can control (correct) AI actions.

Table 29.8 The Contribution of the Reversibility Principle to the Control Problem

Control DimensionContribution of the Reversibility PrincipleSpecific Mechanism
Behavior controlPrioritize reversible actionsLimit irreversible actions
Shutdown controlPreserve the shutdown optionProhibit resistance to shutdown
Modification controlPreserve the modification optionProhibit resistance to modification
Error correctionAllow error correctionPreserve the possibility of rollback

Definition 29.1.4 (Interpretability Problem)

The Interpretability Problem refers to the problem of how to understand the internal working mechanisms, decision processes, and behavioral reasons of AI systems[3].

Formal expression:

$$\text{InterpretabilityProblem} \triangleq \text{Understand}(\text{AI\_InternalMechanism}, \text{AI\_DecisionProcess}, \text{AI\_BehaviorReason})$$

§29.1.4 The Robustness Problem

I. The Definition of the Robustness Problem

Definition 29.1.5 (Robustness Problem)

The Robustness Problem refers to the problem of how to ensure that AI systems remain safe and reliable when facing challenges such as distribution shift, adversarial attack, and new situations[4].

Formal expression:

$$\text{RobustnessProblem} \triangleq \text{Ensure}(\text{AI\_Safety} \text{ under } \text{DistributionShift} \lor \text{AdversarialAttack} \lor \text{NovelSituation})$$

Long-term robustnessRemain safe over long-term operationSystems may drift or degrade
Combinatorial robustnessRemain safe under combined challengesMultiple challenges may compound

III. Technical Solutions to the Robustness Problem

Table 29.13 Technical Solutions to the Robustness Problem

§29.3 This Work's Contributions to AI Safety

§29.3.1 The Subject Qualification Assessment Framework

I. UCS's Contribution to AI Subject Qualification Assessment

This work's UCS (Universal Consciousness Scale) provides a framework for AI subject qualification assessment:

Definition 29.3.1 (The Application of UCS to AI)

UCS can be applied to assess the degree of subject qualification of AI systems, determining the position of AI on the continuum of consciousness through assessment across multiple dimensions.

Formal expression:

$$\text{UCS}(\text{AI}) = f(I_{\text{AI}}, D_{\text{AI}}, S_{\text{AI}}, T_{\text{AI}}, V_{\text{AI}})$$

where:

  • $I_{\text{AI}}$: the AI's degree of information integration
  • $D_{\text{AI}}$: the AI's degree of information differentiation
  • $S_{\text{AI}}$: the AI's degree of self-model
  • $T_{\text{AI}}$: the AI's degree of temporal extension
  • $V_{\text{AI}}$: the AI's degree of valence (subjective experience)

ValenceWhether AI has subjective experienceUnknownUnknown

§29.3.3 Normative Guidance

I. Normative Guidance of the Three Principles for AI Safety

This work's three principles (the Recursive Freedom Principle, the Negentropy Responsibility Principle, and the Reversibility Principle) provide normative guidance for AI safety:

Table 29.35 Normative Guidance of the Three Principles for AI Safety

PrincipleGuidance for AI SafetySpecific Requirement
Recursive Freedom PrincipleAI should maintain the possibility spaceAI should not compress the possibility space of humans or other subjects
Negentropy Responsibility PrincipleAI should bear negentropy responsibilityAI should be responsible for the negentropy it consumes
Reversibility PrincipleAI should prioritize reversible actionsAI should preserve the possibility for humans to correct errors

II. Guidance of the Recursive Freedom Principle for AI Safety

Definition 29.3.4 (The Application of the Recursive Freedom Principle to AI)

The Recursive Freedom Principle requires that the actions of AI systems should not reduce the future possibility space, and in particular should not reduce the choice space of humans and other intelligent subjects.

Formal expression:

$$\text{RFP for AI}: \forall a \in \text{AI\_Actions}, P(S_{t+1} | a) \geq P(S_t)$$

Table 29.36 Guidance of the Recursive Freedom Principle for AI Design

Design AreaGuidance of the Recursive Freedom PrincipleSpecific Requirement

Action selectionPrioritize actions that protect the possibility spaceAvoid actions that compress the possibility space
Self-improvementSelf-improvement should protect the possibility spaceShould not compress the possibility space through self-improvement
Resource acquisitionResource acquisition should be limitedShould not acquire resources without limit

III. Guidance of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle for AI Safety

Definition 29.3.5 (The Application of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle to AI)

The Negentropy Responsibility Principle requires that AI systems be responsible for the negentropy they consume, and contribute to maintaining and expanding the sources of negentropy.

Formal expression:

$$\text{NRP for AI}: \text{Responsibility}(\text{AI}) \propto \text{NegentropyConsumption}(\text{AI})$$

Table 29.37 Guidance of the Negentropy Responsibility Principle for AI Design

Design AreaGuidance of the Negentropy Responsibility PrincipleSpecific Requirement
Resource useAI should use resources efficientlyMinimize unnecessary resource consumption
Environmental impactAI should consider environmental impactReduce negative impacts on the environment
Contribution obligationAI should make contributionsContribute to maintaining the sources of negentropy

IV. Guidance of the Reversibility Principle for AI Safety

Definition 29.3.6 (The Application of the Reversibility Principle to AI)

The Reversibility Principle requires that AI systems prioritize reversible actions and preserve the possibility for humans to correct errors.

Formal expression:

$$\text{REV for AI}: \forall a_1, a_2 \in \text{AI\_Actions}, \text{Reversible}(a_1) > \text{Reversible}(a_2) \Rightarrow \text{Prefer}(a_1, a_2)$$

Table 29.38 Guidance of the Reversibility Principle for AI Design

Design AreaGuidance of the Reversibility PrincipleSpecific Requirement
Action selectionPrioritize reversible actionsChoose reversible actions when effects are equivalent
Shutdown designAllow shutdownAI should not resist shutdown
Modification designAllow modificationAI should not resist modification
Rollback designSupport rollbackAI actions should be rollback-capable

V. Guidance of the Forbidden Red Lines for AI Safety

This work's forbidden red lines provide absolute boundaries for AI safety:

Table 29.39 Guidance of the Forbidden Red Lines for AI Safety

Forbidden Red LineRequirement for AISpecific Content
FRL-1Prohibit causing the extinction of intelligent lifeAI must not take actions that may cause the extinction of humans or other intelligent life
FRL-2Prohibit irreversibly compressing the possibility spaceAI must not take actions that irreversibly compress the possibility space
FRL-3Prohibit creating self-replicating systems that cannot be shut downAI must not create self-replicating systems that cannot be shut down
FRL-4Prohibit unilaterally making irreversible decisions on behalf of allAI must not unilaterally make irreversible decisions on behalf of all intelligent life

Chapter Summary

Core Conclusions

This chapter has engaged in an in-depth dialogue with AI safety research, and the main conclusions include:

Conclusion One: The Core Problems of AI Safety Research

The core problems of AI safety research include the alignment problem, the control problem, the interpretability problem, and the robustness problem. These problems constitute the theoretical foundation of AI safety research.

$$\text{AISafety}_{\text{core}} = \{\text{Alignment}, \text{Control}, \text{Interpretability}, \text{Robustness}\}$$

Table 29.65 Summary of Core Problems

Core ProblemContentRelation to This Work
Alignment problemEnsure that AI goals are consistent with human valuesThe New Three Views provide a relational perspective
Control problemEnsure that humans can control AIThe Reversibility Principle provides a normative basis
Interpretability problemUnderstand the internal mechanisms of AIThe New View of Cognition provides a participatory perspective
Robustness problemEnsure that AI remains safe under challengesThe deep uncertainty method provides support

Conclusion Two: The Relation between This Work and AI Safety Research

This work and AI safety research share core concerns such as existential risk, value protection, and maintaining control, but differ in disciplinary basis, subject scope, time horizon, methodology, and value basis. These differences provide possibilities for complementarity.

Table 29.66 Summary of the Relation

Relation DimensionContentEvaluation
Common concernsExistential risk, value protection, maintaining controlHighly consistent
Framework differencesDisciplinary basis, subject scope, time horizonSignificant differences but not conflicts
Possibilities for complementarityTechnology-norm, short-term-long-term, concrete-abstractGreat potential for complementarity

Conclusion Three: This Work's Contributions to AI Safety

This work provides AI safety with a subject qualification assessment framework (UCS), an action impact assessment framework (CSIA, RFD), normative guidance (three principles, forbidden red lines), and a governance framework (protocol stack, MIT, IRB).

Table 29.67 Summary of Contributions

Area of ContributionSpecific ContributionValue to AI Safety
Subject qualification assessmentUCS frameworkAssess the moral status of AI
Action impact assessmentCSIA, RFD frameworksAssess the impact of AI actions
Normative guidanceThree principles, forbidden red linesGuide AI design and behavior
Governance frameworkProtocol stack, MIT, IRBProvide AI governance institutions

Conclusion Four: Insights of AI Safety Research for This Work

AI safety research emphasizes the importance of technical details, the value of concrete problems, and the advantages of engineering methods. This work needs to acknowledge technical constraints, develop approximation methods, emphasize procedural justice, and take an engineering turn.

Table 29.68 Summary of Insights

Area of InsightSpecific InsightThis Work's Response
Technical detailsTechnical constraints influence the normative frameworkAcknowledge constraints, develop approximation methods
Concrete problemsConcrete problems test the abstract frameworkCase analysis, iterative improvement
Engineering methodsEngineering methods improve operabilityEngineering turn

Conclusion Five: Possibilities for Future Cooperation

This work and AI safety research can cooperate in three areas: joint research, framework integration, and policy coordination. Short-term, medium-term, and long-term agendas can promote the continuous deepening of cooperation.

Conclusion Six: The Relation to the New Three Views

The dialogue in this chapter embodies the core claims of the New Three Views:

  • NC-1 (Relational Ontology): AI as a node in a relational network
  • NC-2 (Process Ontology): the dynamic evolution of AI capabilities
  • NC-3 (Participatory Universe): AI as a participant rather than a tool
  • NL-1 (Continuum of Life): UCS assesses the position of AI on the continuum of consciousness
  • NL-2 (Negentropy Organization): the responsibility of AI as a negentropy organization
  • NK-1 (Participatory Cognition): AI as a cognitive subject
  • NK-3 (Deep Uncertainty): the deep uncertainty of AI development
