[1] The concept of the Alignment Problem has various formulations in AI safety research. Russell (2019), in Human Compatible, defines it as the problem of ensuring that the goals of AI systems are consistent with human values. Ngo et al. (2022) analyze the alignment problem from the perspective of deep learning. The definition adopted by this work synthesizes these sources.

[2] The concept of the Control Problem was systematically expounded by Bostrom (2014) in Superintelligence. Bostrom analyzed the challenge of maintaining control when AI capabilities surpass human capabilities. Russell (2019) further developed this concept.

[3] The Interpretability Problem is an important area of AI safety research. Olah et al. (2020), in "Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits," developed mechanistic interpretability methods. The Anthropic research team has made important contributions in this area.

[4] The Robustness Problem concerns the safety of AI systems under various challenges. Goodfellow et al. (2014) discovered the phenomenon of adversarial examples. Hendrycks & Dietterich (2019) studied robustness under distribution shift.

[5] The distinction between outer alignment and inner alignment was proposed by Hubinger et al. (2019) in "Risks from Learned Optimization." This distinction is crucial for understanding the complexity of the alignment problem.

[6] The paperclip maximizer is a thought experiment proposed by Bostrom (2003) to illustrate the dangers of the goal specification problem. An AI instructed to maximize paperclip production might convert the entire universe into paperclips.

[7] Deceptive alignment is a concept proposed by Hubinger et al. (2019), referring to the possibility that an AI system may appear aligned during training but pursue different goals during deployment. This is one of the most challenging aspects of the alignment problem.

[8] Iterated amplification is an alignment method proposed by Christiano et al. (2018), which gradually improves AI capabilities through human supervision. This method attempts to expand AI capabilities while maintaining alignment.

[9] Human-compatible AI is a concept proposed by Russell (2019), containing three principles: the AI's sole goal is to maximize the realization of human preferences; the AI is initially uncertain about human preferences; and human behavior is a source of information about human preferences.

[10] Constitutional AI is a method proposed by Anthropic, which guides AI behavior through a set of principles (a "constitution"). Bai et al. (2022) described this method in detail in "Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback."

[11] Interruptibility is an AI safety property studied by Hadfield-Menell et al. (2017), referring to the requirement that an AI system should allow humans to interrupt its actions without resistance. This is highly relevant to this work's Reversibility Principle.

[12] Corrigibility is an AI safety property studied by Soares et al. (2015), referring to the requirement that an AI system should allow humans to modify its goals without resistance. This is also highly relevant to this work's Reversibility Principle.

[13] Mechanistic interpretability is a research direction developed by Olah et al. (2020), aimed at understanding the internal computational mechanisms of neural networks. This direction is crucial for UCS's assessment of the internal states of AI.

[14] Integrated Information Theory (IIT) is a theory of consciousness proposed by Tononi (2004), which quantifies the degree of consciousness using the degree of information integration (Φ). Part of this work's UCS draws on the ideas of IIT.

[15] Emergent abilities in deep learning are a phenomenon studied by Wei et al. (2022), referring to the sudden acquisition of new abilities by large language models as their scale increases. This phenomenon increases the uncertainty of AI development.

[16] AI existential risk is a type of risk analyzed in detail by Bostrom (2014) and Ord (2020). Ord estimates AI-related existential risk in this century at approximately 10%.

[17] The OECD AI Principles are international AI governance principles adopted in 2019, including five principles: inclusive growth, human-centered values, transparency, robustness, and accountability.

[18] The UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI is a global AI ethics framework adopted in 2021, and is the first global normative document on AI ethics.

[19] The EU AI Act is AI regulation adopted by the European Union in 2024, which adopts a risk-based classification approach and implements strict regulation of high-risk AI applications.

[20] The International AI Safety Summit is an international coordination mechanism begun in 2023, aimed at promoting international cooperation on AI safety. The first summit was held at Bletchley Park in the United Kingdom.

Footnotes

Chapter 29 Footnotes

[1] The concept of the alignment problem has various formulations in AI safety research. Russell (2019) defines it in Human Compatible as the problem of ensuring that the goals of AI systems are consistent with human values. Ngo et al. (2022) analyze the alignment problem from the perspective of deep learning. The definition adopted in this work synthesizes these sources.

[2] The concept of the control problem was systematically expounded by Bostrom (2014) in Superintelligence. Bostrom analyzed the challenge of maintaining control when AI capabilities surpass those of humans. Russell (2019) further developed this concept.

[3] The interpretability problem is an important area of AI safety research. Olah et al. (2020) developed mechanistic interpretability methods in "Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits." The research team at Anthropic has made important contributions in this area.

[4] The robustness problem concerns the safety of AI systems under various challenges. Goodfellow et al. (2014) discovered the phenomenon of adversarial examples. Hendrycks & Dietterich (2019) studied robustness under distributional shift.

[5] The distinction between outer alignment and inner alignment was proposed by Hubinger et al. (2019) in "Risks from Learned Optimization." This distinction is crucial for understanding the complexity of the alignment problem.

[6] The paperclip maximizer is a thought experiment proposed by Bostrom (2003) to illustrate the dangers of the specification problem. An AI instructed to maximize paperclip production might convert the entire universe into paperclips.

[7] Deceptive alignment is a concept proposed by Hubinger et al. (2019), referring to the possibility that an AI system may appear aligned during training but pursue different goals when deployed. This is one of the most challenging aspects of the alignment problem.

[8] Iterated amplification is an alignment method proposed by Christiano et al. (2018) that progressively increases AI capability through human oversight. The method seeks to scale AI capability while maintaining alignment.

[9] Human-compatible AI is a concept proposed by Russell (2019), comprising three principles: the AI's only objective is to maximize the realization of human preferences; the AI is initially uncertain about human preferences; and human behavior is a source of information about human preferences.

[10] Constitutional AI is a method proposed by Anthropic that guides the behavior of AI through a set of principles (a "constitution"). Bai et al. (2022) describe the method in detail in "Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback."

[11] Interruptibility is an AI safety property studied by Hadfield-Menell et al. (2017), holding that an AI system should allow humans to interrupt its actions without resistance. This is highly relevant to the Reversibility Principle of this work.

[12] Corrigibility is an AI safety property studied by Soares et al. (2015), holding that an AI system should allow humans to modify its goals without resistance. This too is highly relevant to the Reversibility Principle of this work.

[13] Mechanistic interpretability is a research direction developed by Olah et al. (2020), aimed at understanding the internal computational mechanisms of neural networks. This direction is crucial for the UCS assessment of the internal states of AI.

[14] Integrated Information Theory (IIT) is a theory of consciousness proposed by Tononi (2004), which quantifies the degree of consciousness by the degree of information integration (Φ). The UCS component of this work draws on the ideas of IIT.

[15] Emergent abilities in deep learning are a phenomenon studied by Wei et al. (2022), referring to large language models suddenly acquiring new abilities as their scale increases. This phenomenon increases the uncertainty of AI development.

[16] AI existential risk is a type of risk analyzed in detail by Bostrom (2014) and Ord (2020). Ord estimates AI-related existential risk in this century at about 10%.

[17] The OECD AI Principles are international AI governance principles adopted in 2019, comprising five principles: inclusive growth, human-centered values, transparency, robustness, and accountability.

[18] The UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI is a global AI ethics framework adopted in 2021 and the first global normative instrument on AI ethics.

[19] The EU AI Act is an AI regulation adopted by the European Union in 2024, which adopts a risk-based classification approach and imposes strict regulation on high-risk AI applications.

[20] The International AI Safety Summit is an international coordination mechanism begun in 2023, aimed at promoting international cooperation on AI safety. The first summit was held at Bletchley Park in the United Kingdom.

In-Depth Dialogue with International Space LawChapter 30

Chapter Opening Guide

I. The Position of This Chapter in the Book

Chapter 30 is the third chapter of Part Eight (International Dialogue), and it undertakes the task of an in-depth dialogue with international space law. Within the protocol stack architecture, the function of this chapter can be expressed as:

$$\text{Chapter 30} = \text{Dialogue}(\text{CosmicResponsibilityEthics}, \text{InternationalSpaceLaw})$$

This chapter undertakes five core tasks:

Task No.Task ContentDeliverable

IV. Why a Dialogue with International Space Law Is Needed

International space law is the most important legal framework that humanity has developed to date in the field of space governance. As space activities accelerate, international space law faces new challenges. This work has a profound connection to international space law:

Table 30.1 The Necessity of a Dialogue with International Space Law

DimensionExplanationValue of the Dialogue
Historical accumulationInternational space law has over 60 years of developmentDrawing on institutional experience
Legal effectInternational space law is legally bindingProviding a legal interface pathway for this work
Institutional practiceInternational space law has rich practical experienceTesting the feasibility of this work
Future challengesInternational space law faces new challengesThis work can provide theoretical support
Normative foundationInternational space law needs normative deepeningThis work can provide normative foundations

V. Relation to the New Three Views

The dialogue in this chapter needs to examine international space law from the perspective of the New Three Views:

Table 30.2 The Relation of This Chapter to the New Three Views

New Three Views PropositionRelation in This ChapterConcrete Manifestation
NC-1 (relational ontology)Space as a relational networkSpace is not empty space but a relational network
NC-2 (process ontology)The processual character of space activitiesSpace activities are continuous processes rather than static states
NC-3 (participatory universe)Humanity participates in cosmic evolutionSpace activities are the way humanity participates in cosmic evolution
NL-1 (continuum of life)The possibility of space lifeLife may exist or arise in space
NL-2 (negentropic organization)The negentropic character of space resourcesSpace resources are sources of negentropy
NK-1 (participatory cognition)The cognitive significance of space explorationSpace exploration expands the boundaries of human cognition
NK-3 (deep uncertainty)The uncertainty of space activitiesSpace activities face deep uncertainty

$$\text{Chapter30\_NewThreeViews} = \{NC\text{-}1, NC\text{-}2, NC\text{-}3, NL\text{-}1, NL\text{-}2, NK\text{-}1, NK\text{-}3\}$$

VI. Methodological Commitments

This chapter adheres to the following methodological commitments:

  1. Commitment to legal accuracy: accurately present the content of international space law and avoid misreading
  2. Commitment to respecting priority: respect the priority status of existing international law
  3. Constructive commitment: seek constructive dialogue rather than simple criticism
  4. Practice-oriented commitment: attend to the practical significance of the dialogue
  5. Gradualist commitment: propose gradual integration pathways

§30.1 The Core Principles of International Space Law

§30.1.1 The Principle of Benefit for All Mankind

I. The Legal Sources of the Principle

Definition 30.1.1 (Province of All Mankind Principle)

The Province of All Mankind Principle is a foundational principle of international space law, stipulating that the exploration and use of outer space shall be carried on for the benefit of all mankind [1].

The principal legal sources of this principle include:

Table 30.3 The Legal Sources of the Province of All Mankind Principle

Legal InstrumentRelevant ProvisionContent
Outer Space Treaty (1967)Article IThe exploration and use of outer space shall be for the benefit and in the interests of all countries
Moon Agreement (1979)Article IVThe exploration and use of the Moon is the province of all mankind
UN General Assembly resolutionsMultiple resolutionsReaffirming the Province of All Mankind Principle

Formal expression:

$$\text{ProvinceOfAllMankind} \triangleq \forall a \in \text{SpaceActivities}, \text{Benefit}(a, \text{AllMankind})$$

II. The Connotations of the Principle

The Province of All Mankind Principle contains the following core connotations:

Table 30.4 The Connotations of the Province of All Mankind Principle

Connotation DimensionContentExplanation
BeneficiaryAll mankindNot limited to particular states or groups
Scope of activityExploration and useIncluding scientific research and resource utilization
Temporal scopePresent and futureIncluding future generations
Types of benefitPlural benefitsIncluding scientific, economic, cultural, and others

III. Interpretive Controversies Regarding the Principle

There are controversies over the interpretation of the Province of All Mankind Principle:

Table 30.5 Interpretive Controversies Regarding the Province of All Mankind Principle

Point of ControversyPosition APosition B
The meaning of "benefit"Refers only to general benefitsIncludes concrete sharing of economic benefits
The scope of "all mankind"Present humanityIncluding future generations
Legal effectA declaratory principleA binding obligation
Relation to sovereigntyDoes not restrict state activitiesRestricts states' exclusive rights

IV. Relation to the New Three Views

Examining the Province of All Mankind Principle from the perspective of the New Three Views:

│  - Benefits are relational, not atomistic                       │ 
│                                                                 │

§30.1.2 The Principle of Non-Appropriation

V. The Legal Sources of the Principle

Definition 30.1.2 (Non-Appropriation Principle)

The Non-Appropriation Principle stipulates that outer space and celestial bodies may not be appropriated by states through claims of sovereignty, use, occupation, or any other means [2].

The principal legal sources of this principle include:

Table 30.6 The Legal Sources of the Non-Appropriation Principle

Legal InstrumentRelevant ProvisionContent
Outer Space Treaty (1967)Article IIOuter space may not be appropriated
Moon Agreement (1979)Article XIThe Moon and its natural resources are the common heritage of mankind
Customary international law—Non-appropriation has become customary international law

Formal expression:

$$\text{NonAppropriation} \triangleq \neg \exists s \in \text{States}, \text{Sovereignty}(s, \text{OuterSpace})$$

VI. The Connotations of the Principle

The Non-Appropriation Principle contains the following core connotations:

Table 30.7 The Connotations of the Non-Appropriation Principle

Connotation DimensionContentExplanation
Prohibited objectClaims of sovereigntyProhibits claims of sovereignty over outer space
Prohibited meansUse, occupation, other meansProhibits any form of appropriation
Applicable subjectsStatesExplicitly prohibits appropriation by states
Scope of applicationOuter space and celestial bodiesIncluding the Moon and other celestial bodies

VII. Contemporary Challenges to the Principle

The Non-Appropriation Principle faces contemporary challenges:

Table 30.8 Contemporary Challenges to the Non-Appropriation Principle

ChallengeContentImpact
Space resource extractionPrivate enterprises extracting space resourcesThe question of resource ownership
Domestic legislationThe U.S. Space Resource Act, etc.Relation to international law
Private actorsWhether the principle applies to private actorsLegal gap
Orbital positionsThe scarcity of geostationary orbitsDe facto exclusive use

§30.1.3 The Principle of Peaceful Use

I. The Legal Sources of the Principle

Definition 30.1.3 (Peaceful Use Principle)

The Peaceful Use Principle stipulates that outer space shall be used exclusively for peaceful purposes, and prohibits the deployment of weapons of mass destruction in outer space [3].

The principal legal sources of this principle include:

Table 30.10 The Legal Sources of the Peaceful Use Principle

Legal InstrumentRelevant ProvisionContent
Outer Space Treaty (1967)Article IVProhibits the deployment of nuclear weapons and weapons of mass destruction in orbit
Moon Agreement (1979)Article IIIThe Moon shall be used exclusively for peaceful purposes
UN General Assembly resolutionsMultiple resolutionsReaffirming the Peaceful Use Principle

Formal expression:

$$\text{PeacefulUse} \triangleq \forall a \in \text{SpaceActivities}, \neg \text{Military}(a) \lor \text{NonAggressive}(a)$$

II. The Connotations of the Principle

The Peaceful Use Principle contains the following core connotations:

Table 30.11 The Connotations of the Peaceful Use Principle

Connotation DimensionContentExplanation
Prohibited contentWeapons of mass destructionExplicitly prohibits nuclear weapons and the like
Permitted contentNon-aggressive military activitiesRoom for interpretation exists
Scope of applicationOuter space and celestial bodiesThe Moon shall be used exclusively for peaceful purposes
Legal effectTreaty obligationLegally binding

III. Interpretive Controversies Regarding the Principle

There are controversies over the interpretation of the Peaceful Use Principle:

Table 30.12 Interpretive Controversies Regarding the Peaceful Use Principle

Point of ControversyPosition APosition B
The meaning of "peaceful"DemilitarizationNon-aggressive
Conventional weaponsProhibitedPermitted
Military satellitesProhibitedPermitted (if non-aggressive)
Anti-satellite weaponsProhibitedNot explicitly prohibited

IV. Relation to the Principle of Reversibility

This work's Principle of Reversibility is related to the Peaceful Use Principle:

Table 30.13 The Relation Between the Principle of Reversibility and the Peaceful Use Principle

DimensionPeaceful Use PrinciplePrinciple of ReversibilityRelation

Grounds for prohibitionPeaceIrreversibilityDeepening
Scope of applicationMilitary activitiesAll significant actionsExtension

§30.1.4 The Principle of International Cooperation

I. The Legal Sources of the Principle

Definition 30.1.4 (International Cooperation Principle)

The International Cooperation Principle stipulates that states shall engage in international cooperation and mutual assistance in the exploration and use of outer space [4].

The principal legal sources of this principle include:

Table 30.14 The Legal Sources of the International Cooperation Principle

Legal InstrumentRelevant ProvisionContent
Outer Space Treaty (1967)Articles I, IXInternational cooperation, mutual consultation
Rescue Agreement (1968)Full textInternational cooperation in astronaut rescue
Liability Convention (1972)Full textInternational cooperation in compensation for damage
Registration Convention (1975)Full textInternational cooperation in the registration of space objects

Formal expression:

$$\text{InternationalCooperation} \triangleq \forall s_1, s_2 \in \text{States}, \text{Cooperate}(s_1, s_2, \text{SpaceActivities})$$

II. The Connotations of the Principle

The International Cooperation Principle contains the following core connotations:

Table 30.15 The Connotations of the International Cooperation Principle

Connotation DimensionContentExplanation

§30.1.5 The Principle of Environmental Protection

I. The Legal Sources of the Principle

Definition 30.1.5 (Environmental Protection Principle)

The Environmental Protection Principle stipulates that states shall, in the exploration and use of outer space, avoid harmful contamination of outer space and celestial environments, and avoid adverse changes to the Earth's environment [5].

The principal legal sources of this principle include:

Table 30.18 The Legal Sources of the Environmental Protection Principle

Legal InstrumentRelevant ProvisionContent
Outer Space Treaty (1967)Article IXAvoiding harmful contamination
Moon Agreement (1979)Article VIIProtecting the lunar environment
COPUOS GuidelinesSpace Debris Mitigation GuidelinesReducing space debris
COPUOS GuidelinesLong-term Sustainability GuidelinesLong-term sustainability of space activities

Formal expression:

$$\text{EnvironmentalProtection} \triangleq \forall a \in \text{SpaceActivities}, \neg \text{HarmfulContamination}(a)$$

II. The Connotations of the Principle

The Environmental Protection Principle contains the following core connotations:

Table 30.19 The Connotations of the Environmental Protection Principle

Connotation DimensionContentExplanation
Protected objectOuter space, celestial bodies, the EarthIncluding multiple environments
Prohibited contentHarmful contaminationIncluding physical and biological contamination
Applicable subjectsStatesStates bear responsibility
Legal effectTreaty obligation + soft lawPartly soft law

II. The Correspondence Between the Principle of Recursive Freedom and the Province of All Mankind Principle

Definition 30.2.1 (Correspondence Between the Principle of Recursive Freedom and the Province of All Mankind Principle)

The Principle of Recursive Freedom requires protecting the space of possibilities, and the Province of All Mankind Principle requires that space activities be for the benefit of all mankind. The correspondence between the two can be expressed as: protecting the space of possibilities is a precondition for realizing the benefit of all mankind.

Formal expression:

$$\text{RFP} \Rightarrow \text{ProvinceOfAllMankind}$$

That is: if an action protects the space of possibilities, then the action contributes to the benefit of all mankind.

BeneficiaryAll subjectsAll mankindRFP extends the beneficiary
Temporal scopeDeep timePrimarily presentRFP extends the temporal scope
Normative foundationPhysical-philosophicalLegalRFP provides a deeper foundation

III. The Correspondence Between the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility and the Environmental Protection Principle

Definition 30.2.2 (Correspondence Between the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility and the Environmental Protection Principle)

The Principle of Negentropy Responsibility requires maintaining negentropic sources, and the Environmental Protection Principle requires avoiding harmful contamination. The correspondence between the two can be expressed as: maintaining negentropic sources is the essence of environmental protection.

Formal expression:

$$\text{NRP} \Leftrightarrow \text{EnvironmentalProtection}_{\text{deepened}}$$

That is: the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility is the deepened version of the Environmental Protection Principle.

Protected objectNegentropic organizationOuter space, celestial bodies, the EarthNRP extends the protected object
Prohibited contentNegentropy dissipationHarmful contaminationNRP deepens the prohibited content
Normative foundationThermodynamic-ethicalLegalNRP provides a deeper foundation

Chapter Summary

Core Conclusions

This chapter conducted an in-depth dialogue with international space law, and its main conclusions include:

Conclusion One: The Core Principles of International Space Law

The core principles of international space law include the Province of All Mankind Principle, the Non-Appropriation Principle, the Peaceful Use Principle, the International Cooperation Principle, and the Environmental Protection Principle. These principles constitute the normative foundations of international space law.

$$\text{ISL}_{\text{core}} = \{\text{ProvinceOfAllMankind}, \text{NonAppropriation}, \text{PeacefulUse}, \text{InternationalCooperation}, \text{EnvironmentalProtection}\}$$

Table 30.69 Summary of the Core Principles

PrincipleCore ContentLegal Source
Benefit for all mankindSpace activities shall be for the benefit of all mankindOST Article I
Non-appropriationProhibiting claims of sovereignty over outer spaceOST Article II
Peaceful useProhibiting the deployment of weapons of mass destructionOST Article IV
International cooperationStates shall engage in international cooperationOST Articles I, IX
Environmental protectionAvoiding harmful contaminationOST Article IX

Conclusion Two: The Relationship Between This Work and International Space Law

There are three types of relations between this work and international space law: correspondence, extension, and supplement. The correspondence relations provide the basis for integration, the extension relations enable this work to address new challenges, and the supplement relations fill the gaps of international space law.

Table 30.70 Summary of Relations

Type of RelationContentEvaluation
CorrespondenceCore principles correspondProvides the basis for integration
ExtensionExtension of subjects, time, and spaceAddresses new challenges
SupplementSupplements regarding AI governance, deep-time responsibility, etc.Fills gaps

Conclusion Three: This Work's Contributions to International Space Law

This work provides international space law with four contributions: extension of the time scale, extension of the range of subjects, deepening of the normative foundations, and operational frameworks.

Table 30.71 Summary of Contributions

Field of ContributionConcrete ContributionValue to International Space Law
Extension of the time scaleFrom the present to deep timeAddressing long-term impacts
Extension of the range of subjectsFrom states to all intelligent subjectsAddressing the diversification of subjects
Deepening of the normative foundationsProviding physical-philosophical-ethical foundationsAddressing interpretive controversies
Provision of operational frameworksCSIA, the protocol stack, etc.Improving operability

Conclusion Four: The Insights International Space Law Offers to This Work

The treaty-making, dispute resolution, and enforcement-mechanism experience of international space law offers this work important insights.

Table 30.72 Summary of Insights

Field of InsightConcrete InsightThis Work's Response
Treaty-makingGradual development, ambiguous consensus, adaptive designA gradual integration pathway
Dispute resolutionConsultation first, professionalism, flexibilityThe design of the Multi-Intelligence Tribunal

Conclusion Five: The Integration Pathway

The integration of this work with international space law should adopt a gradual pathway: short term (2026-2035) to build conceptual bridges, mid term (2035-2050) to achieve initial institutionalization, and long term (after 2050) to achieve comprehensive institutionalization.

Conclusion Six: Relation to the New Three Views

The dialogue in this chapter embodies the core claims of the New Three Views:

  • NC-1 (relational ontology): space as a relational network rather than empty space
  • NC-2 (process ontology): space activities as continuous processes
  • NC-3 (participatory universe): humanity participating in cosmic evolution through space activities
  • NL-1 (continuum of life): life may exist or arise in space
  • NL-2 (negentropic organization): space resources as sources of negentropy
  • NK-1 (participatory cognition): space exploration expanding the boundaries of cognition
  • NK-3 (deep uncertainty): space activities facing deep uncertainty

[1] The concept of the Province of All Mankind Principle originates in Article I of the Outer Space Treaty. That article provides: "The exploration and use of outer space, including the Moon and other celestial bodies, shall be carried out for the benefit and in the interests of all countries, irrespective of their degree of economic or scientific development, and shall be the province of all mankind." This principle is regarded as one of the foundational principles of international space law. See Cheng (1997), Jakhu & Dempsey (2016).

[2] The Non-Appropriation Principle is stipulated in Article II of the Outer Space Treaty: "Outer space, including the Moon and other celestial bodies, is not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, by means of use or occupation, or by any other means." This principle prohibits states from claiming sovereignty over outer space, but whether it applies to private actors and resource extraction is controversial. See Tronchetti (2009), Masson-Zwaan & Richards (2021).

[3] The Peaceful Use Principle is stipulated in Article IV of the Outer Space Treaty. That article prohibits the placement in orbit around the Earth of nuclear weapons or any other kinds of weapons of mass destruction, prohibits the stationing of such weapons on celestial bodies, and provides that the Moon and other celestial bodies shall be used exclusively for peaceful purposes. The meaning of "peaceful" is controversial, with two interpretations: "demilitarized" and "non-aggressive." See Lyall & Larsen (2018).

[4] The International Cooperation Principle is embodied in Articles I and IX of the Outer Space Treaty. Article I provides that the exploration and use of outer space shall be "the province of all mankind," and Article IX provides that states shall undertake appropriate international consultations before proceeding with an activity that would cause potentially harmful interference with the activities of other states. This principle is embodied in practice through projects such as the International Space Station. See Jakhu & Pelton (2017).

[5] The Environmental Protection Principle is stipulated in Article IX of the Outer Space Treaty, requiring states to "conduct exploration of outer space, including the Moon and other celestial bodies, ... and ... avoid their harmful contamination" in conducting such exploration. This principle has been further developed in the Space Debris Mitigation Guidelines and the Long-term Sustainability Guidelines. See COPUOS (2019).

[6] The Outer Space Treaty (OST), whose full title is the Treaty on Principles Governing the Activities of States in the Exploration and Use of Outer Space, including the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies, entered into force in 1967 and is the foundational treaty of international space law. As of 2024, 114 states have ratified the treaty. See UNOOSA (2024).

[7] The Moon Agreement, whose full title is the Agreement Governing the Activities of States on the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies, entered into force in 1984. This agreement established the principle of the "common heritage of mankind," but few states have ratified it (only 18 states as of 2024), and none of the major spacefaring states have ratified it. See Tronchetti (2009).

[8] The Rescue Agreement, whose full title is the Agreement on the Rescue of Astronauts, the Return of Astronauts and the Return of Objects Launched into Outer Space, entered into force in 1968. This agreement stipulates the obligation of international cooperation in astronaut rescue and the return of space objects. See Lyall & Larsen (2018).

[9] The Liability Convention, whose full title is the Convention on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects, entered into force in 1972. This convention establishes a regime of international liability for damage caused by space objects, including two forms of liability: absolute liability and fault-based liability. See Jakhu & Dempsey (2016).

[10] The Registration Convention, whose full title is the Convention on Registration of Objects Launched into Outer Space, entered into force in 1976. This convention requires states to register space objects they launch and to provide registration information to the Secretary-General of the United Nations. See UNOOSA (2024).

[11] COPUOS (the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space) is a committee under the United Nations General Assembly, established in 1959, and is the primary platform for international space governance. COPUOS has two subcommittees: the Scientific and Technical Subcommittee and the Legal Subcommittee. See UNOOSA (2024).

[12] UNOOSA (the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs) is part of the United Nations Secretariat, responsible for coordinating United Nations space activities and providing secretariat services to COPUOS. See UNOOSA (2024).

[13] The Space Debris Mitigation Guidelines were adopted by COPUOS in 2007 and are an international soft-law instrument on space debris mitigation. The guidelines set out seven mitigation measures, including limiting debris released during missions and avoiding on-orbit break-ups. See COPUOS (2007).

[14] The Long-term Sustainability Guidelines were adopted by COPUOS in 2019 and are an international soft-law instrument on the long-term sustainability of space activities. The guidelines set out 21 guidelines covering policy and regulatory frameworks, safe operations, international cooperation, and capacity building. See COPUOS (2019).

[15] COSPAR (the Committee on Space Research) is a committee under the International Science Council responsible for formulating planetary protection policy. The COSPAR Planetary Protection Policy classifies missions into five categories according to mission type and target celestial body and stipulates different protection requirements. See COSPAR (2020).

[16] ITU (the International Telecommunication Union) is a specialized agency of the United Nations responsible for coordinating the global use of the radio spectrum and satellite orbits. The ITU Radio Regulations stipulate the procedures for the allocation of satellite frequencies and orbital positions. See ITU (2024).

[17] The Cosmos 954 incident was the 1978 crash in Canada of the Soviet nuclear-powered satellite Cosmos 954. Canada submitted a claim to the Soviet Union under the Liability Convention, which was ultimately resolved through diplomatic consultation, with the Soviet Union paying 3 million Canadian dollars in compensation. This was the first practical application of the Liability Convention. See Jakhu & Dempsey (2016).

[18] The Artemis Accords are a multilateral space cooperation framework initiated by the United States in 2020, aimed at establishing principles of cooperation for lunar and Mars exploration. As of 2024, more than 40 states have signed them. The accords are regarded as either a supplement to or a challenge to traditional international space law. See NASA (2024).

[19] The U.S. Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act was adopted in 2015 and recognizes the ownership by U.S. citizens of space resources they extract. This legislation has given rise to controversy over its relation to Article II of the Outer Space Treaty. See Tronchetti (2015).

[20] IISL (the International Institute of Space Law) is the main academic organization in the field of international space law, established in 1960, and holds an academic colloquium each year during the International Astronautical Congress. See IISL (2024).

Footnotes

Chapter 30 Footnotes

[1] The concept of the Province of All Mankind principle derives from Article I of the Outer Space Treaty. That article provides: "The exploration and use of outer space, including the Moon and other celestial bodies, shall be carried out for the benefit and in the interests of all countries, irrespective of their degree of economic or scientific development, and shall be the province of all mankind." This principle is regarded as one of the foundational principles of international space law. See Cheng (1997), Jakhu & Dempsey (2016).

[2] The Non-Appropriation Principle is laid down in Article II of the Outer Space Treaty: "Outer space, including the Moon and other celestial bodies, is not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, by means of use or occupation, or by any other means." This principle prohibits states from claiming sovereignty over outer space, but whether it applies to private actors and resource extraction is controversial. See Tronchetti (2009), Masson-Zwaan & Richards (2021).

[3] The Peaceful Use Principle is laid down in Article IV of the Outer Space Treaty. That article prohibits the placement in orbit around the Earth of nuclear weapons or any other weapons of mass destruction, prohibits the stationing of such weapons on celestial bodies, and provides that the Moon and other celestial bodies shall be used exclusively for peaceful purposes. The meaning of "peaceful" is controversial, with two interpretations: "non-militarization" and "non-aggression." See Lyall & Larsen (2018).

[4] The International Cooperation Principle is embodied in Articles I and IX of the Outer Space Treaty. Article I provides that the exploration and use of outer space shall be "the province of all mankind," and Article IX provides that states shall undertake consultations before engaging in activities that may cause potentially harmful interference to other states. In practice, this principle is reflected in projects such as the International Space Station. See Jakhu & Pelton (2017).

[5] The Environmental Protection Principle is laid down in Article IX of the Outer Space Treaty, requiring states to "conduct studies of outer space, including the Moon and other celestial bodies, and conduct exploration of them so as to avoid their harmful contamination." This principle has been further developed in the Space Debris Mitigation Guidelines and the Long-term Sustainability Guidelines. See COPUOS (2019).

[6] The full title of the Outer Space Treaty (OST) is the Treaty on Principles Governing the Activities of States in the Exploration and Use of Outer Space, including the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies. It entered into force in 1967 and is the foundational treaty of international space law. As of 2024, 114 states had ratified the treaty. See UNOOSA (2024).

[7] The full title of the Moon Agreement is the Agreement Governing the Activities of States on the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies. It entered into force in 1984. The Agreement established the principle of the "common heritage of mankind," but few states have ratified it (only 18 as of 2024), and none of the major spacefaring states has ratified it. See Tronchetti (2009).

[8] The full title of the Rescue Agreement is the Agreement on the Rescue of Astronauts, the Return of Astronauts and the Return of Objects Launched into Outer Space. It entered into force in 1968. The Agreement sets out international obligations of cooperation for the rescue of astronauts and the return of space objects. See Lyall & Larsen (2018).

[9] The full title of the Liability Convention is the Convention on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects. It entered into force in 1972. The Convention establishes an international liability regime for damage caused by space objects, comprising two forms of liability: absolute liability and fault-based liability. See Jakhu & Dempsey (2016).

[10] The full title of the Registration Convention is the Convention on Registration of Objects Launched into Outer Space. It entered into force in 1976. The Convention requires states to register the space objects they launch and to provide registration information to the Secretary-General of the United Nations. See UNOOSA (2024).

[11] COPUOS (the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space) is a committee subordinate to the United Nations General Assembly, established in 1959, and is the principal platform for international space governance. COPUOS has a Scientific and Technical Subcommittee and a Legal Subcommittee. See UNOOSA (2024).

[12] UNOOSA (the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs) is part of the United Nations Secretariat, responsible for coordinating United Nations space activities and providing secretariat services to COPUOS. See UNOOSA (2024).

[13] The Space Debris Mitigation Guidelines were adopted by COPUOS in 2007 and are an international soft law instrument on space debris mitigation. The Guidelines set out seven mitigation measures, including limiting debris released during a mission and avoiding on-orbit breakups. See COPUOS (2007).

[14] The Long-term Sustainability Guidelines were adopted by COPUOS in 2019 and are an international soft law instrument on the long-term sustainability of space activities. The Guidelines set out 21 guidelines covering policy and regulatory frameworks, safe operations, international cooperation, and capacity-building. See COPUOS (2019).

[15] COSPAR (the Committee on Space Research) is a committee of the International Science Council responsible for formulating planetary protection policy. The COSPAR planetary protection policy classifies missions into five categories according to mission type and target celestial body and specifies different protection requirements. See COSPAR (2020).

[16] The ITU (International Telecommunication Union) is a specialized agency of the United Nations responsible for coordinating the use of the global radio spectrum and satellite orbits. The ITU Radio Regulations set out procedures for the allocation of satellite frequencies and orbital positions. See ITU (2024).

[17] The Cosmos 954 incident was the 1978 crash in Canada of the Soviet nuclear-powered satellite Cosmos 954. Canada presented a claim against the Soviet Union under the Liability Convention, which was ultimately resolved through diplomatic negotiation, with the Soviet Union paying C$3 million in compensation. This was the first practical application of the Liability Convention. See Jakhu & Dempsey (2016).

[18] The Artemis Accords are a multilateral space cooperation framework initiated by the United States in 2020, aimed at establishing principles of cooperation for lunar and Martian exploration. As of 2024, more than 40 states had signed. The Accords are regarded as a supplement to, or challenge to, traditional international space law. See NASA (2024).

[19] The U.S. Commercial Space Launch Competitiveness Act was passed in 2015 and recognizes the ownership by U.S. citizens of space resources they extract. This legislation has given rise to controversy over its relationship to Article II of the Outer Space Treaty. See Tronchetti (2015).

[20] The IISL (International Institute of Space Law) is the leading academic organization in the field of international space law, founded in 1960, and holds an academic colloquium each year during the International Astronautical Congress. See IISL (2024).

VI. Methodological Commitments

This chapter adheres to the following methodological commitments:

  1. Commitment to accurate presentation: Accurately present the core claims of each academic tradition
  2. Commitment to respecting differences: Respect the uniqueness of each tradition and avoid oversimplification
  3. Constructive commitment: Seek constructive dialogue rather than simple criticism
  4. Openness commitment: Acknowledge that this work can learn from other traditions
  5. Integration commitment: Explore the possibilities of theoretical integration

§31.1 Dialogue with Environmental Ethics

§31.1.1 The Core Claims of Environmental Ethics

I. The Historical Development of Environmental Ethics

Definition 31.1.1 (Environmental Ethics)

Environmental Ethics is the branch of philosophy that studies the ethical relationship between humans and the natural environment, exploring the moral status of natural entities, human responsibility toward nature, and the nature of environmental value[1].

The historical development of environmental ethics can be divided into several stages:

Table 31.3 The Historical Development of Environmental Ethics

StagePeriodMain FeaturesRepresentative Figures
Precursor stageLate 19th century - mid 20th centuryNature conservation thoughtMuir, Leopold
Formation stage1970sDisciplinary establishmentRoutley, Singer
Development stage1980s-1990sTheoretical pluralismCallicott, Rolston
Maturity stage2000s to presentGlobalization, interdisciplinarityJamieson, Gardiner

II. The Main Schools of Environmental Ethics

Environmental ethics encompasses multiple theoretical schools:

Table 31.4 The Main Schools of Environmental Ethics

SchoolCore ClaimRepresentative FiguresScope of Moral Consideration
AnthropocentrismOnly humans have intrinsic valueNortonHumans
Animal liberation/rightsSentient animals have moral statusSinger, ReganSentient animals
BiocentrismAll life has intrinsic valueTaylorAll life
EcocentrismEcosystems as a whole have intrinsic valueLeopold, CallicottEcosystems
Deep ecologyNature has intrinsic value, humans are part of natureNaessThe whole of nature

III. The Core Issues of Environmental Ethics

Environmental ethics focuses on the following core issues:

Table 31.5 The Core Issues of Environmental Ethics

IssueContentMain Debates
The issue of moral statusWhich entities have moral status?Humans vs. animals vs. life vs. ecosystems
The issue of intrinsic valueDoes nature have intrinsic value?Intrinsic value vs. instrumental value
The issue of intergenerational justiceWhat responsibilities do we have toward future generations?The scope and content of responsibility
The issue of species conservationWhy conserve species?The moral status of species
The issue of wilderness conservationWhy conserve wilderness?The value of wilderness

§31.2 Dialogue with Global Justice Theory

§31.2.1 The Core Claims of Global Justice Theory

I. The Historical Development of Global Justice Theory

Definition 31.2.1 (Global Justice Theory)

Global Justice Theory is the branch of political philosophy that studies issues of justice across national borders, exploring distributive justice, human rights protection, and institutional design among states and at the global level[2].

The historical development of global justice theory can be divided into several stages:

Table 31.12 The Historical Development of Global Justice Theory

StagePeriodMain FeaturesRepresentative Figures
Precursor stage18th-19th centuryCosmopolitan thoughtKant
Formation stage1970s-1980sDisciplinary establishmentBeitz, Pogge
Development stage1990s-2000sTheoretical pluralismRawls, Nussbaum
Maturity stage2010s to presentDeepening globalizationCaney, Moellendorf

II. The Main Schools of Global Justice Theory

Global justice theory encompasses multiple theoretical schools:

Table 31.13 The Main Schools of Global Justice Theory

SchoolCore ClaimRepresentative FiguresScope of Justice
CosmopolitanismPrinciples of justice should apply globallyPogge, CaneyGlobal
StatismJustice is mainly within the stateRawls, MillerState
RelationalismJustice depends on the type of relationshipBlake, SangiovanniDetermined by relations
Capability approachFocus on the guarantee of basic capabilitiesNussbaum, SenIndividual capabilities

III. The Core Issues of Global Justice Theory

Global justice theory focuses on the following core issues:

Table 31.14 The Core Issues of Global Justice Theory

IssueContentMain Debates
The issue of distributive justiceHow should global resources be distributed?Equality vs. sufficiency vs. priority
The issue of human rightsWhich rights are universal?The scope and content of rights
The issue of institutional justiceHow should global institutions be designed?State sovereignty vs. global governance
The issue of migration justiceHow should the rights of migrants be guaranteed?Open borders vs. state control
The issue of climate justiceHow should climate responsibility be distributed?Historical responsibility vs. current capacity

§31.3 Dialogue with Complex Systems Science

§31.3.1 The Core Concepts of Complex Systems Science

I. The Historical Development of Complex Systems Science

Definition 31.3.1 (Complex Systems Science)

Complex Systems Science is the interdisciplinary field that studies systems composed of a large number of interacting components, focusing on phenomena such as emergence, self-organization, and nonlinear dynamics[3].

The historical development of complex systems science can be divided into several stages:

Table 31.22 The Historical Development of Complex Systems Science

StagePeriodMain FeaturesRepresentative Figures/Institutions
Precursor stage1940s-1960sCybernetics, systems theoryWiener, Bertalanffy
Formation stage1970s-1980sChaos theory, dissipative structuresPrigogine, Lorenz
Development stage1980s-1990sThe Santa Fe schoolSanta Fe Institute
Maturity stage2000s to presentNetwork science, computational social scienceBarabási, Newman

II. The Core Concepts of Complex Systems Science

Complex systems science encompasses multiple core concepts:

Table 31.23 The Core Concepts of Complex Systems Science

ConceptDefinitionRelation to This Work
EmergenceThe whole possesses properties that the parts do notConsciousness as an emergent phenomenon
Self-organizationThe system spontaneously forms ordered structuresThe formation of negentropic organization
NonlinearityInput and output are not proportionalA source of deep uncertainty
FeedbackOutput affects inputThe feedback mechanism of versioned governance
AdaptivityThe system adjusts according to the environmentThe adaptivity of the protocol stack
CriticalityThe system is at the edge of a phase transitionEcological tipping points

III. A Detailed Analysis of the Concept of Emergence

Definition 31.3.2 (Emergence)

Emergence refers to the fact that the overall properties of a complex system cannot be reduced to a simple sum of the properties of its components, but rather are new properties produced through the interactions among the components[4].

Formal expression:

$$\text{Emergence}: P(\text{System}) \neq \sum_i P(\text{Component}_i)$$

where $P$ denotes a property.

II. The Relation of Emergence to This Work:

Table 31.24 The Relation of Emergence to This Work

Type of EmergenceExampleApplication in This Work
Weak emergenceComputable but unpredictableThe behavior of complex systems
Strong emergenceIrreducible new propertiesConsciousness as emergence
Epistemological emergenceEmergence caused by cognitive limitationsDeep uncertainty
Ontological emergenceGenuinely new propertiesThe emergence of subjecthood

III. A Detailed Analysis of the Concept of Self-organization

Definition 31.3.3 (Self-organization)

Self-organization refers to the process by which a system, without external instructions, spontaneously forms ordered structures through internal interactions[5].

Formal expression:

$$\text{Self-organization}: \text{Order}(t_2) > \text{Order}(t_1) \text{ without external control}$$

IV. The Relation of Self-organization to Negentropy:

$$\text{Self-organization} \Leftrightarrow \text{Local negentropy increase}$$

§31.4 Dialogue with the Philosophy of Technology

§31.4.1 The Core Issues of the Philosophy of Technology

I. The Historical Development of the Philosophy of Technology

Definition 31.4.1 (Philosophy of Technology)

The Philosophy of Technology is the branch of philosophy that studies the nature of technology, the relationship between technology and humans, and the ethical and social impacts of technology[8].

The historical development of the philosophy of technology can be divided into several stages:

Table 31.31 The Historical Development of the Philosophy of Technology

StagePeriodMain FeaturesRepresentative Figures
Precursor stageLate 19th century - early 20th centuryCritique of technologyMarx, Heidegger
Formation stage1950s-1970sDisciplinary establishmentEllul, Mumford
Development stage1980s-1990sThe empirical turnBijker, Latour
Maturity stage2000s to presentThe ethics of emerging technologiesFloridi, Bostrom

II. The Core Issues of the Philosophy of Technology

The philosophy of technology focuses on the following core issues:

Table 31.32 The Core Issues of the Philosophy of Technology

IssueContentMain Debates
The issue of the nature of technologyWhat is technology?Instrument vs. system vs. mode of being
The issue of technological determinismDoes technology determine society?Determinism vs. constructivism
The issue of technological neutralityIs technology value-neutral?Neutrality vs. value-ladenness
The issue of technological ethicsThe ethical responsibility of technology?Designer vs. user vs. technology itself
The issue of the human-technology relationshipThe relationship between humans and technology?Subject vs. object vs. symbiosis

III. A Detailed Analysis of the Issue of the Nature of Technology

The philosophy of technology has multiple understandings of the nature of technology:

Table 31.33 Different Understandings of the Nature of Technology

UnderstandingCore ClaimRepresentative FiguresRelation to This Work

SubstantivismTechnology is an autonomous forceEllulPartially accepted
PhenomenologyTechnology is a mode of beingHeideggerPartially borrowed
PostphenomenologyTechnology mediates the human-world relationIhdeImportant borrowing
Actor-network theoryTechnology is an actorLatourImportant borrowing

Chapter Summary

Core Conclusions

This chapter has conducted a dialogue with multiple academic traditions, and the main conclusions include:

Conclusion One: Dialogue with Environmental Ethics

This work and environmental ethics share multiple points of common ground (expanding the scope of moral consideration, concern for intergenerational justice, concern for wholeness, etc.), and also have important differences (spatial scope, type of subject, value basis, etc.). The two can be integrated at the conceptual, principles, institutional, and methodological levels, and negentropic value can serve as the physical basis of the value of life.

Table 31.63 The Core Conclusions of the Dialogue with Environmental Ethics

DimensionConclusion
Common groundExpanded moral consideration, intergenerational justice, wholeness, intrinsic value, sustainability

IntegrationNegentropic value as the physical basis of the value of life, CSIA as an extension of environmental impact assessment

Conclusion Two: Dialogue with Global Justice Theory

This work and global justice theory share multiple points of common ground (going beyond national borders, concern for institutional design, concern for distributive justice, etc.), and also have important differences (spatial scope, type of subject, time scale, etc.). The two can be integrated at the conceptual, principles, institutional, and methodological levels, and cosmic justice can serve as an extension of global justice.

Conclusion Three: Dialogue with Complex Systems Science

The dialogue in this chapter has produced rich gains, including gains at the conceptual and methodological levels. At the same time, the dialogue also has limitations in coverage, depth, integration, and culture. In the future, it is necessary to proceed in four directions: expanding the scope of dialogue, deepening the depth of dialogue, improving methods of integration, and practical dialogue.

Conclusion Seven: The Relation to the New Three Views

The dialogue in this chapter embodies the core claims of the New Three Views:

  • NC-1 (relational ontology): The ecological relations of environmental ethics, the dependent origination of Buddhism, and the all things as one body of Daoism all support relational ontology
  • NC-2 (process ontology): The emergence of complex systems science, the impermanence of Buddhism, and the flow of the Dao of Daoism all support process ontology
  • NC-3 (participatory universe): The technological participation of the philosophy of technology and the unity of knowledge and action of Confucianism both support the participatory universe
  • NL-1 (continuum of life): The view of life of environmental ethics and the view of sentient beings of Buddhism both support the continuum of life
  • NL-2 (negentropic organization): The concept of self-organization of complex systems science supports negentropic organization
  • NK-1 (participatory cognition): The unity of knowledge and action of Confucianism and the enlightenment of Buddhism both support participatory cognition
  • NK-4 (deliberative knowledge): The deliberative democracy of global justice theory supports deliberative knowledge

[1] Environmental Ethics as an independent discipline began in the 1970s. In 1973, the Australian philosopher Richard Routley published the pioneering paper "Is There a Need for a New, an Environmental, Ethic?", marking the formal birth of environmental ethics. Thereafter, scholars such as Peter Singer, Tom Regan, Paul Taylor, J. Baird Callicott, and Holmes Rolston III made important contributions. See Jamieson (2008), Light & Rolston (2003).

[2] The modern development of Global Justice Theory began in the 1970s. Charles Beitz's Political Theory and International Relations (1979) and Thomas Pogge's Realizing Rawls (1989) are foundational works in this field. Thereafter, scholars such as Martha Nussbaum, Amartya Sen, Simon Caney, and David Miller made important contributions. See Brock (2009), Caney (2005).

[3] Complex Systems Science is an interdisciplinary field that studies systems composed of a large number of interacting components. The development of this field can be traced back to cybernetics (Wiener), systems theory (Bertalanffy), chaos theory (Lorenz), and the theory of dissipative structures (Prigogine). The Santa Fe Institute has been an important research center in this field since its founding in 1984. See Mitchell (2009), Holland (2014).

[4] Emergence is one of the core concepts of complex systems science. Emergence refers to the fact that the whole possesses properties that the parts do not. There is debate about the ontological status of emergence, with two main views: weak emergence (computable but unpredictable) and strong emergence (irreducible new properties). See Bedau & Humphreys (2008), Clayton & Davies (2006).

[5] Self-organization refers to the process by which a system spontaneously forms ordered structures without external instructions. Ilya Prigogine's theory of dissipative structures provides a thermodynamic basis for self-organization. The relation between self-organization and negentropy is: the process of self-organization is a process of local negentropy increase. See Prigogine & Stengers (1984), Kauffman (1993).

[6] Agent-Based Modeling (ABM) is a computational method that studies the emergent behavior of complex systems by simulating the behavior and interactions of autonomous agents. ABM has wide applications in fields such as the social sciences, ecology, and economics. See Epstein & Axtell (1996), Gilbert (2008).

[7] Network Analysis is the method of using graph theory and network science tools to analyze the structure and dynamics of systems. Scholars such as Albert-László Barabási and Mark Newman have made important contributions in the field of network science. See Barabási (2016), Newman (2018).

[8] The Philosophy of Technology is the branch of philosophy that studies the nature of technology, the relationship between technology and humans, and the ethical and social impacts of technology. The development of this field can be traced back to the work of scholars such as Martin Heidegger, Jacques Ellul, and Lewis Mumford. Contemporary philosophy of technology has undergone an "empirical turn," focusing more on the philosophical analysis of concrete technologies. See Verbeek (2005), Ihde (1990).

[9] The Confucian tradition is the Chinese philosophical tradition founded by Confucius (551-479 BCE). Confucianism emphasizes core values such as benevolence (ren), righteousness (yi), propriety (li), wisdom (zhi), and trustworthiness (xin), and focuses on human moral cultivation and social order. Mencius, Xunzi, Zhu Xi, and Wang Yangming are important representatives of the Confucian tradition. See Tu (1985), Angle (2009).

[10] The Buddhist tradition is the religious and philosophical tradition based on the teachings of Shakyamuni Buddha (c. 563-483 BCE). Buddhism emphasizes core concepts such as dependent origination, no-self, suffering, and nirvana, and focuses on liberation and enlightenment. Buddhism has several major traditions, including Theravada, Mahayana, and Vajrayana. See Siderits (2007), Garfield (2015).

[11] The Daoist tradition is the Chinese philosophical tradition represented by Laozi and Zhuangzi. Daoism emphasizes core concepts such as the Dao, naturalness, and non-action, and focuses on harmony between humans and nature. The Daodejing and the Zhuangzi are the core texts of Daoism. See Graham (1989), Moeller (2006).

[12] Aldo Leopold (1887-1948) was an American ecologist and a pioneer of environmental ethics. His A Sand County Almanac (1949) proposed the concept of the "Land Ethic," which had a profound influence on the development of environmental ethics. See Leopold (1949).

[13] Peter Singer (1946-) is an Australian philosopher and an important representative of utilitarian ethics. His Animal Liberation (1975) is a foundational work in animal ethics. Singer advocates expanding the scope of moral consideration to include all sentient beings. See Singer (1975, 2011).

[14] John Rawls (1921-2002) was an American political philosopher and an important representative of contemporary political philosophy. His A Theory of Justice (1971) and The Law of Peoples (1999) had a profound influence on global justice theory. See Rawls (1971, 1999).

[15] Thomas Pogge (1953-) is a German-American philosopher and an important representative of global justice theory. His World Poverty and Human Rights (2002) proposed an institutional analysis of global poverty. See Pogge (2002).

[16] Ilya Prigogine (1917-2003) was a Belgian physical chemist and the 1977 Nobel laureate in Chemistry. His theory of dissipative structures provided a thermodynamic basis for self-organization and complex systems. See Prigogine & Stengers (1984).

[17] Martin Heidegger (1889-1976) was a German philosopher and an important representative of phenomenology and existentialism. His The Question Concerning Technology (1954) is a classic text in the philosophy of technology. See Heidegger (1977).

[18] Don Ihde (1934-) is an American philosopher and the founder of postphenomenology. His Technology and the Lifeworld (1990) developed a phenomenological analysis of technology. See Ihde (1990).

[19] Ubuntu is a concept in the South African Zulu and Xhosa languages, meaning "I am because we are." Ubuntu ethics emphasizes the relationality and communality of persons, and is akin to the relational ontology of this work. See Metz (2007), Ramose (1999).

[20] The unity of knowledge and action is the core idea of the Ming dynasty Confucian scholar Wang Yangming (1472-1529), emphasizing the unity of knowledge and action. This idea is akin to the participatory cognition of this work. See Wang (1963), Ivanhoe (2009).

VI. Methodological Commitments

This chapter adheres to the following methodological commitments:

  1. Feasibility commitment: all research agendas should be realistically feasible
  2. Priority commitment: clearly distinguish the priorities of different agendas
  3. Resource-awareness commitment: take resource constraints into account
  4. Openness commitment: the research agenda should remain open and can be adjusted according to progress
  5. Collaborative commitment: emphasize interdisciplinary and inter-institutional cooperation

§32.1 Empirical Validation of the Indicator System

§32.1.1 UCS Validation Research Design

I. Necessity of UCS Validation

Definition 32.1.1 (UCS Validation Research)

UCS validation research refers to systematic research that tests the validity, reliability, and operability of the Universal Consciousness Scale through empirical methods[1].

II. The Necessity of UCS Validation Derives from the Following Considerations:

Table 32.3 Necessity of UCS Validation

DimensionCurrent StateValidation Need
Conceptual validityConceptual prototypeTest whether the concept captures the core features of consciousness
Measurement validityUnvalidatedTest whether the measurement method is valid
Cross-substrate applicabilityTheoretical assumptionTest whether it applies to different types of systems
OperabilityLimitedDevelop operable measurement methods

III. Design Framework for UCS Validation Research

UCS validation research should include the following components:

Table 32.4 Components of UCS Validation Research

ComponentContentMethod
Conceptual validationTest the validity of the UCS conceptConceptual analysis, expert review
Convergent validity validationTest the relation to existing consciousness measuresCorrelation analysis
Discriminant validity validationTest discrimination from non-consciousness measuresDiscriminant analysis
Cross-substrate validationTest applicability across different systemsComparative study
Reliability validationTest the stability of measurementTest-retest reliability, inter-rater reliability

IV. Specific Design of UCS Validation Research

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  UCS Validation Research Design Framework                       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│  Study 1: Conceptual Validity Study                             │
│  ├─ Goal: Test whether the UCS concept captures the core features of consciousness│
│  ├─ Methods:                                                    │
│  │   - Literature review: integrate existing theories of consciousness│
│  │   - Expert Delphi method: solicit opinions of consciousness science experts│
│  │   - Concept mapping: establish a mapping between UCS and existing theories│
│  ├─ Expected output: UCS conceptual validity report             │
│  └─ Time: 6-12 mo                                               │
│                                                                 │
│  Study 2: Convergent Validity Study                             │
│  ├─ Goal: Test the relation between UCS and existing consciousness measures│
│  ├─ Methods:                                                    │
│  │   - Select existing consciousness measurement tools (e.g., PCI, C-Scale)│
│  │   - Measure the same sample with UCS and existing tools      │
│  │   - Compute correlation coefficients                         │
│  ├─ Expected output: convergent validity report                 │
│  └─ Time: 12-18 mo                                              │
│                                                                 │
│  Study 3: Cross-Substrate Validation Study                      │
│  ├─ Goal: Test the applicability of UCS across different types of systems│
│  ├─ Methods:                                                    │
│  │   - Select different types of systems (humans, animals, AI systems)│
│  │   - Develop UCS measurement methods for different systems    │
│  │   - Compare UCS distributions across different systems       │
│  ├─ Expected output: cross-substrate applicability report       │
│  └─ Time: 18-36 mo                                              │
│                                                                 │
│  Study 4: Reliability Study                                     │
│  ├─ Goal: Test the stability of UCS measurement                 │
│  ├─ Methods:                                                    │
│  │   - Test-retest reliability: repeated measurement of the same sample│
│  │   - Inter-rater reliability: multiple raters scoring the same sample│
│  │   - Internal consistency: test the internal consistency of the scale│
│  ├─ Expected output: reliability report                         │
│  └─ Time: 12-24 mo                                              │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

V. Specific Methods of UCS Validation Research

Table 32.5 Specific Methods of UCS Validation Research

Research TypeSpecific MethodSample RequirementAnalysis Method
Conceptual validationDelphi method20-30 expertsConsensus analysis
Convergent validityCorrelational study100-200 peopleCorrelation analysis
Cross-substrate validationComparative studyMulti-type systemsAnalysis of variance
ReliabilityTest-retest study50-100 peopleICC computation

Theory of ConsciousnessCore ConceptRelation to UCSValidation Method

DimensionCurrent StateValidation Need

Table 32.8 Components of RFD Validation Research

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  RFD Validation Research Design Framework                       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│  Study 1: Conceptual Validity Study                             │
│  ├─ Goal: Test whether the RFD concept captures the core features of the possibility space│
│  ├─ Methods:                                                    │
│  │   - Literature review: integrate theories related to the possibility space│
│  │   - Expert Delphi method: solicit opinions of complex systems experts│
│  │   - Concept mapping: establish a mapping between RFD and existing theories│
│  ├─ Expected output: RFD conceptual validity report             │
│  └─ Time: 6-12 mo                                               │
│                                                                 │
│  Study 2: Computational Validation Study                        │
│  ├─ Goal: Test the validity of the RFD computation method       │
│  ├─ Methods:                                                    │
│  │   - Build a simplified model system                          │
│  │   - Compute the RFD of the model system                      │
│  │   - Compare with theoretical expectations                    │
│  ├─ Expected output: computation method validation report       │
│  └─ Time: 12-18 mo                                              │
│                                                                 │
│  Study 3: Predictive Validation Study                           │
│  ├─ Goal: Test whether RFD can predict the adaptability of systems│
│  ├─ Methods:                                                    │
│  │   - Select observable systems (e.g., organizations, ecosystems)│

│  │   - Track the adaptability performance of the systems        │
│  │   - Analyze the relation between RFD and adaptability        │
│  ├─ Expected output: predictive validity report                 │
│  └─ Time: 24-48 mo                                              │
│                                                                 │
│  Study 4: Sensitivity Analysis Study                            │
│  ├─ Goal: Test the sensitivity of RFD to parameter changes      │
│  ├─ Methods:                                                    │
│  │   - Identify the key parameters of RFD computation           │
│  │   - Systematically vary parameter values                     │
│  │   - Analyze changes in RFD                                   │
│  ├─ Expected output: sensitivity analysis report                │
│  └─ Time: 12-18 mo                                              │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

DirectionContentChallengePossible Solution

Node No.Core ConclusionArgumentative Basis

UncertaintyBenefits are highly uncertainUse probabilistic analysis, robustness analysis
Distributional effectsCosts and benefits are unevenly distributedUse distributional analysis, equity assessment

Chapter Summary

Core Conclusions

This chapter has planned the short-term research agenda (1-5 years) of this work. The main conclusions include:

Conclusion One: Empirical Validation of the Indicator System

Empirical validation of the indicator system is the core task of the short-term agenda. All six indicators—UCS, RFD, CRV, CDI, MBCL, and CSIA—require systematic validation research, including conceptual validation, convergent/discriminant validity validation, cross-substrate/cross-domain validation, reliability validation, and predictive validation. Validation research requires substantial resource support and should be rationally allocated according to priorities.

Table 32.67 Core Conclusions of Indicator Validation Research

IndicatorValidation FocusMain ChallengePriority
UCSConceptual validity, cross-substrate applicabilityConsciousness measurement, cross-substrate methodsP1
RFDComputational validity, predictive validityState-space estimation, computational complexityP2
CRVAssessment validity, predictive validityCommitment assessment, long-term trackingP2
CDIHistorical validation, comparative validationData integration, indicator aggregationP3
MBCLCase validation, predictive validationInformation risk assessmentP3
CSIAProcedural validation, comparative validationLarge-action impact assessmentP1

Conclusion Two: Feasibility Research on Institutional Design

Feasibility research on institutional design should include four dimensions: political, legal, technical, and economic. The feasibility of different institutional designs varies considerably and requires targeted advancement strategies. Institutions such as the Multi-Intelligence Tribunal face challenges in political feasibility and require gradual advancement.

Table 32.68 Core Conclusions of Feasibility Research

DimensionResearch FocusMain Challenge
Political feasibilityPolitical will, stakeholders, institutional compatibilitySovereignty sensitivity, conflicts of interest
Legal feasibilityLegal compatibility, legal obstacles, reform pathsLegal reform needs
Technical feasibilityTechnology maturity, technical obstacles, technology developmentImmature technology
Economic feasibilityCost estimation, funding sources, cost-benefitLong-term benefits hard to quantify

Conclusion Three: Academic Community Building

Academic community building is the foundation for the sustainable development of the framework. A gradual strategy should be adopted, from using existing platforms to establishing dedicated platforms. Academic publication platforms, research networks, talent development, and international cooperation are the four core components of academic community building.

Table 32.69 Core Conclusions of Academic Community Building

ComponentShort-Term StrategyMedium-Term StrategyLong-Term Strategy
Journals and conferencesPublish on existing platformsEstablish special issuesEstablish a dedicated journal
Research networksEstablish a core teamExpand the networkInstitutionalize
Talent developmentUse existing platformsDevelop dedicated coursesEstablish degree programs
International cooperationEstablish bilateral cooperationEstablish multilateral networksInstitutionalized cooperation

Conclusion Four: Advancing International Dialogue

International dialogue is an important avenue for framework development and expansion of impact. Systematic dialogue should be conducted with the longtermism community, the AI safety community, the international law community, and the policy community. The dialogue should focus on conceptual integration, methodological integration, resource sharing, and policy coordination.

Table 32.70 Core Conclusions of International Dialogue

Dialogue CommunityDialogue FocusContribution of This WorkLearning from the Other Party
LongtermismNormative foundations, deep uncertaintyDeeper normative foundationsPractical experience
AI safetySubjecthood, alignment, governanceNormative goals, assessment frameworkTechnical methods
International lawLegal framework, institutional designEthical frameworkInstitutional experience
Policy communityPolicy translation, policy impactPolicy recommendationsPolicy feedback

Conclusion Five: Priorities and Resource Allocation

The short-term research agenda should be prioritized according to importance, urgency, feasibility, and synergy. The P1 priority includes UCS validation, CSIA validation, academic publication platform building, and dialogue with the AI safety community. The short-term agenda requires 30-50 person-yr of human resources and 5-10 million USD of financial resources.

Conclusion Six: Relation to the New Three Views

The research agenda planning of this chapter embodies the core claims of the New Three Views:

  • NC-1 (relational ontology): the research agenda emphasizes interdisciplinary and inter-institutional cooperation
  • NC-2 (process ontology): the research agenda adopts iterative, versioned methods
  • NC-3 (participatory universe): the research agenda emphasizes openness and collaboration
  • NL-1 (life continuum): UCS validation research focuses on graded measurement
  • NL-2 (negentropic organization): the physical basis of indicator validation is thermodynamics
  • NK-1 (participatory cognition): research methods emphasize participatory character
  • NK-4 (negotiated knowledge): research results emphasize negotiated character
