[1] The design of UCS validation research draws on the classic methods of psychometrics. Psychometrics emphasizes the validation of validity and reliability. Validity includes content validity, construct validity, convergent validity, and discriminant validity. Reliability includes test-retest reliability, inter-rater reliability, and internal consistency. See Cronbach & Meehl (1955), Messick (1995).

[2] The core challenge facing RFD validation research is the computation of the possibility space. The possibility space is a high-dimensional concept that is hard to compute precisely in actual systems. Possible solutions include dimensionality reduction methods, sampling methods, and approximation algorithms. See Kauffman (1993), Holland (2014).

[3] CRV validation research needs to draw on research in commitment theory and responsibility theory. Commitment theory studies the formation, maintenance, and fulfillment of commitments. Responsibility theory studies the attribution and distribution of responsibility. See Searle (1969), Hart (1968).

[4] Political feasibility is one of the core concepts of policy analysis. Political feasibility analysis focuses on the possibility that a policy will be accepted and implemented in the political environment. See Kingdon (1984), Sabatier & Jenkins-Smith (1993).

[5] Legal feasibility analysis is an important component of institutional design. Legal feasibility analysis focuses on the compatibility of an institutional design with the existing legal framework, as well as the legal reforms required. See Mashaw (1983), Sunstein (1996).

[6] Technical feasibility analysis usually uses the Technology Readiness Level (TRL) as an assessment tool. TRL is a standardized method developed by NASA for assessing technology maturity, divided into levels 1-9. See Mankins (1995).

[7] Economic feasibility analysis includes cost estimation, funding source analysis, and cost-benefit analysis. Cost-benefit analysis is a standard method for assessing the economic value of a project, but it faces challenges when long-term benefits are hard to quantify. See Boardman et al. (2018).

[8] Academic publication platforms are the core infrastructure of the academic community. Academic journals and conferences are the main mechanisms for knowledge accumulation, quality control, and academic dialogue. See Merton (1973), Ziman (2000).

[9] Research networks are an important organizational form of scientific knowledge production. Research networks can integrate dispersed resources, promote interdisciplinary cooperation, and accelerate knowledge sharing. See Powell & Grodal (2005), Borgatti & Halgin (2011).

[10] Talent development is the foundation for the sustainable development of an academic community. Talent development includes formal education (courses, degree programs) and informal education (workshops, internships). See Becher & Trowler (2001).

[11] International cooperation is an important feature of contemporary scientific research. International cooperation can integrate global resources, incorporate diverse perspectives, and expand research impact. See Wagner (2008), Adams (2013).

[12] Longtermism is an ethical and policy stance concerned with the long-term future. The longtermism community includes institutions such as the Future of Humanity Institute (FHI) at Oxford University, the Centre for the Study of Existential Risk (CSER) at Cambridge University, and Open Philanthropy. See MacAskill (2022), Ord (2020).

[13] AI safety research focuses on technical and policy issues that ensure AI systems are safe and beneficial. The AI safety community includes institutions such as the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI), Anthropic, and DeepMind AI Safety. See Russell (2019), Amodei et al. (2016).

[14] International space law is a branch of international law that regulates space activities. The international space law community includes institutions such as the International Institute of Space Law (IISL) and the International Institute of Air and Space Law (IIASL). See Masson-Zwaan & Freeland (2010).

[15] The policy community is a network of actors involved in policy-making and implementation. The policy community includes policy-makers, policy researchers, policy advocates, and stakeholders. See Sabatier (1988), Haas (1992).

[16] Priority ranking is a core method of project management and strategic planning. Priority ranking is usually based on criteria such as importance, urgency, and feasibility. See Covey (1989), Eisenhower Matrix.

[17] The Delphi Method is a structured expert consultation method that converges expert opinions through multiple rounds of anonymous surveys. The Delphi Method is widely used in technology forecasting, policy analysis, and conceptual validation. See Linstone & Turoff (1975).

[18] Integrated Information Theory (IIT) is a theory of consciousness proposed by Giulio Tononi that quantifies the degree of consciousness with Φ (phi). IIT provides the theoretical basis for the D₁ dimension of UCS (degree of information integration). See Tononi (2004), Oizumi et al. (2014).

[19] Global Workspace Theory (GWT) is a theory of consciousness proposed by Bernard Baars that emphasizes the relation between consciousness and global information integration. GWT provides support for the theoretical basis of UCS. See Baars (1988), Dehaene & Naccache (2001).

[20] The Technology Readiness Level (TRL) is a standardized method developed by NASA for assessing technology maturity. TRL is divided into 9 levels, from basic research (TRL 1) to practical application (TRL 9). See Mankins (1995), NASA (2012).

Footnotes

Chapter 32 Footnotes

[1] The design of the UCS validation study draws on classic methods in psychometrics. Psychometrics emphasizes the validation of validity and reliability. Validity includes content validity, construct validity, convergent validity, and discriminant validity. Reliability includes test-retest reliability, inter-rater reliability, and internal consistency. See Cronbach & Meehl (1955), Messick (1995).

[2] The core challenge facing the RFD validation study is the computation of the possibility space. The possibility space is a high-dimensional concept that is difficult to compute exactly in real systems. Possible solutions include dimensionality reduction methods, sampling methods, and approximation algorithms. See Kauffman (1993), Holland (2014).

[3] The CRV validation study needs to draw on research in commitment theory and responsibility theory. Commitment theory studies the formation, maintenance, and fulfillment of commitments. Responsibility theory studies the attribution and distribution of responsibility. See Searle (1969), Hart (1968).

[4] Political feasibility is one of the core concepts of policy analysis. Political feasibility analysis is concerned with the likelihood that a policy will be accepted and implemented in a political environment. See Kingdon (1984), Sabatier & Jenkins-Smith (1993).

[5] Legal feasibility analysis is an important component of institutional design. Legal feasibility analysis is concerned with the compatibility of an institutional design with the existing legal framework and with the legal reforms required. See Mashaw (1983), Sunstein (1996).

[6] Technical feasibility analysis usually uses the Technology Readiness Level (TRL) as an assessment tool. TRL is a standardized method developed by NASA for assessing technological maturity, divided into levels 1-9. See Mankins (1995).

[7] Economic feasibility analysis includes cost estimation, funding source analysis, and cost-benefit analysis. Cost-benefit analysis is the standard method for assessing the economic value of a project, but it faces challenges where long-term benefits are difficult to quantify. See Boardman et al. (2018).

[8] Academic publication platforms are the core infrastructure of the academic community. Academic journals and conferences are the principal mechanisms of knowledge accumulation, quality control, and academic dialogue. See Merton (1973), Ziman (2000).

[9] Research networks are an important organizational form of scientific knowledge production. Research networks can integrate dispersed resources, promote interdisciplinary cooperation, and accelerate knowledge sharing. See Powell & Grodal (2005), Borgatti & Halgin (2011).

[10] Talent development is the foundation of the sustainable development of the academic community. Talent development includes formal education (courses, degree programs) and informal education (workshops, internships). See Becher & Trowler (2001).

[11] International cooperation is an important feature of contemporary scientific research. International cooperation can integrate global resources, incorporate diverse perspectives, and expand research impact. See Wagner (2008), Adams (2013).

[12] Longtermism is an ethical and policy position concerned with the long-term future. The longtermism community includes institutions such as the Future of Humanity Institute (FHI) at Oxford, the Centre for the Study of Existential Risk (CSER) at Cambridge, and Open Philanthropy. See MacAskill (2022), Ord (2020).

[13] AI safety research is concerned with the technical and policy problems of ensuring that AI systems are safe and beneficial. The AI safety community includes institutions such as the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI), Anthropic, and DeepMind AI Safety. See Russell (2019), Amodei et al. (2016).

[14] International space law is the branch of international law governing space activities. The international space law community includes institutions such as the International Institute of Space Law (IISL) and the International Institute of Air and Space Law (IIASL). See Masson-Zwaan & Freeland (2010).

[15] A policy community is a network of actors involved in the formulation and implementation of policy. A policy community includes policymakers, policy researchers, policy advocates, and stakeholders. See Sabatier (1988), Haas (1992).

[16] Prioritization is a core method of project management and strategic planning. Prioritization is usually based on criteria such as importance, urgency, and feasibility. See Covey (1989), Eisenhower Matrix.

[17] The Delphi Method is a structured method of expert consultation that converges expert opinion through multiple rounds of anonymous survey. The Delphi Method is widely used in technology forecasting, policy analysis, and proof of concept. See Linstone & Turoff (1975).

[18] Integrated Information Theory (IIT) is a theory of consciousness proposed by Giulio Tononi that quantifies the degree of consciousness by Φ (phi). IIT provides the theoretical foundation for the D₁ dimension of the UCS (degree of information integration). See Tononi (2004), Oizumi et al. (2014).

[19] Global Workspace Theory (GWT) is a theory of consciousness proposed by Bernard Baars that emphasizes the relationship between consciousness and global information integration. GWT provides support for the theoretical foundations of the UCS. See Baars (1988), Dehaene & Naccache (2001).

[20] The Technology Readiness Level (TRL) is a standardized method developed by NASA for assessing technological maturity. TRL is divided into nine levels, from basic research (TRL 1) to practical application (TRL 9). See Mankins (1995), NASA (2012).

III. Core Tasks of This Chapter

This chapter undertakes five core tasks:

T-2Explore policy translation pathsPolicy translation roadmap

T-5Set medium-term milestonesMilestone system

Time Span and Characteristics of the Medium-Term Agenda

The medium-term agenda covers a time span of 5-20 years and has the following characteristics:

Table 33.1 Characteristics of the Medium-Term Agenda

CharacteristicShort-Term Agenda (1-5 yr)Medium-Term Agenda (5-20 yr)Long-Term Agenda (20 yr+)
Core taskFoundation-layingDevelopmentMaturation
UncertaintyRelatively lowMediumRelatively high
Planning precisionHighMediumLow
Flexibility requirementRelatively lowMediumHigh
Milestone typeConcretePhasedDirectional

The choice of the time span of the medium-term agenda is based on the following considerations:

  1. Technology development cycle: major technological breakthroughs (such as AGI) may occur during this period
  2. Institutional change cycle: major changes in international institutions usually take 10-20 years
  3. Disciplinary construction cycle: a new discipline usually takes 15-20 years from emergence to initial maturity
  4. Generational replacement cycle: the academic career of one generation of scholars is about 20-30 years

IV. Relation to the New Three Views

The medium-term agenda planning of this chapter needs to proceed from the perspective of the New Three Views:

V. Methodological Commitments

This chapter adheres to the following methodological commitments:

  1. Adaptability commitment: the medium-term agenda should be adaptable and can be adjusted according to environmental changes
  2. Phasing commitment: set clear phased milestones
  3. Evaluability commitment: each phase should have evaluable indicators
  4. Openness commitment: remain open to new scenarios and new challenges
  5. Collaborative commitment: emphasize interdisciplinary, inter-institutional, and cross-border collaboration

§33.1 Continuous Revision and Refinement of the Framework

§33.1.1 Revision Based on Empirical Research

I. Necessity of Revision Based on Empirical Research

Definition 33.1.1 (Revision Based on Empirical Research)

Revision based on empirical research refers to the process of adjusting and refining a theoretical framework according to the results of empirical research, and is the core mechanism of theoretical development[1].

Table 33.3 Necessity of Empirical Research Revision

DimensionExplanationSignificance for This Work
Validation functionTest theoretical predictionsConfirm or falsify the core claims of the framework
Calibration functionCalibrate parameters and weightsOptimize the parameters of the indicator system
Extension functionDiscover new phenomenaExtend the scope of application of the framework
Correction functionCorrect errorsRectify the defects of the framework

II. Sources of Empirical Research Revision

Table 33.4 Sources of Empirical Research Revision

Source TypeContentExpected Time
Indicator validation researchValidation results of indicators such as UCS, RFD, and CRV5-10 yr
Case studiesEarth-scale application cases5-15 yr
Simulation researchResults of computer simulation5-10 yr
Natural experimentsNatural experiments provided by technological development and social changeContinuous

│        │                                                        │
│        ↓                                                        │
│  Phase 2: Deviation Diagnosis                                   │
│  ├─ Diagnose the sources of deviation                           │
│  │   - Measurement error                                        │
│  │   - Theoretical defects                                      │
│  │   - Boundary conditions not satisfied                        │
│  └─ Determine revision needs                                    │
│        │                                                        │
│        ↓                                                        │
│  Phase 3: Revision Proposal                                     │
│  ├─ Propose revision options                                    │
│  ├─ Assess the impact of the revision options                   │
│  └─ Select the optimal revision option                          │
│        │                                                        │
│        ↓                                                        │

§33.1.4 Version Management

I. Necessity of Version Management

Definition 33.1.4 (Version Management)

Version management refers to the method of systematically managing different versions of a theoretical framework using semantic version numbers, ensuring the traceability and rollback capability of revisions[4].

Table 33.12 Necessity of Version Management

DimensionExplanationSignificance for This Work
TraceabilityTrace the revision historyUnderstand the evolution of the framework
Rollback capabilityRoll back to an earlier versionRespond to revision failure
Compatibility managementManage version compatibilityEnsure the stability of applications
Collaboration supportSupport multi-party collaborationPromote open collaboration

II. Version Number Rules

This work adopts Semantic Versioning:

Table 33.13 Version Number Rules

Version TypeChange TypeExampleExplanation

PATCHBackward-compatible bug fixv1.0.0 → v1.0.1Fix errors, clarify wording

│  └─ 6. Tag the version                                          │

│  └─ Effect: Ensure that the framework can continuously evolve   │
│                                                                 │

│  ├─ Content: Design redundancy at key links to enhance robustness│
│  ├─ Methods:                                                    │
│  │   - Identify key links of the framework                      │
│  │   - Design alternative options for key links                 │
│  │   - Establish failover mechanisms                            │
│  └─ Effect: Improve the robustness of the framework under unexpected scenarios│

Chapter Summary

Core Conclusions

This chapter has planned the medium-term research agenda (5-20 years) of this work. The main conclusions include:

Conclusion One: Continuous Revision and Refinement of the Framework

Continuous revision and refinement of the framework is the core task of the medium-term agenda. Revision should be based on three sources: empirical research, stress testing, and international dialogue. A systematic revision mechanism should be established, and version management should be adopted to ensure the traceability and rollback capability of revisions.

Table 33.51 Core Conclusions of Framework Revision

Revision SourceRevision ContentRevision MechanismExpected Version
Empirical researchIndicator parameters, computation methodsData-driven revisionv1.1.0
Stress testingWeakness patching, robustness enhancementWeakness-driven revisionv1.2.0
International dialogueConceptual integration, methodological borrowingDialogue-driven revisionv1.3.0
SynthesisMajor version updateComprehensive revisionv2.0.0

Conclusion Two: Exploration of Policy Translation

Policy translation is an important task of the medium-term agenda. Policy translation should be advanced through four links: pilot projects, policy experiments, impact evaluation, and lessons learned. Pilot projects test feasibility, policy experiments assess causal effects, impact evaluation tests actual effects, and lessons learned distills scalable knowledge.

Table 33.52 Core Conclusions of Policy Translation

LinkPurposeMethodOutput
Pilot projectsTest feasibilityLimited-scope implementationPilot report
Policy experimentsAssess causal effectExperimental methodsExperiment report
Impact evaluationTest actual effectMulti-tiered evaluationEvaluation report
Lessons learnedDistill scalable knowledgeSystematic summarizationBest practice guide

Conclusion Three: Deepening Interdisciplinary Integration

Interdisciplinary integration is a key task of the medium-term agenda. Deep integration should be conducted with the natural sciences, the social sciences, and the humanities. An integration methodology should be developed to ensure the systematicity, consistency, and effectiveness of integration.

Table 33.53 Core Conclusions of Interdisciplinary Integration

Discipline TypeIntegration AreaExpected ContributionIntegration Method
Natural sciencesPhysics, biology, neuroscienceDeepen the scientific basisConceptual interfacing, level correspondence
Social sciencesEconomics, political science, sociologyDeepen the social basisTheoretical integration, methodological borrowing
HumanitiesPhilosophy, history, religious studiesDeepen the humanistic basisConceptual dialogue, cultural sensitivity

Conclusion Four: Response to New Scenarios

Response to new scenarios is a continuous challenge of the medium-term agenda. Attention should be paid to three types of new scenarios: technological development, social change, and environmental change. The adaptability of the framework should be enhanced through five strategies: modular design, parameterized design, scenario-branch design, continuous learning mechanisms, and redundancy design.

Table 33.54 Core Conclusions of Response to New Scenarios

Scenario TypeMain ChallengeResponse StrategyAdaptability Enhancement
Technological developmentAGI, biotechnology, neurotechnologyAdvance preparation, adaptive designModularization, parameterization
Social changePolitical landscape, cultural changePluralistic participation, cultural adaptationScenario branching, continuous learning
Environmental changeClimate change, ecological tipping pointsFramework application, emergency mechanismsRedundancy design

Conclusion Five: Milestones of the Medium-Term Agenda

The medium-term agenda should set clear phased milestones. The 5-year milestone focuses on completing the foundation-laying, the 10-year milestone focuses on deepening development, the 15-year milestone focuses on translation breakthroughs, and the 20-year milestone focuses on maturation and transition.

Table 33.55 Core Conclusions of Medium-Term Agenda Milestones

MilestoneCore ThemeKey ResultSuccess Criterion
5 yrFoundation-laying completedv1.1.0, validation report, pilot reportFoundation work completed
10 yrDeepening of developmentv1.2.0, experiment report, integration reportGood development momentum
15 yrTranslation breakthroughv1.3.0, policy cases, institutional prototypeSubstantive impact
20 yrMaturation and transitionv2.0.0, disciplinary maturation, long-term preparationReady to enter the long term

Conclusion Six: Relation to the New Three Views

The medium-term agenda planning of this chapter embodies the core claims of the New Three Views:

  • NC-1 (relational ontology): framework revision emphasizes multi-party dialogue and relationality
  • NC-2 (process ontology): framework development adopts versioned, iterative methods
  • NC-3 (participatory universe): framework development emphasizes open collaboration and co-construction
  • NL-1 (life continuum): interdisciplinary integration expands the scope of subjects
  • NL-2 (negentropic organization): framework development enhances the adaptability of civilization
  • NK-1 (participatory cognition): policy translation emphasizes action research and collaborative research
  • NK-4 (negotiated knowledge): international dialogue emphasizes interdisciplinary and cross-cultural negotiation

[1] Revision based on empirical research is the core mechanism of scientific theory development. Popper emphasized that theories should be falsifiable, and the results of empirical research can falsify or support a theory. Kuhn emphasized the importance of paradigm shifts. This work adopts a method of gradual revision, adjusting specific content according to the results of empirical research while keeping the core propositions stable. See Popper (1959), Kuhn (1962).

[2] Revision based on stress testing draws on the stress testing methods of engineering and finance. Stress testing identifies the weaknesses and boundaries of a system by testing it under extreme conditions. This work conducted stress tests under four extreme scenarios in Part V, identifying the main weaknesses of the framework. See Taleb (2012), Bank for International Settlements (2009).

[3] Revision based on international dialogue embodies the social character of knowledge production. Scientific knowledge is not produced in isolation, but develops through dialogue and criticism within the academic community. This work conducted dialogue with the communities of longtermism, AI safety, and international space law in Part VIII. See Longino (1990), Kitcher (2001).

[4] Version management draws on the version control methods of software engineering. Semantic Versioning is a widely used version number specification that represents different types of changes through major, minor, and patch numbers. See Preston-Werner (2013).

[5] Pilot projects are a common method of policy implementation. Pilot projects implement a policy within a limited scope to test its feasibility and effect, providing a basis for large-scale scaling up. See Pressman & Wildavsky (1984), Bardach (1977).

[6] Policy experiments are the core method of evidence-based policy-making. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are regarded as the "gold standard" for assessing causal effects, but their application in the policy field faces ethical and practical challenges. See Banerjee & Duflo (2011), Cartwright & Hardie (2012).

[7] Impact evaluation is the core method of project management and policy analysis. Impact evaluation usually includes tiers such as output evaluation, outcome evaluation, impact evaluation, and sustainability evaluation. See Rossi et al. (2004), Weiss (1998).

[8] Lessons learned is the core mechanism of organizational learning. Lessons learned transforms tacit knowledge into explicit knowledge, so that experience can be passed on and scaled up. See Nonaka & Takeuchi (1995), Argyris & Schön (1978).

[9] Integration with the natural sciences is an important direction of interdisciplinary research. The framework of this work is built on physics (thermodynamics, information theory), biology (evolutionary theory, ecology), and neuroscience (consciousness science). See Wilson (1998), Gell-Mann (1994).

[10] Integration with the social sciences is an important basis of institutional design. Institutional economics, political science, and sociology provide theoretical foundations and empirical evidence for institutional design. See North (1990), Ostrom (1990), Acemoglu & Robinson (2012).

[11] Integration with the humanities is an important basis of normative argumentation. Philosophy (ethics, metaphysics, epistemology) provides the theoretical basis for normative principles. History and religious studies provide perspectives for cultural sensitivity. See MacIntyre (1981), Taylor (1989).

[12] Integration methodology is the methodological basis of interdisciplinary research. Interdisciplinary integration faces challenges such as conceptual incompatibility and methodological inconsistency, and requires systematic methodological guidance. See Klein (1990), Repko (2012).

[13] New scenarios of technological development are one of the main challenges facing the medium-term agenda. Breakthroughs in areas such as AGI, biotechnology, and neurotechnology may occur within the medium-term time span, posing new challenges to the framework. See Bostrom (2014), Russell (2019).

[14] New scenarios of social change are an important challenge facing the medium-term agenda. Changes in demographic structure, political landscape, economic structure, and cultural change may affect the applicability of the framework. See Castells (2010), Beck (1992).

[15] New scenarios of environmental change are an urgent challenge facing the medium-term agenda. Environmental problems such as climate change, biodiversity loss, and resource depletion may intensify within the medium-term time span. See IPCC (2021), Rockström et al. (2009).

[16] Framework adaptability is a core concept of complex systems theory. Adaptive systems can adjust their own structure and behavior according to environmental changes. The framework of this work should be adaptable and capable of responding to the challenges of new scenarios. See Holland (1995), Gunderson & Holling (2002).

[17] Milestones are a core tool of project management. A milestone is a key node in a project, marking the completion of an important phase. Milestones should have clear deliverables and verification criteria. See Project Management Institute (2017).

[18] The 10-year milestone marks the midpoint of the medium-term agenda. At this node, the framework should have completed revision based on stress testing, policy experiments should have begun to produce results, and interdisciplinary integration should have made substantive progress. See Mintzberg (1994).

[19] The 15-year milestone marks the translation breakthrough phase of the medium-term agenda. At this node, policy translation should have produced substantive impact, the institutional prototype should have begun to operate, and Interstellar Civilization Studies should have taken initial shape. See Kingdon (1984).

[20] The 20-year milestone marks the end of the medium-term agenda and the beginning of the long-term agenda. At this node, the framework should have reached a mature state, the discipline should have become a recognized discipline, and preparations for the long-term agenda should have been made. See Sabatier (1988).

[1] Revision based on empirical research is a core mechanism of the development of scientific theory. Popper emphasized that theories should be falsifiable and that the results of empirical research can falsify or support a theory. Kuhn, by contrast, emphasized the importance of paradigm shifts. This work adopts a method of gradual revision, adjusting specific content in the light of empirical research results while keeping the core propositions stable. See Popper (1959), Kuhn (1962).

[2] Revision based on stress testing draws on stress testing methods in engineering and finance. Stress testing identifies the weaknesses and boundaries of a system by testing it under extreme conditions. In Part Five, this work conducts stress tests of four extreme scenarios, identifying the main weaknesses of the framework. See Taleb (2012), Bank for International Settlements (2009).

[3] Revision based on international dialogue reflects the social character of knowledge production. Scientific knowledge is not produced in isolation but develops through dialogue and criticism within the academic community. In Part Eight, this work engages in dialogue with the longtermism, AI safety, and international space law communities. See Longino (1990), Kitcher (2001).

[4] Version management draws on version control methods in software engineering. Semantic versioning is a widely used specification for version numbers, expressing different types of changes through the major, minor, and patch numbers. See Preston-Werner (2013).

[5] Pilot projects are a common method of policy implementation. A pilot project implements a policy on a limited scale in order to test its feasibility and effects, providing the basis for large-scale rollout. See Pressman & Wildavsky (1984), Bardach (1977).

[6] Policy experimentation is a core method of evidence-based policymaking. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are regarded as the "gold standard" for assessing causal effects, but their application in the policy domain faces ethical and practical challenges. See Banerjee & Duflo (2011), Cartwright & Hardie (2012).

[7] Impact evaluation is a core method of project management and policy analysis. Impact evaluation usually comprises tiers such as output evaluation, outcome evaluation, impact evaluation, and sustainability evaluation. See Rossi et al. (2004), Weiss (1998).

[8] Lesson learning is a core mechanism of organizational learning. Lesson learning converts tacit knowledge into explicit knowledge, enabling experience to be transmitted and generalized. See Nonaka & Takeuchi (1995), Argyris & Schön (1978).

[9] Integration with the natural sciences is an important direction of interdisciplinary research. The framework of this work is built on the foundations of physics (thermodynamics, information theory), biology (evolutionary theory, ecology), and neuroscience (consciousness science). See Wilson (1998), Gell-Mann (1994).

[10] Integration with the social sciences is an important foundation of institutional design. Institutional economics, political science, and sociology provide the theoretical foundations and empirical evidence for institutional design. See North (1990), Ostrom (1990), Acemoglu & Robinson (2012).

[11] Integration with the humanities is an important foundation of normative argumentation. Philosophy (ethics, metaphysics, epistemology) provides the theoretical foundations for normative principles. History and religious studies provide perspectives on cultural sensitivity. See MacIntyre (1981), Taylor (1989).

[12] Integration methodology is the methodological foundation of interdisciplinary research. Interdisciplinary integration faces challenges such as conceptual incompatibility and methodological inconsistency, requiring systematic methodological guidance. See Klein (1990), Repko (2012).

[13] New contexts of technological development are one of the main challenges facing the mid-term agenda. Breakthroughs in areas such as AGI, biotechnology, and neurotechnology may occur within the mid-term time span, posing new challenges to the framework. See Bostrom (2014), Russell (2019).

[14] New contexts of social change are an important challenge facing the mid-term agenda. Changes in demographics, political configuration, economic structure, and cultural transformation may affect the applicability of the framework. See Castells (2010), Beck (1992).

[15] New contexts of environmental change are an urgent challenge facing the mid-term agenda. Environmental problems such as climate change, biodiversity loss, and resource depletion may intensify within the mid-term time span. See IPCC (2021), Rockström et al. (2009).

[16] Framework adaptability is a core concept of complex systems theory. Adaptive systems are able to adjust their own structure and behavior in response to environmental change. The framework of this work should be adaptive, able to meet the challenges of new contexts. See Holland (1995), Gunderson & Holling (2002).

[17] Milestones are a core tool of project management. A milestone is a key node in a project, marking the completion of an important stage. A milestone should have clear deliverables and verification criteria. See Project Management Institute (2017).

[18] The 10-year milestone marks the midpoint of the mid-term agenda. At this node, the framework should have completed revision based on stress testing, policy experiments should be beginning to produce results, and interdisciplinary integration should have made substantive progress. See Mintzberg (1994).

[19] The 15-year milestone marks the phase of translational breakthrough in the mid-term agenda. At this node, policy translation should be producing substantive impact, institutional prototypes should be beginning to operate, and interstellar civilization studies should be taking initial shape. See Kingdon (1984).

[20] The 20-year milestone marks the end of the mid-term agenda and the beginning of the long-term agenda. At this node, the framework should have reached a state of maturity, the discipline should have become a recognized discipline, and preparation should be made for the long-term agenda. See Sabatier (1988).

(ii) The Time Span and Characteristics of the Long-Term Agenda

The long-term agenda covers a time span of more than 20 years and has the following characteristics:

Table 34.1 Characteristics of the Long-Term Agenda

(iii) The choice of the time span of the long-term agenda is based on the following considerations:

  1. Disciplinary maturation cycle: a new discipline typically requires 30-50 years from emergence to maturity
  2. Institutional evolution cycle: fundamental change in international institutions typically requires several decades
  3. Paradigm shift cycle: the shift of a scientific paradigm typically requires more than one generation
  4. Civilizational development cycle: major civilizational transformations typically occur on a century scale

(iv) The Epistemological Challenge of Long-Term Planning

Definition 34.0.1 (The Epistemological Challenge of Long-Term Planning)

Long-term planning faces a fundamental epistemological challenge: we cannot accurately predict the future more than 20 years ahead, yet we still need to provide directional guidance for long-term development[1].

V. Methodological Commitments

This chapter follows the following methodological commitments:

  1. Directional commitment: the long-term agenda provides direction rather than a concrete plan
  2. Scenario-based commitment: adopts scenario planning methods to cope with uncertainty
  3. Openness commitment: maintains openness to new scenarios and new paradigms
  4. Humility commitment: acknowledges the limitations of long-term prediction
  5. Revisability commitment: the long-term agenda itself should be revisable

§34.1 Advancement of Disciplinary Building

§34.1.1 Disciplinary Positioning

I. The Disciplinary Positioning of Interstellar Civilization Studies

Definition 34.1.1 (Interstellar Civilization Studies)

Interstellar Civilization Studies (Astropolitics and Interstellar Civilization Studies, abbreviated AICS) is an interdisciplinary academic field that studies the existence, development, governance, and ethical problems of civilization at the cosmic scale[2].

Table 34.4 The Disciplinary Positioning of Interstellar Civilization Studies

Positioning DimensionContentExplanation
Object of studyThe existence and development of civilization at the cosmic scaleIncludes human civilization and potential non-human civilizations
Core questionHow can civilization exist responsibly in the universe?Covers ontology, ethics, and governance studies
Disciplinary natureA combination of normative and descriptiveStudies both "what is" and "what ought to be"
Time scaleDeep time (hundreds to thousands of years)A time horizon transcending generations
Spatial scaleThe cosmos (solar system to galaxy)A spatial horizon transcending the Earth

├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│  Stage One: Anomaly Identification                              │
│  ├─ Identify anomalies that the current paradigm cannot explain │

│  ├─ Propose a new paradigm                                      │

│  └─ The new paradigm demonstrates other advantages              │
│                                                                 │

│  ├─ Competition between the old and new paradigms               │
│  ├─ The academic community evaluates and selects                │
│  └─ The new paradigm gradually gains acceptance                 │
│                                                                 │

│  ├─ The new paradigm becomes mainstream                         │
│  ├─ Textbooks and courses are updated                           │
│  └─ A new normal science begins                                 │
│                                                                 │

Chapter Summary

Core Conclusions

This chapter has planned the long-term research agenda (20 years+) of this work. The main conclusions include:

Conclusion One: Advancement of Disciplinary Building

Interstellar Civilization Studies is an interdisciplinary academic field that studies the existence, development, governance, and ethical problems of civilization at the cosmic scale. Disciplinary building should pass through four stages—the emergence period, the formation period, the maturity period, and the stability period—establishing institutional elements such as academic organizations, degree programs, journals, and conferences.

Table 34.38 Core Conclusions on Disciplinary Building

ElementContentExpected Time
Disciplinary positioningStudy the existence and development of civilization at the cosmic scaleDetermined
Disciplinary boundariesPermeable, evolving, negotiatedContinuously delimited
Disciplinary methodologyInterdisciplinarity, normativity, foresightContinuously developed
Disciplinary institutionalizationAcademic organizations, degree programs, journals, conferences30-50 years

Conclusion Two: Development of International Institutions

The transformation from academic proposals to international norms is a long-term process that needs to pass through five stages: academic research, policy advocacy, soft law formation, hard law formation, and institutional operation. Institutional evolution may follow a gradual integration, parallel development, crisis-driven, or hybrid path.

Table 34.39 Core Conclusions on the Development of International Institutions

StageContentExpected Time
Academic researchProduce academic results1-10 years
Policy advocacyPromote to policymakers5-15 years
Soft law formationForm non-binding guidelines10-20 years
Hard law formationForm binding treaties20-40 years
Institutional operationInstitutions formally operate30 years+

Conclusion Three: Fundamental Revision of Theory

This work's framework may face paradigm shifts in physics, consciousness science, ethics, or technology. The core concepts (consciousness, life, subject, freedom, responsibility) may need to be reconstructed in light of academic development. The revision of normative principles should follow four constraints: consistency, continuity, procedure, and effectiveness.

Table 34.40 Core Conclusions on Theoretical Revision

Revision TypeTrigger ConditionRevision Procedure
Paradigm shiftFundamental change in the relevant fieldMonitoring, preparation, participation, adaptation
Concept reconstructionAcademic development, empirical researchIdentification, proposal, deliberation, implementation, evaluation
Principle revisionEmpirical research, criticism, new scenariosFollow four constraints
Maintaining opennessContinuous needFour mechanisms

Conclusion Four: Exploration of New Paradigms

The current framework has limitations in four respects: ontological, normative, epistemological, and operational. The possible paths for transcending the current framework include internal development, extension and integration, paradigm shift, and comprehensive transcendence. Openness to new paradigms should be maintained, following four principles: humility, curiosity, fairness, and courage.

Table 34.41 Core Conclusions on the Exploration of New Paradigms

Conclusion Five: Long-Term Vision

The long-term vision should maintain a balance between humility and ambition. The 50-year vision includes disciplinary maturity, institutional operation, theoretical maturity, social impact, and technological application. The 100-year vision faces extremely high uncertainty, and the possible scenarios include interstellar civilization, multi-intelligence coexistence, civilizational contact, civilizational crisis, and paradigm transcendence. The longer-term outlook should maintain fundamental humility.

Conclusion Six: Relation to the New Three Views

The long-term agenda planning of this chapter embodies the core claims of the New Three Views:

  • NC-1 (relational ontology): The relational positioning of the discipline, interdisciplinary integration
  • NC-2 (process ontology): The processual development of the discipline, continuous evolution
  • NC-3 (participatory universe): The participatory construction of the discipline, open collaboration
  • NL-1 (continuum of life): The continuous expansion of the scope of subjecthood
  • NL-2 (negentropic organization): The negentropic contribution of the discipline, enhancing civilizational adaptability
  • NK-1 (participatory cognition): The participatory nature of knowledge production
  • NK-4 (deliberative knowledge): The deliberative nature of knowledge, interdisciplinary and cross-cultural deliberation

[1] The epistemological challenge of long-term planning is one of the core problems of planning theory. Mintzberg (1994) criticized the limitations of traditional strategic planning and emphasized the importance of adaptability and learning. This work adopts a scenario planning approach to cope with long-term uncertainty. See Mintzberg (1994), Schwartz (1991).

[2] The disciplinary positioning of Interstellar Civilization Studies draws on the experience of several related fields. Futures Studies, Existential Risk Studies, and Longtermism Studies provide important references for this discipline. See Bell (1997), Bostrom (2002), MacAskill (2022).

[3] The delimitation of disciplinary boundaries is an important research topic in the sociology of science. Gieryn (1983) proposed the concept of "boundary work," emphasizing that disciplinary boundaries are the result of social construction. This work adopts an open view of boundaries. See Gieryn (1983), Abbott (2001).

[4] Interdisciplinary methodology is the core challenge of interdisciplinary research. Klein (1990) systematically discussed the history, theory, and practice of interdisciplinary research. Repko (2012) provided a practical guide to interdisciplinary research. See Klein (1990), Repko (2012).

[5] Disciplinary institutionalization is a classic research topic in the sociology of science. Ben-David & Collins (1966) studied the social origins of a new science. Whitley (1984) analyzed the social organization of science. See Ben-David & Collins (1966), Whitley (1984).

[6] The transformation from academic proposals to international norms is an important topic in international relations research. Finnemore & Sikkink (1998) proposed the norm life cycle theory. Haas (1992) studied the role of epistemic communities in policymaking. See Finnemore & Sikkink (1998), Haas (1992).

[7] Institutional evolution is a core topic of institutional theory. Mahoney & Thelen (2010) proposed a theory of gradual institutional change. Streeck & Thelen (2005) analyzed multiple modes of institutional change. See Mahoney & Thelen (2010), Streeck & Thelen (2005).

[8] Institutional effectiveness evaluation is a core method of policy analysis. Rossi et al. (2004) provided a systematic approach to evaluation research. Young (1999) specifically discussed the effectiveness evaluation of international institutions. See Rossi et al. (2004), Young (1999).

[9] Continuous institutional improvement draws on the idea of adaptive governance. Dietz et al. (2003) discussed adaptive management in the governance of public resources. Folke et al. (2005) analyzed the adaptive governance of social-ecological systems. See Dietz et al. (2003), Folke et al. (2005).

[10] Paradigm shift is a core concept of the philosophy of science. Kuhn (1962) proposed the paradigm theory of scientific revolutions. Lakatos (1978) developed the methodology of research programmes. See Kuhn (1962), Lakatos (1978).

[11] Core concept reconstruction is an important mechanism of theoretical development. Laudan (1977) discussed conceptual change in scientific progress. Thagard (1992) analyzed the cognitive mechanisms of conceptual revolutions. See Laudan (1977), Thagard (1992).

[12] Normative principle revision is an important mechanism of ethical development. Rawls (1971) proposed the method of reflective equilibrium. Daniels (1979) further developed the method of wide reflective equilibrium. See Rawls (1971), Daniels (1979).

[13] Theoretical openness is an important condition for scientific progress. Popper (1959) emphasized the importance of falsifiability and criticism. Feyerabend (1975), by contrast, advocated methodological pluralism. See Popper (1959), Feyerabend (1975).

[14] Transcending the current framework is a natural process of theoretical development. Laudan (1977) discussed the problem-solving model of scientific progress. Kitcher (1993) analyzed multiple modes of scientific progress. See Laudan (1977), Kitcher (1993).

[15] The characteristics of new paradigms are an important research topic in the philosophy of science. Kuhn (1962) discussed the characteristics and functions of paradigms. Hacking (1983) analyzed paradigm change in scientific practice. See Kuhn (1962), Hacking (1983).

[16] The conditions for paradigm shift are an important research topic in the sociology of science. Kuhn (1962) discussed the conditions for scientific crises and revolutions. Collins (1998) analyzed the social conditions of scientific revolutions. See Kuhn (1962), Collins (1998).

[17] Openness to new paradigms is an important attitude for scientific progress. Popper (1959) emphasized the importance of critical rationalism. Longino (1990) discussed the social nature and openness of scientific knowledge. See Popper (1959), Longino (1990).

[18] The choice of the time span of the 50-year vision is based on the historical experience of disciplinary development and institutional evolution. A new discipline typically requires 30-50 years from emergence to maturity. Fundamental change in international institutions typically requires several decades. See Ben-David & Collins (1966), Finnemore & Sikkink (1998).

[19] The 100-year vision faces fundamental uncertainty. Technological prediction on a 100-year scale is almost impossible to make accurately. Social and cultural change is likewise difficult to predict. See Tetlock (2005), Taleb (2007).

[20] The longer-term outlook exceeds the scope of current cognitive capacity. Deep time thinking is an important cognitive capacity, but its predictive capacity is limited. See Gould (1987), Ord (2020).

[21] The humility of vision is an important quality of responsible long-term planning. Epistemic humility is an important theme of contemporary epistemology. See Whitcomb et al. (2017), Hazlett (2012).

[17] Openness to new paradigms is an important attitude of scientific progress. Popper (1959) emphasized the importance of critical rationalism. Longino (1990) discussed the social character and openness of scientific knowledge. See Popper (1959), Longino (1990).

[18] The choice of a 50-year time span for the vision is based on the historical experience of disciplinary development and institutional evolution. It usually takes 30-50 years for a new discipline to go from emergence to maturity. Fundamental change in international institutions usually takes decades. See Ben-David & Collins (1966), Finnemore & Sikkink (1998).

[19] The 100-year vision faces fundamental uncertainty. Technological prediction on a 100-year scale is almost impossible to make accurately. Social and cultural change is equally difficult to predict. See Tetlock (2005), Taleb (2007).

[20] Longer-term prospects lie beyond the scope of current cognitive capacity. Deep time thinking is an important cognitive capacity, but its predictive power is limited. See Gould (1987), Ord (2020).

[21] Humility in vision is an important quality of responsible long-term planning. Epistemic humility is an important theme in contemporary epistemology. See Whitcomb et al. (2017), Hazlett (2012).

§35.1 Open Questions at the Conceptual Level

§35.1.1 The Question of the Nature of Consciousness

I. The Core of the Question

Definition 35.1.1 (The Question of the Nature of Consciousness)

The question of the nature of consciousness refers to questions concerning the fundamental properties, origins, and boundaries of consciousness, and these questions directly affect this work's New View of Life and the UCS indicator[2].

Table 35.3 Sub-Questions of the Question of the Nature of Consciousness

Sub-QuestionContentImpact on This Work
Definition of consciousnessWhat is consciousness?Affects the definitional basis of UCS
Origin of consciousnessHow does consciousness arise?Affects the theoretical basis of the continuum of life
Boundary of consciousnessWhich entities possess consciousness?Affects the determination of subjecthood
Measurement of consciousnessHow is consciousness measured?Affects the operationalization of UCS
Function of consciousnessWhat function does consciousness serve?Affects the status of consciousness in governance

II. The Current Position of This Work

This work adopts Integrated Information Theory (IIT) as a working definition of consciousness:

$$\Phi = \text{integrated information}$$

Where $\Phi$ is the integrated information of a system, reflecting the degree of information integration by which the system as a whole exceeds the sum of its parts.

§35.1.2 The Precise Definition of the Possibility Space

I. The Core of the Question

Definition 35.1.2 (The Question of the Precise Definition of the Possibility Space)

The question of the precise definition of the possibility space refers to how to precisely define and measure the possibility space, and how to operationalize the concept of the possibility space into a computable indicator[3].

Table 35.5 Sub-Questions of the Definition of the Possibility Space

Sub-QuestionContentImpact on This Work
The ontological status of possibilityIs possibility real or epistemological?Affects the theoretical basis of the possibility space
The dimensions of the possibility spaceHow many dimensions does the possibility space have?Affects the computation of RFD
The metric of the possibility spaceHow should the size of the possibility space be measured?Affects the operationalization of RFD
The dynamics of the possibility spaceHow does the possibility space change over time?Affects the Principle of Reversibility
The comparison of possibility spacesHow should the possibility spaces of different subjects be compared?Affects the Principle of Recursive Freedom

II. The Current Position of This Work

This work defines the possibility space as:

$$\mathcal{P}(A, t) = \{s \in S : s \text{ is a state realizable by subject } A \text{ at time } t\}$$

The Recursive Freedom Degree (RFD) is defined as:

$$\text{RFD}(A, t) = \log_2 |\mathcal{P}(A, t)|$$

III. The Limitations of the Current Position

│  ├─ Or is it merely an epistemological concept?                 │
│  └─ Different ontological positions lead to different theoretical consequences │
│                                                                 │
│  Limitation Two: The Boundaries of the Possibility Space Are Unclear │
│  ├─ What counts as a "realizable state"?                        │
│  ├─ The distinction among physical possibility, technological possibility, and social possibility │
│  └─ The vagueness of boundaries affects the computation of RFD  │
│                                                                 │
│  Limitation Three: The Difficulty of Measuring the Possibility Space │
│  ├─ The possibility space is usually infinite-dimensional       │
│  ├─ How should the weights of different dimensions be determined? │
│  └─ The legitimacy of discretization and approximation          │
│                                                                 │
│  Limitation Four: The Subjectivity of the Possibility Space     │
│  ├─ Does the possibility space depend on the subject's cognition? │

§35.1.3 The Question of the Distribution of Negentropy Responsibility

I. The Core of the Question

Definition 35.1.3 (The Question of the Distribution of Negentropy Responsibility)

The question of the distribution of negentropy responsibility refers to how to distribute the responsibility for maintaining and increasing the negentropy of the universe among different subjects, and how to handle the fairness issues in the distribution of responsibility[4].

The conflict of responsibilitiesHow should conflicts of responsibility be handled?Affects institutional design

II. The Current Position of This Work

This work proposes the Principle of Negentropy Responsibility (NRP):

$$\text{NRP}: \forall A \in \mathcal{A}, \text{Responsibility}(A) \propto \text{Capability}(A) \times \text{Impact}(A)$$

Where:

  • $\text{Capability}(A)$ is the capability of subject $A$
  • $\text{Impact}(A)$ is the impact of subject $A$

I. The Core of the Question

Definition 35.1.4 (The Cross-Substrate Subjecthood Question)

The cross-substrate subjecthood question refers to how to determine whether entities on different material substrates (biological, silicon-based, quantum, etc.) possess moral subjecthood, and how to compare subjects on different substrates[5].

AI subjecthoodDo AI systems possess subjecthood?Affects AI governance
Extraterrestrial subjecthoodDoes extraterrestrial life possess subjecthood?Affects First Contact

II. The Current Position of This Work

This work adopts a functionalist position:

$$\text{subjecthood} = f(\text{functional features}) \neq f(\text{material substrate})$$

That is, subjecthood depends on functional features rather than the material substrate.

§35.2 Open Questions at the Methodological Level

§35.2.1 The Verification of Deep-Time Prediction

I. The Core of the Question

Definition 35.2.1 (The Verification of Deep-Time Prediction)

The problem of the verification of deep-time prediction refers to how to verify predictions concerning time scales of centuries or even longer, and how to assess the reliability of predictions when direct verification is impossible[6].

Table 35.12 Sub-Questions of the Verification of Deep-Time Prediction

Sub-QuestionContentImpact on This Work
The possibility of verificationCan deep-time predictions be verified?Affects the scientific character of the framework
The method of verificationHow can deep-time predictions be verified?Affects methodology
Reliability assessmentHow can the reliability of deep-time predictions be assessed?Affects the basis for decision-making
Historical analogyAre historical analogies valid?Affects argumentative method
Simulation verificationCan simulation replace empirical verification?Affects stress testing

II. The Current Position of This Work

This work adopts the following strategies to address the problem of verifying deep-time prediction:

  1. Scenario planning: instead of making a single prediction, construct multiple scenarios
  2. Robustness analysis: assess the robustness of the framework under different scenarios
  3. Historical analogy: draw on historical experience for analogical reasoning
  4. Simulation modeling: explore possible futures through simulation

§35.2.2 The Question of Handling Deep Uncertainty

I. The Core of the Question

Definition 35.2.2 (The Question of Handling Deep Uncertainty)

The question of handling deep uncertainty refers to how to make reasonable decisions when uncertainty cannot be described by a probability distribution[7].

Table 35.14 Sub-Questions of Handling Deep Uncertainty

Sub-QuestionContentImpact on This Work
Identification of deep uncertaintyHow can deep uncertainty be identified?Affects the premise of decision-making
Classification of deep uncertaintyWhat types of deep uncertainty are there?Affects handling strategies
Decision methodsHow should decisions be made under deep uncertainty?Affects normative principles
Robustness and adaptabilityHow should robustness and adaptability be balanced?Affects institutional design
Learning and updatingHow should learning occur under deep uncertainty?Affects versioned governance

II. The Current Position of This Work

This work adopts the following strategies to handle deep uncertainty:

  1. The Principle of Reversibility: prioritize reversible actions
  2. Robust decision-making: choose strategies that perform well under multiple scenarios
  3. Adaptive governance: establish governance mechanisms that can adapt to change
  4. Versioned updating: allow the framework to be updated with new information

Formalized expression:

$$\text{Decision}^ = \arg\max_d \min_s U(d, s)$$

Where $d$ is the decision, $s$ is the scenario, and $U$ is the utility function.

§35.4 Open Questions at the Meta Level

§35.4.1 The Sufficiency of the Normative Foundation

I. The Core of the Question

Definition 35.4.1 (The Sufficiency of the Normative Foundation)

The question of the sufficiency of the normative foundation refers to whether this work's normative foundation (the bridge principle and the three principles) is sufficient, and whether it can provide a solid foundation for Cosmic Responsibility Ethics[14].

Table 35.31 Sub-Questions of the Sufficiency of the Normative Foundation

Sub-QuestionContentImpact on This Work
The legitimacy of the bridge principleIs the bridge principle legitimate?Affects the derivation from the descriptive to the normative
The completeness of the three principlesAre the three principles complete?Affects the coverage of normative guidance
The consistency of the three principlesAre the three principles consistent?Affects the coherence of normative guidance
The source of normativityWhat is the ultimate source of normativity?Affects the ground of normativity
The relationship to other ethical theoriesWhat is the relationship to other ethical theories?Affects theoretical positioning

II. The Current Position of This Work

This work proposes three bridge principles:

  • BP-1 (Principle of Persistence Rationality): a rational subject with a will to persist ought to maintain its conditions of persistence
  • BP-2 (Principle of Cognitive Humility): under deep uncertainty one ought to be cautious and avoid irreversible catastrophic consequences
  • BP-3 (Principle of Inter-Subjectivity): in multi-subject situations one ought to adopt principles that can be reasonably accepted by other rational subjects

§35.5.4 The Dynamic Adjustment of Priority

I. The Necessity of the Dynamic Adjustment of Priority

Definition 35.5.4 (The Dynamic Adjustment of Priority)

The dynamic adjustment of priority refers to adjusting the priority of research directions in light of research progress, changes in the external environment, and new information[19].

Table 35.44 Triggering Conditions for the Dynamic Adjustment of Priority

Triggering ConditionContentDirection of Adjustment
Research breakthroughA research direction makes a major breakthroughLower the priority of that direction and raise the priority of other directions dependent on it
Research difficultyA research direction encounters major difficultiesLower the priority of that direction and seek alternatives
External changeThe external environment undergoes major changeAdjust the priority of related directions in light of the change
Emergence of a new problemA new important problem emergesAdd a new research direction and adjust the overall priority
Resource changeAvailable resources changeAdjust the feasibility assessment in light of resources

II. The Mechanisms of the Dynamic Adjustment of Priority

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  The Mechanisms of the Dynamic Adjustment of Priority           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│  Mechanism One: Periodic Review                                 │
│  ├─ Conduct a comprehensive review of the priority once a year  │
│  ├─ Assess the progress and changes of each research direction  │
│  └─ Adjust the priority in light of the review results          │
│                                                                 │
│  Mechanism Two: Triggered Adjustment                            │
│  ├─ Adjust when the triggering conditions are satisfied         │
│  ├─ No need to await periodic review                            │
│  └─ Maintain the timeliness of the priority                     │
│                                                                 │
│  Mechanism Three: Negotiated Adjustment                         │
│  ├─ Priority adjustment requires negotiation within the academic community │
│  ├─ Collect different opinions and suggestions                  │
│  └─ Reach consensus through negotiation                         │
│                                                                 │
│  Mechanism Four: Transparency and Openness                      │
│  ├─ The process and results of priority adjustment should be transparent and open │
│  ├─ Explain the reasons for the adjustment                      │
│  └─ Accept oversight by the academic community                  │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Chapter Summary

Core Conclusions

This chapter has systematically sorted out the open questions of this work and planned the research directions. The main conclusions include:

Conclusion One: Open Questions at the Conceptual Level

This work faces four core open questions at the conceptual level: the question of the nature of consciousness, the question of the precise definition of the possibility space, the question of the distribution of negentropy responsibility, and the cross-substrate subjecthood question. These questions are interrelated and require systematic study.

Table 35.46 Summary of Open Questions at the Conceptual Level

QuestionCore ChallengeResearch Direction
The nature of consciousnessThe contested nature of IIT, the computational difficulty of ΦBehavioral markers of consciousness, approximate computation methods
Possibility spaceUnclear ontological status, measurement difficultyFormalized definition, measurement methods
Distribution of negentropy responsibilityContested basis of responsibility, measurement difficultyPhilosophical argumentation, measurement methods
Cross-substrate subjecthoodFunctionalism controversy, identification difficultyCriteria of determination, boundary cases

Conclusion Two: Open Questions at the Methodological Level

This work faces four core open questions at the methodological level: the verification of deep-time prediction, the handling of deep uncertainty, the feasibility of index calculation, and the validity of simulation methods. These questions affect the operability and verifiability of the framework.

Table 35.47 Summary of Open Questions at the Methodological Level

QuestionCore ChallengeResearch Direction
Verification of deep-time predictionFundamental epistemological difficultyScenario planning, robustness analysis
Handling of deep uncertaintyRestriction of reversibility, difficulty of learningDecision theory, adaptive governance
Feasibility of index calculationLack of data, insufficient operationalizationProxy indicators, measurement tools
Validity of simulation methodsModel simplification, difficulty of verificationVerification methods, multi-model comparison

Conclusion Three: Open Questions at the Application Level

This work faces four core open questions at the application level: the policy translation pathway, institutional articulation, political feasibility, and cultural adaptability. These questions affect the practical value of the framework.

Table 35.48 Summary of Open Questions at the Application Level

QuestionCore ChallengeResearch Direction
Policy translation pathwayUnclear translation mechanism, numerous obstaclesTranslation mechanism, pilot research
Institutional articulationDifficulty of articulation with existing institutionsArticulation path, study of legitimacy
Political feasibilityLack of political will, conflicts of interestInterest analysis, political strategy
Cultural adaptabilityRisk of Western-centrismCross-cultural comparison, bias identification

Conclusion Four: Open Questions at the Meta Level

This work faces four core open questions at the meta level: the sufficiency of the normative foundation, cultural bias, speculativeness and falsifiability, and the theory-practice relationship. These questions affect the overall effectiveness of the framework.

Table 35.49 Summary of Open Questions at the Meta Level

QuestionCore ChallengeResearch Direction
Sufficiency of the normative foundationContested bridge principle, conflicts among principlesDeepened argumentation, dialogue with metaethics
Cultural biasHiddenness of bias, Western dominanceBias identification, cross-cultural dialogue
Speculativeness and falsifiabilityHigh speculativeness, difficulty of verificationTestability, empirical connection
Theory-practice relationshipAbstractness of theory, lack of feedbackOperationalization, action research

Conclusion Five: The Priority of Research Directions

According to the four criteria of importance, urgency, feasibility, and influence, this work has determined research directions at three priority levels: high, medium, and low. There are 10 high-priority research directions, 12 medium-priority research directions, and 10 low-priority research directions. The priority should be dynamically adjusted in light of research progress and external changes.

Table 35.50 Summary of the Priority of Research Directions

PriorityNumberCharacteristicTime Frame
High10Critically important, relatively feasible1-5 years
Medium12Important but not urgent5-15 years
Low10Lower in importance or feasibility15 years+

Conclusion Six: Relation to the New Three Views

The sorting out of open questions in this chapter embodies the core claims of the New Three Views:

  • NC-1 (relational ontology): The mutual dependence among conceptual problems
  • NC-2 (process ontology): Questions evolve over time, and priority is dynamically adjusted
  • NC-3 (participatory universe): Problem solving requires multi-party participation
  • NL-1 (continuum of life): The cross-substrate subjecthood question
  • NL-2 (negentropic organization): The question of the distribution of negentropy responsibility
  • NK-1 (participatory cognition): The participatory nature of knowledge production
  • NK-4 (deliberative knowledge): The deliberative nature of problem solving

[1] The identification and sorting out of open questions is an important link in theoretical development. Kuhn (1962) pointed out that an important task of scientific research is to identify and resolve "puzzles." Lakatos (1978), by contrast, emphasized that a research programme should be able to identify and handle "anomalies." The sorting out of open questions in this chapter draws on these insights from the philosophy of science. See Kuhn (1962), Lakatos (1978).

[2] The question of the nature of consciousness is one of the most difficult problems in philosophy and science. Chalmers (1996) called it the "hard problem." The Integrated Information Theory (IIT) adopted by this work is a theory of consciousness proposed by Tononi (2004, 2008). For comparisons of theories of consciousness, see Baars (1988), Dehaene & Changeux (2011), Koch et al. (2016).

[3] The concept of the possibility space involves core problems of modal metaphysics. Lewis (1986) proposed modal realism, holding that possible worlds really exist. Kripke (1980), by contrast, took a more moderate position. The concept of the possibility space in this work draws on these philosophical discussions but adopts a more operationalized definition. See Lewis (1986), Kripke (1980), Plantinga (1974).

[4] The question of the distribution of negentropy responsibility involves core problems of distributive justice. Rawls's (1971) theory of justice provides important theoretical resources. For discussions of intergenerational justice, see Parfit (1984), Gosseries & Meyer (2009). The discussion of cross-civilizational responsibility is an innovation of this work, but it draws on the literature on global justice; see Pogge (2002), Beitz (1979).

[5] The cross-substrate subjecthood question involves core debates in the philosophy of mind. For classic formulations of functionalism, see Putnam (1967), Fodor (1974). For the Chinese room argument, see Searle (1980). For discussions of AI subjecthood, see Floridi & Sanders (2004), Gunkel (2018).

[6] The verification of deep-time prediction is a core methodological problem in Futures Studies and longtermism research. Tetlock (2005) studied the accuracy of expert prediction. Taleb (2007) discussed the unpredictability of "black swan" events. For scenario planning methods, see Schwartz (1991), van der Heijden (2005).

[7] The handling of deep uncertainty is a frontier problem in decision theory. Walker et al. (2013) proposed a definition and classification of deep uncertainty. Lempert et al. (2003) developed the robust decision-making (RDM) method. Decision Making under Deep Uncertainty, edited by Marchau et al. (2019), is an important review in this field.

[8] The feasibility of index calculation involves measurement theory and operationalization methods. On the computational complexity of Φ, see Tegmark (2016), Oizumi et al. (2014). On general methods of indicator operationalization, see Adcock & Collier (2001), Goertz (2006).

[9] The validity of simulation methods is a core methodological problem in computational social science. On simulation verification, see Sargent (2013), Windrum et al. (2007). On multi-agent simulation, see Epstein & Axtell (1996), Gilbert & Troitzsch (2005).

[10] The policy translation pathway is a core problem of policy science. On the translation from knowledge to policy, see Weiss (1979), Nutley et al. (2007). On evidence-based policymaking, see Pawson (2006), Cartwright & Hardie (2012).

[11] The question of institutional articulation involves international institutional theory and institutional change theory. On the articulation of international institutions, see Young (1996), Oberthür & Stokke (2011). On institutional change, see Mahoney & Thelen (2010), Streeck & Thelen (2005).

[12] The question of political feasibility is a core problem of political science and policy analysis. On political feasibility analysis, see Majone (1989), Kingdon (1984). On policy windows, see Kingdon (1984), Zahariadis (2014).

[13] The question of cultural adaptability involves cross-cultural research and comparative philosophy. On cross-cultural ethics, see Wiredu (1996), Nussbaum (1997). On comparative philosophy, see Mou (2001), Angle & Tiwald (2017).

[14] The question of the sufficiency of the normative foundation involves core debates in metaethics. On the naturalistic fallacy, see Moore (1903), Frankena (1939). On contemporary metaethics, see Miller (2013), Shafer-Landau (2012).

[15] The question of cultural bias involves postcolonial theory and critical theory. On critiques of Western-centrism, see Said (1978), Chakrabarty (2000). On cultural bias in philosophy, see Park (2013), Garfield & Van Norden (2016).

[16] The questions of speculativeness and falsifiability involve core problems of the philosophy of science. Popper (1959) proposed the criterion of falsifiability. On the status of speculative theories, see Laudan (1977), Kitcher (1993). On the testability of normative theories, see Rawls (1971), Daniels (1979).

[17] The theory-practice relationship is a classic problem of philosophy. On the relationship between theory and practice, see Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics; Marx, Theses on Feuerbach. On action research, see Lewin (1946), Reason & Bradbury (2008).

[18] The determination of research priorities is an important problem of science policy and research management. On methods for determining research priorities, see Fleurence & Torgerson (2004), Viergever et al. (2010). On setting research agendas, see Kingdon (1984), Baumgartner & Jones (1993).

[19] The dynamic adjustment of priority is a core principle of adaptive management. On adaptive management, see Holling (1978), Walters (1986). On the dynamic adjustment of research agendas, see Sarewitz & Pielke (2007).
