Footnotes

Chapter 35 Footnotes

[1] The identification and organization of open problems is an important part of theoretical development. Kuhn (1962) pointed out that an important task of scientific research is to identify and solve "puzzles." Lakatos (1978) emphasized that a research programme should be able to identify and deal with "anomalies." The organization of open problems in this chapter draws on these insights from the philosophy of science. See Kuhn (1962), Lakatos (1978).

[2] The problem of the nature of consciousness is one of the most difficult problems in philosophy and science. Chalmers (1996) called it the "hard problem." Integrated Information Theory (IIT), adopted in this work, is a theory of consciousness proposed by Tononi (2004, 2008). For a comparison of theories of consciousness, see Baars (1988), Dehaene & Changeux (2011), Koch et al. (2016).

[3] The concept of the possibility space involves core problems of modal metaphysics. Lewis (1986) proposed modal realism, holding that possible worlds really exist. Kripke (1980) took a more moderate position. The concept of the possibility space in this work draws on these philosophical discussions but adopts a more operational definition. See Lewis (1986), Kripke (1980), Plantinga (1974).

[4] The problem of allocating negentropy responsibility involves core problems of distributive justice. Rawls's (1971) theory of justice provides important theoretical resources. For discussion of intergenerational justice, see Parfit (1984), Gosseries & Meyer (2009). The discussion of cross-civilizational responsibility is an innovation of this work but draws on the global justice literature; see Pogge (2002), Beitz (1979).

[5] The problem of cross-substrate subjecthood involves core disputes in the philosophy of mind. For the classic formulation of functionalism, see Putnam (1967), Fodor (1974). For the Chinese room argument, see Searle (1980). For discussion of AI subjecthood, see Floridi & Sanders (2004), Gunkel (2018).

[6] The problem of validating deep-time predictions is a core methodological problem in futures studies and longtermism research. Tetlock (2005) studied the accuracy of expert prediction. Taleb (2007) discussed the unpredictability of "black swan" events. For the scenario planning method, see Schwartz (1991), van der Heijden (2005).

[7] The handling of deep uncertainty is a frontier problem in decision theory. Walker et al. (2013) proposed a definition and classification of deep uncertainty. Lempert et al. (2003) developed Robust Decision Making (RDM). Marchau et al. (2019), eds., Decision Making under Deep Uncertainty, is an important survey in the field.

[8] The problem of the feasibility of indicator computation involves measurement theory and operationalization methods. On the computational complexity of Φ, see Tegmark (2016), Oizumi et al. (2014). On general methods of indicator operationalization, see Adcock & Collier (2001), Goertz (2006).

[9] The problem of the validity of simulation methods is a core methodological problem in computational social science. On simulation validation, see Sargent (2013), Windrum et al. (2007). On agent-based simulation, see Epstein & Axtell (1996), Gilbert & Troitzsch (2005).

[10] The problem of the pathway of policy translation is a core problem of policy science. On the translation of knowledge into policy, see Weiss (1979), Nutley et al. (2007). On evidence-based policymaking, see Pawson (2006), Cartwright & Hardie (2012).

[11] The problem of institutional articulation involves international institutional theory and institutional change theory. On the articulation of international institutions, see Young (1996), Oberthür & Stokke (2011). On institutional change, see Mahoney & Thelen (2010), Streeck & Thelen (2005).

[12] The problem of political feasibility is a core problem of political science and policy analysis. On political feasibility analysis, see Majone (1989), Kingdon (1984). On policy windows, see Kingdon (1984), Zahariadis (2014).

[13] The problem of cultural adaptability involves cross-cultural research and comparative philosophy. On cross-cultural ethics, see Wiredu (1996), Nussbaum (1997). On comparative philosophy, see Mou (2001), Angle & Tiwald (2017).

[14] The problem of the sufficiency of normative foundations involves core disputes in metaethics. On the naturalistic fallacy, see Moore (1903), Frankena (1939). On contemporary metaethics, see Miller (2013), Shafer-Landau (2012).

[15] The problem of cultural bias involves postcolonial theory and critical theory. On critiques of Western-centrism, see Said (1978), Chakrabarty (2000). On cultural bias in philosophy, see Park (2013), Garfield & Van Norden (2016).

[16] The problem of speculation versus falsifiability involves core problems of the philosophy of science. Popper (1959) proposed the criterion of falsifiability. On the status of speculative theories, see Laudan (1977), Kitcher (1993). On the testability of normative theories, see Rawls (1971), Daniels (1979).

[17] The problem of the relationship between theory and practice is a classic problem of philosophy. On the relationship between theory and practice, see Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and Marx's Theses on Feuerbach. On action research, see Lewin (1946), Reason & Bradbury (2008).

[18] The determination of research priorities is an important problem of science policy and research management. On methods for determining research priorities, see Fleurence & Torgerson (2004), Viergever et al. (2010). On setting research agendas, see Kingdon (1984), Baumgartner & Jones (1993).

[19] The dynamic adjustment of priorities is a core principle of adaptive management. On adaptive management, see Holling (1978), Walters (1986). On the dynamic adjustment of research agendas, see Sarewitz & Pielke (2007).

Conclusion and OutlookConclusion

"Freedom is the Stewardship of Possibility."

"Freedom is the Stewardship of Possibility."

------ Core Maxim of Interstellar Civilization Studies

When we look back from the starting point of the entire work—from the three-fold pressures and the three puzzles raised in the preface, to the diagnosis of existing paths in the introduction, and further to the onto-epistemological foundation of the New Three Views, the operational development of the indicator system, the rigorous derivation of normative principles, the engineering construction of institutional design, and finally to the systematic examination of stress tests and the in-depth unfolding of international dialogue—we can clearly discern a complete chain of derivation from "what is" to "what ought to be":

$$L_0 \xrightarrow{\text{Explanation}} L_1 \xrightarrow{\text{Bridge Principle}} L_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Institutionalization}} L_3 \xrightarrow{\text{Operationalization}} L_4$$

Every link in this chain has undergone rigorous argumentation, and every crossing is accompanied by an explicit boundary statement. Now we need to step back, examine the overall outline of this theoretical edifice, assess its contributions and limitations, and look ahead to its future directions of development.

Core Tasks of the Conclusion

TaskContentCorresponding Section
ReviewWhat has this work accomplished?§I
AcknowledgeWhat has this work failed to accomplish?§II
InviteJoin this open research programme§III
ConcludeFrom grand narrative to auditable protocol§IV

Methodological Commitments of the Conclusion

This conclusion continues the engineering-style narrative of the whole book and follows the following principles:

  1. Principle of honesty: do not exaggerate contributions, do not conceal limitations
  2. Principle of traceability: every assessment can be traced back to arguments in the main text
  3. Principle of openness: position the theoretical framework as a revisable research programme rather than a closed dogma
  4. Principle of invitation: explicitly invite criticism, cooperation, and practice

I. Core Contributions of This Work

1.1 Theoretical Contributions
1.1.1 Establishment of the Framework of the New Three Views

The primary theoretical contribution of this work is to propose and systematically argue for the framework of the "New Three Views"—the New Cosmological View, the New View of Life, and the New View of Cognition—as the ontological-epistemological foundation of the interstellar civilization era.

Table C.1 Core Propositions of the New Three Views

New Three ViewsCore PropositionRelation to the Old Three ViewsArgumentation Chapter
New Cosmological ViewNC-1: relations precede entities; NC-2: processes precede states; NC-3: participation precedes observationDimension-raising extension of the worldviewChapter 1
New View of LifeNL-1: life is a graded continuum; NL-2: the essence of life is negentropic organization; NL-3: subjecthood is functionalDimension-raising extension of the view of lifeChapter 2
New View of CognitionNK-1: cognition is intervention; NK-2: knowledge is a social achievement; NK-3: rationality is ecological; NK-4: truth is negotiativeDimension-raising extension of the view of valueChapter 3

The theoretical contribution of the New Three Views can be formalized as:

$$\text{NewThreeViews} = \{NC, NL, NK\} \supset \{WV, LV, VV\}_{\text{OldThreeViews}}$$

Here, the relation between the New Three Views and the Old Three Views is one of "dimension-raising extension" rather than "replacement"—at the Earth scale and within human society, the Old Three Views remain valid; the New Three Views are the extension of the Old Three Views to the interstellar scale. This relation is analogous to that between Newtonian mechanics and relativity:

$$\lim_{\text{scale} \to \text{Earth}} \text{NewThreeViews} = \text{OldThreeViews}$$

1.1.2 Derivation of the Three Principles

The second theoretical contribution of this work is the derivation of three core normative principles from the New Three Views:

Table C.2 Derivation Path of the Three Principles

PrincipleContentBasis of DerivationArgumentation Chapter
Principle of Recursive Freedom (RFP)No action should systematically reduce the possibility space of other subjectsNC-1, NC-3, NL-1Chapter 11
Principle of Negentropy Responsibility (NRP)Negentropic organizations bear responsibility for maintaining the negentropic structure of the cosmosNL-2, NC-2Chapter 12
Principle of Reversibility (REV)Under deep uncertainty, reversible actions should be preferredNK-1, NK-3Chapter 13

The derivation of the three principles depends on the bridge principles (Chapter 5):

$$\text{BridgePrinciples} = \{BP\text{-}1, BP\text{-}2, BP\text{-}3\}$$

Where:

  • BP-1 (principle of persistence rationality): a rational subject with a will to persist ought to maintain its conditions of persistence
  • BP-2 (principle of epistemic humility): under deep uncertainty one ought to be cautious and avoid irreversible catastrophic consequences
  • BP-3 (principle of intersubjectivity): in multi-subject scenarios one ought to adopt principles that can be reasonably accepted by other rational subjects

1.2 Methodological Contributions
1.2.1 Protocol Stack Methodology

The primary methodological contribution of this work is to propose and develop the "protocol stack" methodology (Chapters 16, 17). Drawing on modular design in computer science, this methodology proposes a five-layer governance architecture:

Table C.4 The Five-Layer Architecture of the Protocol Stack

LayerNameContentStabilityRevision Condition
L₀Physical constraint layerLaws of thermodynamics, boundaries of information theoryHighestChange in scientific consensus
L₁Onto-epistemological framework layerNew Three Views (NC, NL, NK)HighMajor theoretical breakthrough
L₂Normative principle layerRFP, NRP, REVMediumArgumentative flaw or new scenario
L₃Institutional design layerMulti-Intelligence Tribunal, Cosmic-Scale IRBRelatively lowPractical feedback
L₄Operational protocol layerUCS, RFD, CRV, CDI, MBCL, CSIALowestContinuous iteration

Design principles of the protocol stack:

$$\text{ProtocolStack} = \text{LayerSeparation} + \text{LoadConstraint} + \text{VersionedRollback}$$

Where:

  • Layer separation: contents of different stabilities are placed in different layers
  • Load constraint: lower layers bear upper layers, and upper layers must not violate lower layers
  • Versioned rollback: each layer can be revised while keeping lower layers unchanged
1.2.2 Development of the Indicator System

The second methodological contribution of this work is the development of six major indicator systems (Chapters 6–10), which transform abstract philosophical principles into operable tools:

Table C.5 The Six Major Indicator Systems

IndicatorFull NameFunctionMaturity
UCSUniversal Consciousness ScaleAssesses the degree of consciousness of a subjectTRL 2
RFDRecursive Freedom DegreeAssesses the impact of an action on the possibility spaceTRL 2
CRVCommitment-Reversibility-VerificationA verifiability framework for commitmentsTRL 2
CDICivilizational Diversity IndexAssesses the diversity of civilizationsTRL 2
MBCLMinimum Biosphere Carrying LimitAssesses the carrying capacity of ecosystemsTRL 2
CSIACosmic-Scale Impact AssessmentAssesses the cross-scale impact of actionsTRL 2

Design principles of the indicator system:

$$\text{IndexDesign} = \text{Operationalization} + \text{Measurability} + \text{Revisability}$$

II. Limitations of This Work

2.1 Theoretical Limitations
2.1.1 Contestability of the Normative Foundation

The normative foundation of this work—deriving normativity from the conditions of persistence of negentropic organizations—remains contested:

Table C.10 Controversies over the Normative Foundation

Point of ControversyContentResponse of This WorkLimitation of the Response
Naturalistic fallacyIs deriving "ought" from "is" valid?The argument from bridge principlesThe bridge principles themselves require defense
Preference for persistenceWhy is persistence good?Persistence is a precondition of normativityThere may be circular reasoning
Priority of negentropyWhy do negentropic organizations have a special status?Negentropic organizations are carriers of complexityThe value of complexity requires argumentation

Formal expression:

$$\text{NormativeFoundation} = f(\text{BridgePrinciples}) \leftarrow \text{Controversial}$$

2.1.2 Speculativeness of the New Three Views

Some claims of the New Three Views are highly speculative and have not yet gained sufficient empirical support:

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Speculativeness of the New Three Views                          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                 │
│  Speculativeness of the New Cosmological View:                   │
│  ├─ Empirical support for relational ontology is limited         │
│  ├─ The interpretation of the participatory cosmology is         │
│  │  contested                                                      │
│  └─ Its relation to mainstream physics needs clarification         │
│                                                                 │
│  Speculativeness of the New View of Life:                        │
│  ├─ The nature of consciousness remains an unsolved mystery      │
│  ├─ The possibility of cross-substrate life is unconfirmed       │
│  └─ The boundaries of the life continuum are unclear             │
│                                                                 │
│  Speculativeness of the New View of Cognition:                   │
│  ├─ The scope of participatory cognition is contested            │
│  ├─ The standard of negotiative truth is unclear                 │
│  └─ The tension with scientific realism                           │
│                                                                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
2.1.3 Weaknesses in Cross-Civilizational Applicability

The stress tests (Chapter 24) revealed the weaknesses of the framework in cross-civilizational scenarios:

Table C.11 Weaknesses in Cross-Civilizational Applicability

WeaknessContentImpactRevision Direction
Communication assumptionAssumes cross-civilizational communication is possibleIf communication is impossible, the framework failsDevelop responses for non-communication scenarios
Ontological assumptionAssumes a shared ontological basis existsIf ontologies are incompatible, the framework failsDevelop a minimal common ontology
Value assumptionAssumes a shared value basis existsIf values are incompatible, the framework failsDevelop value pluralism
2.1.4 Residual Anthropocentrism

Although this work strives to transcend anthropocentrism, residuals may still exist:

  • Conceptual framework: core concepts (such as "freedom" and "responsibility") originate in human experience
  • Value presuppositions: the emphasis on complexity and diversity may reflect human preferences
  • Methodology: the argumentative method is based on the human tradition of rationality
2.2 Methodological Limitations

2.2.3 Limitations of Simulation Methods

The simulation methods on which the stress tests depend have inherent limitations:

  • Model simplification: simulation models are simplifications of reality and may omit important factors
  • Parameter uncertainty: many parameters lack an empirical basis
  • Difficulty of validation: simulation results are hard to validate with empirical data
  • Risk of extrapolation: simulation results may not apply to reality

IV. Final Words

4.1 Humility and Ambition
4.1.1 An Acknowledgment of Humility

This work acknowledges its limitations with humility:

This work is a "first-generation draft model," not the ultimate truth. It is an open research programme, not a closed dogmatic system. It welcomes criticism, revision, and iteration, and regards itself as an updatable "protocol stack."

Formal expression:

$$\text{ThisWork} = \text{FirstGenerationDraft} \neq \text{FinalTruth}$$

$$\text{Status} = \text{OpenResearchProgram} \neq \text{ClosedDoctrine}$$

4.1.2 A Persistence in Ambition

At the same time, this work persists in its ambition:

This work attempts to provide normative guidance for the interstellar civilization era. This ambition is not arrogance but a responsibility toward the future of human and posthuman civilization. Under conditions of deep uncertainty, we need a governance framework that can develop continuously, rather than waiting for problems to arise and then responding in haste.

Table C.23 The Balance of Humility and Ambition

DimensionExpression of HumilityExpression of Ambition
Theoretical statusAcknowledge it is a draft modelPursue systematicity
Empirical basisAcknowledge insufficient validationPursue testability
Scope of applicationAcknowledge boundariesPursue universality
Attitude toward revisionWelcome criticismHold to the core
4.2 The Present and the Future
4.2.1 The Responsibility of the Present

This work emphasizes the responsibility of the present:

We are the first generation of humanity to face the possibility of interstellar civilization. Our choices will affect civilizational development for centuries and even longer. This responsibility cannot be shifted onto future generations, because some choices are irreversible once made.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Responsibility}_{\text{Now}} = f(\text{Impact}_{\text{Future}}, \text{Irreversibility})$$

This work maintains a cautious optimism about the future:

4.3 The Individual and the Cosmos
4.3.1 The Place of the Individual

This work repositions the individual in the cosmos:

From the perspective of the New Three Views, the individual is not an isolated atom but a node in a relational network; not a static entity but a dynamic process; not a detached observer but a participating agent. The action of every individual participates in shaping the possibility space of the cosmos.

Formal expression:

$$\text{Individual} = \text{Node}(\text{RelationalNetwork}) \cap \text{Process}(\text{DynamicBecoming}) \cap \text{Agent}(\text{ParticipatoryCosmos})$$

4.3.2 The Meaning of the Cosmos

This work endows the cosmos with a new meaning:

The cosmos is not an indifferent collection of matter but a field of possibility. Negentropic organizations—including life, consciousness, and civilization—are the way the cosmos realizes its possibilities. To maintain and expand the possibility space is to participate in the self-realization of the cosmos.

4.3.3 Restatement of the Core Maxim

This work concludes with its core maxim:

"Freedom is the Stewardship of Possibility."

"Freedom is the Stewardship of Possibility."

This maxim condenses the essence of this work:

  • Freedom: not unconstrained arbitrariness, but creation within constraints
  • Possibility: not an abstract concept, but the essence of the cosmos
  • Stewardship: not possession or control, but maintenance and expansion

Formal expression:

$$\text{Freedom} = \text{Stewardship}(\mathcal{P})$$

Here $\mathcal{P}$ is the possibility space.

4.3.4 The Final Appeal

This work ends with a final appeal:

We invite every reader to become a steward of possibility. Whether you are a philosopher, a scientist, a policymaker, or an ordinary citizen, your thinking and your action participate in shaping the future of the cosmos. Let us jointly shoulder this responsibility and prepare for the advent of the interstellar civilization era.

This is not an end, but a beginning.

$$\text{End} = \text{Beginning}$$

About the Author

Xue Zhixin Independent scholar, entrepreneur. Born in China on October 23, 1962.

I. A Life Trajectory Across Boundaries

The author's life trajectory is itself a narrative of "crossing boundaries"—and this boundary-crossing life experience ultimately crystallized into the core concern of this book: how to build normative bridges between different forms of intelligence, different civilizational forms, and different time scales.

After graduating from medical university, he entered the field of gastroenterology for clinical work. In his daily dealings with disease and death, he began to ponder questions that medical textbooks could not answer: What is the nature of life? What is the true meaning of healing? Where are the boundaries of medicine?

At the same time, he also served as a university teacher of English and pharmacology. This unique combination of "medicine + language + pharmacology" cultivated his habit of interdisciplinary thinking and laid the foundation for his later reading and integration of multilingual academic literature.

After being promoted to attending physician, he made his first important career leap—leaving the clinical front line to join a foreign-funded pharmaceutical enterprise engaged in biopharmaceutical research and development. This shift moved him from "treating disease" to "creating means of treatment," and his vision expanded from the individual patient to the entire biomedical industry chain.

Thereafter, as a principal founding partner, he successively founded life science and bioengineering investment enterprises and ecological construction investment enterprises. He has long been engaged in angel investment, venture capital, and risk investment, and has been deeply involved in the early development of China's life science industry. It is worth noting that the enterprises he founded were also among the earliest enterprises in China to implement climate change response projects—this concern with long-term, systemic risk already foreshadowed his later theoretical interest in "interstellar civilization" and "deep-time responsibility."

II. Questions at the Threshold of Life and Death

To understand the author's intellectual journey, one must return to a key node in his life.

Before graduating from university, the young author was diagnosed with a malignant tumor and underwent resection surgery. For a young person about to enter the medical profession, this experience had a twofold impact: as a patient, he faced the possibility of death directly; as a future doctor, he experienced the boundaries of medicine.

After recovering, he did not choose to forget this experience but transformed it into the starting point of a lifelong inquiry. He began to practice his own distinctive methods for recovering from such diseases and continuously deepened his theoretical understanding in his work practice. More importantly, this experience prompted him to inquire into fundamental questions that transcend the medical domain:

  • What exactly is life? Is it merely a biochemical process?
  • Where does consciousness come from? What is its relation to the material world?
  • In the face of finitude, how should one live? What should one pursue?
  • What connection exists between an individual life and the larger cosmic order?

III. An Intellectual Turn from Buddhism to Philosophy of Science

Carrying these questions, the author embarked on a long intellectual exploration.

He first started from his own expertise in biology, attempting to find answers in the latest advances in the life sciences. However, he soon realized that purely scientific description cannot answer the normative question of "what ought to be done."

He then turned to Eastern wisdom and began more than a decade of Buddhist practice. In Buddhism he found a mode of thinking that transcends binary oppositions, an attitude toward life in the face of impermanence, and a cosmology that integrates the individual into a larger whole. This period of practice profoundly shaped his way of thinking, and its influence is visible throughout this book—for example, the emphasis on "relationality," the claim of the priority of "process" over "substance," and the preference for "continuum" thinking.

However, more than twenty years ago, he made an important intellectual turn—abandoning Buddhism and turning to the fields of philosophy of science and philosophy of consciousness.

This turn was not a negation of Buddhism but arose from his judgment about the times: humanity is becoming an interstellar species, technological breakthroughs such as AI herald the arrival of a "singularity," and traditional wisdom traditions—whether Eastern or Western—need to be re-examined and transformed in a new context. He realized that in the face of this unprecedented future, what is needed is a normative framework capable of dialogue with modern science, shareable across different civilizations, and translatable into operable institutions.

IV. A Decade of Sharpening a Single Sword

This book is the crystallization of the author's more than ten years of conception.

Over these more than ten years, he has continuously tracked frontier advances in multiple fields such as physics, complex systems science, consciousness science, ethics, and international law, and maintained dialogue with the international academic community. He integrated his biology background, Buddhist practice, entrepreneurial experience, and investment practice into a unique perspective, attempting to answer the question he began to ask in his youth—except that now the scale of this question has expanded from "individual life" to "interstellar civilization."

The "New Three Views" framework proposed in the book embodies his unique intellectual integration:

  • The emphasis on the "participatory cosmos" in the New Cosmological View has both a scientific basis in quantum mechanics and an intellectual echo of the Buddhist idea of "dependent origination and emptiness"
  • The discussion of "cross-substrate life" and "negentropy flow" in the New View of Life originates in his scientific literacy as a scholar with a background in biology
  • The claim that "cognition is intervention" in the New View of Cognition integrates his understanding of the Buddhist tradition of "mindfulness" and contemporary embodied cognitive science

The "protocol stack" governance methodology embodies his practical wisdom as an entrepreneur—he knows well that no matter how good an idea is, if it cannot be translated into operable institutions, it can only remain on paper.

V. A Book of Life

In a sense, The Normative Reconstruction of Interstellar Civilization is not only an academic work but also a "book of life."

It is a cancer survivor's deep response to the meaning of life—when you have faced death directly, you will inquire more seriously: for what, exactly, does life exist?

It is a boundary-crossing scholar's theoretical exploration—when you have crossed the boundaries of medicine, business, investment, Buddhism, and philosophy, you will long all the more to find a framework capable of integrating all of them.

It is an entrepreneur's assumption of responsibility for the future of human civilization—when you have participated in early practice in responding to climate change, you will realize all the more clearly that the decisions of our generation will affect the fate of countless future generations.

As the book says: "Freedom is the stewardship of possibility." The author has spent his life practicing this sentence—he constantly crosses boundaries and keeps possibility open; he transforms personal life experience into reflection on human civilization; in an age of deep uncertainty, he attempts to leave behind for the future a "protocol stack" that can be revised, developed, and surpassed.

This, perhaps, is the greatest contribution that an independent scholar can make to the world.

Final Maxim

"Freedom is the Stewardship of Possibility."

"Freedom is the Stewardship of Possibility."

This maxim condenses the essence of this work. At the threshold of the interstellar civilization era, every one of us is a steward of possibility. Let us, with a humble attitude, an open mind, and responsible action, jointly safeguard the possibility space of the cosmos.

This is not an end, but a beginning.

$$\text{End} \equiv \text{Beginning}$$
